title: Analyzing New York City taxi trips
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README. The spatial work runs in DuckDB through geolattice.geolatticedb, so no PostGIS server is required for these cells.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

from geolattice import geolatticedb as pdb  # GeoLattice spatial database tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution




Code
import zipfile  # unpack the TLC zone shapefile
import urllib.request  # download the shapefile once
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds Data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
TRIPS = DATA / "yellow_taxi_2023-01_clean.parquet"  # cleaned January 2023 yellow trips
ZLOOKUP = DATA / "taxi_zone_lookup.parquet"  # LocationID, borough, zone name
TINY = DATA / "nyc-taxi-tiny" / "year=2015" / "month=*" / "part-0.parquet"  # 2015 sample, with coordinates

def taxi_zone_shp():  # TLC taxi zone polygons
    """Return the TLC taxi zone shapefile, downloading it once if it is missing."""
    folder = DATA / "taxi_zones"  # local cache
    found = sorted(folder.rglob("taxi_zones.shp"))  # already extracted, any nesting
    if found:  # nothing to download
        return found[0]
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
    zip_path = folder / "taxi_zones.zip"  # the TLC archive
    url = "https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/misc/taxi_zones.zip"  # official TLC zones
    print("Downloading taxi zone shapefile ...")  # progress
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, zip_path)  # copy the archive
    with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path) as zf:  # open it
        zf.extractall(folder)  # shapefile, index, and projection
    found = sorted(folder.rglob("taxi_zones.shp"))  # the extracted layer
    if not found:  # the archive layout changed
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"taxi_zones.shp not found after extracting {url}")
    return found[0]

ZONES = taxi_zone_shp()  # path used by pdb.load
print("Repository:", ROOT)  # where the data are read from
print("Zone shapefile:", ZONES.name)  # the layer that was found


Repository: /home/zia207/Github/GeoLattice
Zone shapefile: taxi_zones.shp

title: Analyzing New York City taxi trips
text:
One kilometre squares
Esri’s sample calls aggregate_points and asks for 1 km squares. The processing CRS has to be projected: a degree of longitude is not a kilometre. Their sample uses Web Mercator. The query below uses NAD83 / New York Long Island, EPSG:32118, where the unit is the metre, so a bin of 1,000 is a 1 km square on that projection.
DuckDB spatial has ST_Point, ST_Transform, and ST_MakeEnvelope. It has no ST_SquareGrid. floor(ST_X(g) / 1000) is the column of the square, and ST_MakeEnvelope builds the polygon. In PostGIS the same grid is one function, which notebook 06_03_04 used on the county layer:
SELECT g.i, g.j, count(*) AS pickups
FROM pickups AS p
JOIN ST_SquareGrid(
    1000,
    ST_Transform(ST_MakeEnvelope(-74.3, 40.4, -73.6, 41.0, 4326), 32118)
) AS g
  ON ST_Intersects(ST_Transform(p.geom, 32118), g.geom)
GROUP BY g.i, g.j
The points are the 2015 sample. A bounding box drops coordinates that fall outside the city, including the bad GPS values TLC files contain. Esri symbolized each square by its maximum tip divided by its maximum trip distance. The second map uses the mean tip divided by the mean distance, and only in squares with at least 30 pickups, so one large tip does not paint the cell.


Code
db = pdb.connect("duckdb")  # DuckDB with the spatial extension, through geolatticedb
db.load(ZONES, "taxi_zones", srid=4326)  # TLC zone polygons, stored as WGS84
zones = db.query("SELECT LocationID, zone, borough, geom FROM taxi_zones")  # polygons for the maps

n_trips = db.query(  # January 2023 yellow trips
    f"SELECT count(*) AS n FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}')"
).n.iloc[0]
n_pts = db.query(f"""
    SELECT count(*) AS n
    FROM read_parquet('{TINY.as_posix()}')
    WHERE pickup_longitude BETWEEN -74.3 AND -73.6
      AND pickup_latitude BETWEEN 40.4 AND 41.0
""").n.iloc[0]  # 2015 pickups inside the city box
print(f"{n_trips:,.0f} yellow trips in January 2023")
print(f"{n_pts:,.0f} pickups with coordinates inside the city box, 2015 sample")
print(f"{len(zones):,} taxi zones")


2,940,393 yellow trips in January 2023
143,744 pickups with coordinates inside the city box, 2015 sample
263 taxi zones




Code
# 1 km squares. ix and iy are the column and row on EPSG:32118.
squares = db.query(f"""
WITH pts AS (
    SELECT ST_Transform(
               ST_Point(pickup_longitude, pickup_latitude),
               'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:32118', always_xy := true
           ) AS g,                                    -- pickup, in metres
           tip_amount,
           trip_distance
    FROM read_parquet('{TINY.as_posix()}')
    WHERE pickup_longitude BETWEEN -74.3 AND -73.6    -- city box, west to east
      AND pickup_latitude BETWEEN 40.4 AND 41.0       -- city box, south to north
),
binned AS (
    SELECT floor(ST_X(g) / 1000)::INTEGER AS ix,      -- 1 km column
           floor(ST_Y(g) / 1000)::INTEGER AS iy,      -- 1 km row
           count(*) AS pickups,
           avg(tip_amount) AS mean_tip,
           avg(trip_distance) AS mean_miles
    FROM pts
    GROUP BY ix, iy
)
SELECT pickups, mean_tip, mean_miles,
       mean_tip / nullif(mean_miles, 0) AS tip_per_mile,   -- mean tip per mean mile
       ST_Transform(
           ST_MakeEnvelope(ix * 1000, iy * 1000, (ix + 1) * 1000, (iy + 1) * 1000),
           'EPSG:32118', 'EPSG:4326', always_xy := true
       ) AS geom                                      -- the square, for the map
FROM binned
""")
print(f"{len(squares):,} squares, busiest square {int(squares.pickups.max()):,} pickups")


403 squares, busiest square 7,796 pickups




Code
mapped = squares.copy()  # a copy, so the filter below does not change the table
mapped.loc[mapped.pickups < 30, "tip_per_mile"] = None  # thin squares stay blank on the tip map

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.6))  # count, then tip per mile
squares.plot(  # every square that had a pickup
    "pickups", ax=axes[0], cmap="YlOrRd", legend=True,
    legend_kwds={"label": "pickups", "shrink": 0.7},
)
zones.boundary.plot(ax=axes[0], color="0.25", linewidth=0.25)  # zone outlines
axes[0].set_axis_off()
axes[0].set_title("Pickups per 1 km square, 2015 sample")

mapped.plot(  # tip per mile where the square has enough trips
    "tip_per_mile", ax=axes[1], cmap="YlGnBu", legend=True,
    missing_kwds={"color": "#f2f2f2"},
    legend_kwds={"label": "mean tip per mile ($)", "shrink": 0.7},
)
zones.boundary.plot(ax=axes[1], color="0.25", linewidth=0.25)  # same outlines
axes[1].set_axis_off()
axes[1].set_title("Mean tip per mile, squares with at least 30 pickups")
fig.tight_layout()









The 2015 sample puts 143,744 pickups into 403 squares. The busiest square has 7,795 pickups and sits in Midtown, near Herald Square and Penn Station (about 40.75 N, 73.99 W). The dense squares follow Manhattan south of Central Park. Mean tip per mile is highest in that same Midtown core, where a short trip still carries a tip of a dollar or two. Squares toward the airports sit lower on this scale, because the distance in the denominator is much longer.

title: Analyzing New York City taxi trips
text:
Zones and boroughs
Hsu ranked zones by pickups and by drop-offs, then totaled the boroughs. January 2023 joins PULocationID and DOLocationID to taxi_zone_lookup.parquet. TLC zones 264 and 265 are stored with borough Unknown (the zone name is NV or blank) when the zone was not recorded. Those rows stay out of the ranking. The choropleth uses the TLC polygons, so a zone id that has no polygon does not appear on the map.


Code
top_pu = db.query(f"""
SELECT z.Zone AS zone, z.Borough AS borough, count(*) AS pickups
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}') AS t
JOIN read_parquet('{ZLOOKUP.as_posix()}') AS z
  ON z.LocationID = t.PULocationID
WHERE z.Borough <> 'Unknown'          -- drop TLC zones 264 and 265
GROUP BY z.Zone, z.Borough
ORDER BY pickups DESC
LIMIT 8
""")
top_do = db.query(f"""
SELECT z.Zone AS zone, z.Borough AS borough, count(*) AS dropoffs
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}') AS t
JOIN read_parquet('{ZLOOKUP.as_posix()}') AS z
  ON z.LocationID = t.DOLocationID
WHERE z.Borough <> 'Unknown'
GROUP BY z.Zone, z.Borough
ORDER BY dropoffs DESC
LIMIT 8
""")
boroughs = db.query(f"""
SELECT z.Borough AS borough,
       count(*) AS pickups
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}') AS t
JOIN read_parquet('{ZLOOKUP.as_posix()}') AS z
  ON z.LocationID = t.PULocationID
GROUP BY z.Borough
ORDER BY pickups DESC
""")
print("Most pickups")
print(top_pu.to_string(index=False))
print()
print("Most drop-offs")
print(top_do.to_string(index=False))
print()
print("Pickups by borough")
print(boroughs.to_string(index=False))

pu = db.query(f"""
SELECT PULocationID AS LocationID, count(*) AS pickups
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}')
GROUP BY PULocationID
""")  # one count per zone id
zmap = zones.merge(pu, on="LocationID", how="left")  # counts onto the polygons
zmap["pickups"] = zmap["pickups"].fillna(0)  # a zone with no January pickup

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.35, 1]})

JFK Airport is the busiest pickup zone in this month (151,267 trips), then Upper East Side South, Upper East Side North, and Midtown Center. Drop-offs concentrate on the Upper East Side and Midtown. Manhattan has 2,616,013 pickups. Staten Island has 217. Hsu’s first half of 2017 put Upper East Side South first, with JFK first among zones outside Manhattan. One January is enough to put the airport at the top of the pickup list.

title: Analyzing New York City taxi trips
text:
Peak hours
The pickup timestamp is a column, so the daily pattern is hour(tpep_pickup_datetime) and a count. Hsu’s first half of 2017 peaked around 18:00-19:00 and was quietest around 05:00.


Code
hours = db.query(f"""
SELECT hour(tpep_pickup_datetime) AS hour, count(*) AS trips
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}')
GROUP BY hour
ORDER BY hour
""")  # 24 rows, one per hour of the day

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
ax.plot(hours.hour, hours.trips, color="#1f4e79", marker="o", markersize=3.5)  # trips by hour
ax.set_xticks(range(0, 24, 2))  # labels every two hours
ax.set_xlabel("hour of pickup")
ax.set_ylabel("trips")
ax.set_title("Yellow taxi pickups by hour, January 2023")
fig.tight_layout()

peak = hours.loc[hours.trips.idxmax()]  # the busiest hour
quiet = hours.loc[hours.trips.idxmin()]  # the quietest hour
print(f"Busiest hour: {int(peak.hour):02d}:00, {int(peak.trips):,} trips")
print(f"Quietest hour: {int(quiet.hour):02d}:00, {int(quiet.trips):,} trips")


Busiest hour: 18:00, 207,726 trips
Quietest hour: 04:00, 16,506 trips









January 2023 is busiest at 18:00 (207,726 trips) and quietest at 04:00 (16,506). The evening peak matches Hsu’s longer series. The quiet hour sits one hour earlier than the 05:00 she reported for 2017.

title: Analyzing New York City taxi trips
text:
Short trips and long trips
Hsu split trips at 30 miles, about the distance across the city. The same cut is used here. Trips with trip_distance of 0 are left out of the split. The rate codes follow the TLC data dictionary: 1 standard, 2 JFK, 3 Newark, 4 Nassau or Westchester, 5 negotiated. Payment type 1 is a credit card and 2 is cash.


Code
split = db.query(f"""
SELECT
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE trip_distance > 0 AND trip_distance < 30) AS short_trips,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE trip_distance >= 30) AS long_trips,
    quantile_cont(trip_distance, 0.5) FILTER (WHERE trip_distance > 0) AS median_miles
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}')
""")
by_hour = db.query(f"""
SELECT hour(tpep_pickup_datetime) AS hour,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE trip_distance > 0 AND trip_distance < 30) AS short_trips,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE trip_distance >= 30) AS long_trips
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}')
GROUP BY hour
ORDER BY hour
""")
rates = db.query(f"""
SELECT CASE CAST(RatecodeID AS INTEGER)
           WHEN 1 THEN 'standard'
           WHEN 2 THEN 'JFK'
           WHEN 3 THEN 'Newark'
           WHEN 4 THEN 'Nassau or Westchester'
           WHEN 5 THEN 'negotiated'
           ELSE 'other'
       END AS rate,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE trip_distance > 0 AND trip_distance < 30) AS short_trips,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE trip_distance >= 30) AS long_trips
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}')
GROUP BY rate
ORDER BY short_trips DESC
""")
pays = db.query(f"""
SELECT CASE payment_type
           WHEN 1 THEN 'credit card'
           WHEN 2 THEN 'cash'
           WHEN 3 THEN 'no charge'
           WHEN 4 THEN 'dispute'
           ELSE 'other'
       END AS payment,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE trip_distance > 0 AND trip_distance < 30) AS short_trips,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE trip_distance >= 30) AS long_trips
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}')
GROUP BY payment
ORDER BY short_trips DESC
""")

def shares(frame, key):  # percent of each group, so the small long-trip set is readable
    out = frame.copy()
    out["short_pct"] = (100 * out.short_trips / out.short_trips.sum()).round(1)
    out["long_pct"] = (100 * out.long_trips / out.long_trips.sum()).round(1)
    return out[[key, "short_trips", "short_pct", "long_trips", "long_pct"]]

print(
    f"Short trips: {int(split.short_trips.iloc[0]):,}. "
    f"Long trips: {int(split.long_trips.iloc[0]):,}. "
    f"Median distance: {split.median_miles.iloc[0]:.2f} miles."
)
print()
print("Rate code")
print(shares(rates, "rate").to_string(index=False))
print()
print("Payment")
print(shares(pays, "payment").to_string(index=False))


Short trips: 2,938,076. Long trips: 2,317. Median distance: 1.81 miles.

Rate code

             standard      2815954       95.8         387      16.7
                  JFK       106991        3.6         158       6.8
               Newark         7250        0.2         513      22.1
           negotiated         4369        0.1         599      25.9
Nassau or Westchester         3512        0.1         660      28.5

Payment
    payment  short_trips  short_pct  long_trips  long_pct
credit card      2345173       79.8        1737      75.0
       cash       504540       17.2         522      22.5
      other        64106        2.2          10       0.4
    dispute        15686        0.5          37       1.6
  no charge         8571        0.3          11       0.5




Code
short_routes = db.query(f"""
SELECT pz.Zone AS pickup, dz.Zone AS dropoff, count(*) AS trips
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}') AS t
JOIN read_parquet('{ZLOOKUP.as_posix()}') AS pz ON pz.LocationID = t.PULocationID
JOIN read_parquet('{ZLOOKUP.as_posix()}') AS dz ON dz.LocationID = t.DOLocationID
WHERE t.trip_distance > 0 AND t.trip_distance < 30
  AND pz.Borough <> 'Unknown' AND dz.Borough <> 'Unknown'
GROUP BY pickup, dropoff
ORDER BY trips DESC
LIMIT 5
""")
long_routes = db.query(f"""
SELECT CASE WHEN pz.Borough = 'Unknown' THEN 'Unknown zone' ELSE pz.Zone END AS pickup,
       CASE WHEN dz.Borough = 'Unknown' THEN 'Unknown zone' ELSE dz.Zone END AS dropoff,
       count(*) AS trips
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS.as_posix()}') AS t
JOIN read_parquet('{ZLOOKUP.as_posix()}') AS pz ON pz.LocationID = t.PULocationID
JOIN read_parquet('{ZLOOKUP.as_posix()}') AS dz ON dz.LocationID = t.DOLocationID
WHERE t.trip_distance >= 30
GROUP BY pickup, dropoff
ORDER BY trips DESC
LIMIT 5
""")
print("Busiest short routes")
print(short_routes.to_string(index=False))
print()
print("Busiest long routes")
print(long_routes.to_string(index=False))

LaGuardia Airport   Unknown zone    178

LaGuardia Airport Newark Airport     37




Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
# Share of each group, so 2,317 long trips can be read against 2.9 million short ones.
ax.plot(by_hour.hour, 100 * by_hour.short_trips / by_hour.short_trips.sum(),
        color="#1f4e79", marker="o", markersize=3.5, label="under 30 miles")
ax.plot(by_hour.hour, 100 * by_hour.long_trips / by_hour.long_trips.sum(),
        color="#b85c38", marker="o", markersize=3.5, label="30 miles or more")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, 24, 2))
ax.set_xlabel("hour of pickup")
ax.set_ylabel("percent of that group")
ax.set_title("When short trips and long trips are picked up")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
print(
    "Long trips peak at "
    f"{int(by_hour.loc[by_hour.long_trips.idxmax(), 'hour']):02d}:00"
)


Long trips peak at 16:00









Almost every January trip is under 30 miles: 2,938,076 short trips against 2,317 long ones, and the median distance is 1.81 miles. The busiest short route is Upper East Side South to Upper East Side North. The busiest long route is JFK Airport to an unrecorded drop-off zone, then JFK Airport to Newark Airport. Long trips peak at 16:00, in the afternoon, while short trips follow the 18:00 citywide peak.
The rate codes separate the two groups more clearly than the payment type does. About 96% of short trips use the standard rate. About 17% of long trips do. The rest of the long trips are JFK, Newark, Nassau or Westchester, or a negotiated fare. Both groups pay mostly by credit card (about 80% of short trips and about 75% of long trips). Hsu’s 2017 tables showed the same airport pattern for long trips, with a credit-card share slightly higher on the long trips than on the short ones.

title: Analyzing New York City taxi trips
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

A 1 km square grid is a GROUP BY on coordinates projected to metres. PostGIS writes the same grid with ST_SquareGrid.
The January 2023 zone id joins to the TLC zone table. The polygons turn that count into a map. JFK Airport leads pickups in this month, and Manhattan dominates the boroughs.
hour(tpep_pickup_datetime) is enough for the daily cycle: 18:00 is the peak and 04:00 is the trough.
A 30 mile cut leaves a few thousand long trips. They run between airports in the afternoon, and they use the special rate codes.

Functions used: DuckDB ST_Point, ST_Transform, ST_X, ST_MakeEnvelope, read_parquet, hour, quantile_cont; PostGIS ST_SquareGrid (the same grid, shown above); pdb.connect, db.load, db.query (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

Repeat the borough table for drop-offs. Which borough gains the most trips between pickup and drop-off?
Rebuild the squares at 500 m (floor(ST_X(g) / 500)). Does the busiest cell stay in Midtown?
Move the long-trip cut from 30 miles to 10 miles and list the new top origin-destination pair.
Esri’s sample symbolized each square by maximum tip divided by maximum distance. Add those two aggregates to the square query and compare that map with the mean tip per mile.



Code
db.close()  # close the DuckDB file

title: DuckDB spatial and GeoParquet
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import json  # GeoParquet metadata
import subprocess  # a second process for the locking test
import sys  # path of the Python interpreter
import time  # timing
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import pyarrow.parquet as pq  # Parquet metadata
import duckdb  # DuckDB
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

from geolattice import geolatticedb as pdb  # GeoLattice spatial database tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution




Code
import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_03_05"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

def chr_county(year):  # County Health Rankings (CHR) county table of one year, from the Atlas
    """County Health Rankings & Roadmaps measures for all counties in one release year (2020-2025)."""
    d = pd.read_csv(fetch(f"data/county_health_ranking/chr_county_{year}.csv"), dtype={"fips": str}, low_memory=False)
    d["fips"] = d["fips"].str.zfill(5)  # restore leading zeros (01001, ...)
    return d[~d["fips"].str.endswith("000")].reset_index(drop=True)  # drop state and national rows

title: DuckDB spatial and GeoParquet
text:
Querying Parquet files directly
DuckDB treats a file path (or a glob of many files) as a table. Parquet stores data by column in row groups, with minimum and maximum statistics for each column in each group, so DuckDB reads only the columns a query uses (projection pushdown) and skips row groups whose statistics rule out the filter (predicate pushdown). Nothing is loaded in advance:


Code
files = sorted((DATA).glob("yellow_tripdata_2023-*.parquet"))  # the input files
print(f"{len(files)} files, {sum(f.stat().st_size for f in files) / 1e6:,.0f} MB on disk")
t0 = time.perf_counter()
n = con.execute(f"SELECT count(*) FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS}', union_by_name = true)").fetchone()[0]  # metadata only
print(f"{n:,} trips counted in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s (from the row counts in the file footers)")
plan = con.execute(f"""EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT avg(fare_amount) FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS}', union_by_name = true)
                   WHERE tpep_pickup_datetime >= '2023-07-01' AND tpep_pickup_datetime < '2023-07-02'""").fetchall()[0][1]
print("\n".join(l for l in plan.splitlines() if any(k in l for k in ["READ_PARQUET", "Projections", "Filters", "fare", "pickup", "Rows", "Total Time"]))[:1200])

text:
Out-of-core analytics on large tables
Loading all 38.3 million 2023 trips into pandas would need several gigabytes of memory. DuckDB streams the files through its operators in chunks. An aggregation needs memory only for its groups, so summarizing the year by pickup zone, drop-off zone and hour (more than 400,000 groups) runs comfortably within a 1 GB limit:

t0 = time.perf_counter()
od = con.execute(f"""
SELECT PULocationID AS pu, DOLocationID AS do_, hour(tpep_pickup_datetime) AS hour,
       count(*) AS trips, avg(fare_amount) AS mean_fare, sum(total_amount) AS revenue
FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS}', union_by_name = true)
WHERE tpep_pickup_datetime >= '2023-01-01' AND tpep_pickup_datetime < '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY ALL
""").df()
print(f"{len(od):,} zone-to-zone-hour groups from {n:,} trips in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s (1 GB limit)")

Most 2023 yellow taxi trips start in Manhattan, and the busiest zone pairs are short trips within the Upper East Side. Sorting, by contrast, needs to hold everything it sorts. A common job is to rewrite a year of data sorted by time and split into folders by borough and month, so that later queries read only the folders they need. Under a 500 MB limit DuckDB sorts in chunks, writes the chunks it cannot keep to temp_directory, and merges them. A small monitor records how much it spilled:


Code
import threading  # watch the spill folder while the query runs
spill = OUT / "duckdb_tmp"
def watch(stop, peak):  # record the largest size of the spill folder
    while not stop.is_set():
        peak[0] = max(peak[0], sum(f.stat().st_size for f in spill.glob("*") if f.is_file())); time.sleep(0.1)
out_dir = OUT / "trips_2023_by_borough_month"  # Hive-partitioned output dataset
import shutil; shutil.rmtree(out_dir, ignore_errors=True)
con.execute("SET memory_limit = '500MB'")  # cap, so the sort spills to temp_directory
con.execute("SET threads = 2")  # 24 threads fill the cap before a block can be pinned
con.execute("SET preserve_insertion_order = false")  # do not keep the Parquet row order in memory
stop, peak = threading.Event(), [0]; th = threading.Thread(target=watch, args=(stop, peak)); th.start()
t0 = time.perf_counter()
try:
    con.execute(f"""
COPY (
    SELECT z.Borough AS borough, month(t.tpep_pickup_datetime) AS month, t.tpep_pickup_datetime AS pickup_time,
           t.PULocationID AS pu, t.DOLocationID AS do_, t.trip_distance, t.fare_amount, t.total_amount
    FROM read_parquet('{TRIPS}', union_by_name = true) t
    JOIN read_parquet('{DATA / 'taxi_zone_lookup.parquet'}') z ON z.LocationID = t.PULocationID
    WHERE t.tpep_pickup_datetime >= '2023-01-01' AND t.tpep_pickup_datetime < '2024-01-01'
    ORDER BY pickup_time                                                  -- a full sort of the year
) TO '{out_dir}' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (borough, month), COMPRESSION zstd)
""")
finally:
    t_copy = time.perf_counter() - t0; stop.set(); th.join()  # stop the spill monitor
    con.execute("RESET memory_limit"); con.execute("RESET threads"); con.execute("RESET preserve_insertion_order")
parts = list(out_dir.rglob("*.parquet"))  # files written
print(f"sorted and partitioned {n:,} trips in {t_copy:.1f} s with a 500 MB limit; spilled up to {peak[0] / 1e6:,.0f} MB; "
      f"{len(parts)} files, {sum(f.stat().st_size for f in parts) / 1e6:,.0f} MB")
con.execute(f"SELECT borough, count(*) AS trips FROM read_parquet('{out_dir}/*/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true) "
            "WHERE month = 7 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC").df()  # July only: reads 7 of the folders

title: DuckDB spatial and GeoParquet
section: GeoParquet: writing, metadata and row-group pruning
text:
GeoParquet: writing, metadata and row-group pruning
GeoParquet is Parquet with a standard geo metadata entry that names the geometry columns, their encoding (WKB) and CRS. Two layout choices make spatial filters fast:

a bounding-box column (bbox struct with xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax; the GeoParquet 1.1 “covering”), whose row-group statistics let readers skip row groups outside a query box;
spatial ordering of the rows, for example along a Hilbert curve, so that each row group covers a compact area.

We write the 1.16 million 2009-2015 pickups twice, in time order and in Hilbert order, and count how many row groups a box around Times Square has to read:


Code
con.execute(f"""CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE pickups AS
SELECT pickup_datetime AS t, fare_amount AS fare, ST_Point(pickup_longitude, pickup_latitude) AS geom
FROM read_parquet('{TINY}', hive_partitioning = true)
WHERE year BETWEEN 2009 AND 2015
  AND pickup_longitude BETWEEN -74.3 AND -73.6 AND pickup_latitude BETWEEN 40.45 AND 41.0""")
n_pts = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM pickups").fetchone()[0]
bbox_cols = "struct_pack(xmin := ST_XMin(geom), ymin := ST_YMin(geom), xmax := ST_XMax(geom), ymax := ST_YMax(geom)) AS bbox"
layouts = {"time order": "ORDER BY t",
           "Hilbert order": "ORDER BY ST_Hilbert(geom, ST_Extent(ST_MakeEnvelope(-74.3, 40.45, -73.6, 41.0)))"}  # NYC box
for name, order in layouts.items():  # write two GeoParquet files
    path = OUT / f"pickups_{name.split()[0]}.parquet"
    con.execute(f"COPY (SELECT t, fare, geom, {bbox_cols} FROM pickups {order}) TO '{path}' "
                f"(FORMAT parquet, ROW_GROUP_SIZE 25000, COMPRESSION zstd)")
md = pq.read_metadata(OUT / "pickups_Hilbert.parquet")  # Parquet footer
geo = json.loads(md.metadata[b"geo"])  # the GeoParquet metadata
print(f"{n_pts:,} points; {md.num_row_groups} row groups; geo metadata: primary column {geo['primary_column']!r}, "
      f"encoding {geo['columns']['geom']['encoding']}, types {geo['columns']['geom']['geometry_types']}")


1,155,687 points; 44 row groups; geo metadata: primary column 'geom', encoding WKB, types ['Point']




Code
box = (-73.9915, 40.7535, -73.9795, 40.7625)  # about 1 km x 1 km around Times Square
rows = []  # one row per layout
for name in layouts:
    path = OUT / f"pickups_{name.split()[0]}.parquet"
    st = con.execute(f"""SELECT row_group_id,
           max(CASE WHEN path_in_schema = 'bbox, xmin' THEN stats_min END)::DOUBLE AS xmin,
           max(CASE WHEN path_in_schema = 'bbox, xmax' THEN stats_max END)::DOUBLE AS xmax,
           max(CASE WHEN path_in_schema = 'bbox, ymin' THEN stats_min END)::DOUBLE AS ymin,
           max(CASE WHEN path_in_schema = 'bbox, ymax' THEN stats_max END)::DOUBLE AS ymax
       FROM parquet_metadata('{path}') GROUP BY row_group_id""").df()  # bbox statistics of every row group
    hit = ((st.xmax >= box[0]) & (st.xmin <= box[2]) & (st.ymax >= box[1]) & (st.ymin <= box[3])).sum()  # overlap
    q_ = (f"SELECT count(*) FROM '{path}' WHERE bbox.xmin <= {box[2]} AND bbox.xmax >= {box[0]} "
          f"AND bbox.ymin <= {box[3]} AND bbox.ymax >= {box[1]}")  # filter on the bbox column
    con.execute(q_).fetchall(); t0 = time.perf_counter(); cnt = con.execute(q_).fetchone()[0]; dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
    rows.append({"layout": name, "MB": path.stat().st_size / 1e6, "row groups": len(st),
                 "row groups overlapping the box": int(hit), "pickups found": cnt, "query ms": dt * 1000})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("layout").round(2)

In time order every one of the 44 row groups spans the whole city, so the box query must read all of them. In Hilbert order each row group covers a small area and only 11 overlap the box; the reader skips the rest using the footer statistics alone, and the query is about four times faster. The file is also smaller (31 MB against 40 MB), because neighbouring points compress better. This layout matters most for remote files, where every skipped row group is data that is never downloaded.
The files are standard GeoParquet, so GeoPandas, GDAL/QGIS and other tools read them with their CRS. GeoPandas also writes the bounding-box column and declares it in the metadata as the GeoParquet 1.1 “covering”, which lets read_parquet(bbox=...) filter row groups:


Code

ny = gpd.read_parquet(OUT / "counties.parquet", bbox=(-79.8, 40.5, -71.8, 45.0))  # bbox filter uses the covering

title: DuckDB spatial and GeoParquet
section: Spatial joins and R-tree indexes in DuckDB
text:
Spatial joins and R-tree indexes in DuckDB
DuckDB plans a join on ST_Intersects (and other predicates) as a dedicated spatial join that builds a temporary R-tree on the smaller side, so no index is needed for one-off joins. For repeated filters on a stored table, CREATE INDEX ... USING RTREE adds a persistent R-tree.


Code
con.execute(f"CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE boroughs AS SELECT fips, name, geometry AS geom FROM read_parquet('{OUT / 'counties.parquet'}') "
            "WHERE fips IN ('36005', '36047', '36061', '36081', '36085')")  # the five boroughs from GeoParquet
t0 = time.perf_counter()
by_borough = con.execute("""
SELECT b.name AS county, count(*) AS pickups, round(avg(p.fare), 2) AS mean_fare
FROM pickups p JOIN boroughs b ON ST_Intersects(b.geom, p.geom) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC
""").df()
print(f"spatial join of {n_pts:,} points with 5 polygons in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")
plan = con.execute("EXPLAIN SELECT count(*) FROM pickups p JOIN boroughs b ON ST_Intersects(b.geom, p.geom)").fetchall()[0][1]
print("join operator:", [l.strip(" │─╭╮┴┬") for l in plan.splitlines() if "join" in l.lower()][:1])

Remote data: HTTPS and Overture Maps on S3
With httpfs, a URL is a table. DuckDB downloads only what a query needs: for CSV the whole file streams through once; for Parquet it uses HTTP range requests to read the footer first and then only the needed columns and row groups. A County Health Rankings table straight from the Atlas repository, joined to the local county GeoParquet:

FROM read_csv('{url}', types = {{'fips': 'VARCHAR'}}) h
JOIN read_parquet('{OUT / 'counties.parquet'}') c ON c.fips = lpad(h.fips, 5, '0')
WHERE h.state_abbr = 'NY' ORDER BY ypll DESC LIMIT 5
""").df()

title: DuckDB spatial and GeoParquet
section: When DuckDB is a better choice than PostGIS
text:
When DuckDB is a better choice than PostGIS
DuckDB is a single-process, embedded engine: one process may open a database file for writing at a time. A second process that tries to write to the same file is refused, which is the main practical difference from a PostgreSQL server:


Code
other = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c",
                        f"import duckdb; duckdb.connect(r'{db_file}').execute('CREATE TABLE x (i INT)')"],
                       capture_output=True, text=True)  # a second process tries to write
print("second writer:", (other.stderr.strip().splitlines() or ["succeeded"])[-1][:150])
con.close()  # release the lock

title: DuckDB spatial and GeoParquet
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

DuckDB queries Parquet files in place; projection and predicate pushdown read only the needed columns and row groups, and hive folders become columns.
DuckDB aggregated 38.3 million trips within 1 GB of memory, and sorted and repartitioned the whole year under 500 MB by spilling to temp_directory.
GeoParquet stores geometry as WKB with standard metadata; a bbox column plus Hilbert ordering let readers skip most row groups for a spatial filter.
Spatial joins in DuckDB use a temporary R-tree automatically; CREATE INDEX ... USING RTREE speeds up repeated filters.
httpfs makes URLs and S3 paths tables; Overture Maps’ latest release can be found through its STAC catalog and filtered by bbox without downloading whole files.
Use DuckDB for single-user analytics on files and cloud data, PostGIS for shared, transactional data and services.

Functions used: read_parquet, read_csv, parquet_metadata, COPY ... TO (FORMAT parquet), ST_Point, ST_Hilbert, ST_Extent_Agg, ST_XMin/ST_YMax, ST_Intersects, ST_MakeEnvelope, CREATE INDEX ... USING RTREE, SET memory_limit, EXPLAIN ANALYZE (DuckDB); geopandas.read_parquet(bbox=), GeoDataFrame.to_parquet(write_covering_bbox=True), pyarrow.parquet.read_metadata.
Exercises

Rerun the sorted, partitioned COPY with memory_limit = '250MB' and '2GB'. How do the run time and the spill size change?
Write the pickups ordered by ST_GeoHash instead of ST_Hilbert and compare the number of row groups overlapping the Times Square box.
Compare row group sizes of 5,000, 25,000 and 100,000 rows: file size, row groups read and query time.
Attach the PostGIS database from DuckDB (ATTACH '...' AS pg (TYPE postgres)) and join the npl table from notebook 06_03_03 with the GeoParquet counties.
With internet access, count Overture buildings (theme=buildings/type=building) inside Onondaga County.

import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_03_03"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

def superfund_sites():  # EPA Superfund National Priorities List sites from the Atlas
    """Superfund NPL sites as points (EPSG:4326)."""
    s = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/superfund_npl_data.js")["sites"])  # one row per site
    s = s.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])  # keep sites with coordinates
    s = s[["epa_id", "name", "status", "state", "city", "county", "score", "listed", "lat", "lon"]]  # main fields
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(s, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(s.lon, s.lat), crs=4326)  # points

def chr_county(year):  # County Health Rankings (CHR) county table of one year, from the Atlas
    """County Health Rankings & Roadmaps measures for all counties in one release year (2020-2025)."""
    d = pd.read_csv(fetch(f"data/county_health_ranking/chr_county_{year}.csv"), dtype={"fips": str}, low_memory=False)
    d["fips"] = d["fips"].str.zfill(5)  # restore leading zeros (01001, ...)
    return d[~d["fips"].str.endswith("000")].reset_index(drop=True)  # drop state and national rows

PG_DSN = os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN", "postgresql://postgres:geolattice@localhost:5432/geolattice")

title: Spatiotemporal data
text:
Time-stamped geometries and validity periods
Two kinds of time are common:

Event time: something happened at a moment (a taxi pickup, a measurement). Store a timestamp or timestamptz column next to the geometry.
Validity time: a fact holds during a period (a site is on the National Priorities List from listing to deletion; a monitor operates from its start date to its last date). Store a range (daterange, tstzrange), which PostgreSQL can test with @> (contains), && (overlaps) and index with GiST, together with the geometry.

The Superfund sites carry their dates in the Atlas, so each site gets an NPL validity range from listing to deletion (open-ended if still listed):


Code
sites = superfund_sites()  # sites with dates as text (mm/dd/yyyy)
raw = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/superfund_npl_data.js")["sites"]).set_index("epa_id")  # all fields
for c in ["proposed", "listed", "construction_complete", "deleted"]:  # parse the dates
    sites[c] = pd.to_datetime(raw.loc[sites.epa_id, c].values, format="%m/%d/%Y", errors="coerce")
pg.load(sites.drop(columns="listed").assign(listed=sites.listed), "npl")  # load (dates become timestamps)
pg.execute("""ALTER TABLE npl ADD COLUMN npl_period daterange
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (daterange(listed::date, deleted::date, '[)')) STORED;   -- NULL upper = still listed
CREATE INDEX npl_st_gix ON npl USING GIST (geom, npl_period)""")  # one index on space AND time
q("""SELECT name, state, listed::date, deleted::date, npl_period FROM npl
WHERE deleted IS NOT NULL ORDER BY listed LIMIT 4""")

title: Spatiotemporal data
text:
Trajectories with LINESTRING M
A trajectory is the path of a moving object with a time at every vertex. PostGIS stores it as a LINESTRING M, with the time (as a number, e.g. Unix epoch seconds) in the M coordinate. A valid trajectory has M increasing along the line, which ST_IsValidTrajectory checks. Then:

ST_LocateAlong(traj, t) returns where the object was at time t;
ST_ClosestPointOfApproach(a, b) returns the time when two moving objects were closest, ST_DistanceCPA that distance, and ST_CPAWithin(a, b, d) whether they ever came within d.

A GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) feed gives a bus trip’s path (shapes.txt) and the scheduled times at its stops (stop_times.txt). Interpolating the times along the path gives a scheduled trajectory:


Code
z = zipfile.ZipFile(GEOLATTICE_DATA / "00_shared" / "data_gdal" / "gtfs" / "gtfs_extract.zip")  # GTFS feed (SOLEA, Mulhouse)
shape = pd.read_csv(z.open("shapes.txt")).sort_values("shape_pt_sequence")  # the path, with distance along it
st = pd.read_csv(z.open("stop_times.txt")).sort_values("stop_sequence")  # stop times with distance along the path
day = pd.Timestamp("2023-01-02")  # a service day from calendar.txt (schedule clock times are stored as UTC epochs)
st_sec = pd.to_timedelta(st.arrival_time).dt.total_seconds() + day.timestamp()  # stop times as epoch seconds
shape["t"] = np.interp(shape.shape_dist_traveled, st.shape_dist_traveled, st_sec)  # time at every path vertex
shape = shape.drop_duplicates("t")  # repeated points get the same time; M must increase strictly
xyzm = [(x, y, 0, m) for x, y, m in zip(shape.shape_pt_lon, shape.shape_pt_lat, shape.t)]  # lon, lat, (z), time
traj_wkt = "LINESTRING M (" + ", ".join(f"{x} {y} {m}" for x, y, _, m in xyzm) + ")"  # WKT with M
pg.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS bus_traj")
pg.execute("CREATE TABLE bus_traj (trip_id text PRIMARY KEY, traj geometry(LineStringM, 4326))")
pg.execute("INSERT INTO bus_traj VALUES (%s, ST_GeomFromText(%s, 4326))", (st.trip_id.iloc[0], traj_wkt))
q("""SELECT trip_id, ST_NPoints(traj) AS vertices, ST_IsValidTrajectory(traj) AS valid,
       to_timestamp(ST_M(ST_StartPoint(traj))) AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS departs,
       to_timestamp(ST_M(ST_EndPoint(traj))) AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS arrives,
       round((ST_Length(traj::geography) / 1000)::numeric, 2) AS km FROM bus_traj""")

Each segment’s speed is its length divided by the difference of the M values at its ends. Because the times come from the schedule and are interpolated by distance, speed is constant between two stops; GPS (AVL) records would show the real stops and starts.
Taxi records hold only a pickup and a drop-off, each with a time and a place. As two-point trajectories they assume straight, constant-speed travel, a strong simplification, but enough to show the closest-point-of-approach functions. Which pairs of cabs on the road between 08:00 and 08:30 on 10 January 2012 came within 100 m of each other at the same moment?

wkts = [f"LINESTRING M ({a} {b} {s.timestamp()}, {c} {d} {e.timestamp()})" for a, b, s, c, d, e in zip(
    taxi.pickup_longitude, taxi.pickup_latitude, taxi.pickup_datetime,
    taxi.dropoff_longitude, taxi.dropoff_latitude, taxi.dropoff_datetime)]  # pickup -> drop-off with times
pg.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS taxi_traj")

SELECT a.id AS taxi_a, b.id AS taxi_b,
       date_trunc('second', to_timestamp(ST_ClosestPointOfApproach(a.traj, b.traj)) AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AS closest_at,

ORDER BY distance_m LIMIT 6

title: Spatiotemporal data
text:
TimescaleDB and MobilityDB
Two PostgreSQL extensions specialize in time:



Extension
Adds
Typical use




TimescaleDB
hypertables (tables split automatically into time chunks), time_bucket(), continuous aggregates, compression, retention policies
sensor streams, monitoring, high-rate events


MobilityDB
temporal types such as tgeompoint (a moving point), tfloat; functions atTime, speed, trajectory, tdwithin, temporal aggregates
fleets, GPS tracks, AIS ship data



Neither ships with every PostGIS installation. The Dockerfile in notebook 06_01_02 adds MobilityDB, and its optional timescale service runs TimescaleDB with PostGIS on port 5433. The cells below use the extensions when the server has them and otherwise run the plain-PostgreSQL equivalent, so the notebook works either way.
Time bins. Taxi pickups per hour and borough. TimescaleDB uses time_bucket('1 hour', t) on a hypertable; PostgreSQL 14+ has date_bin('1 hour', t, origin) for the same bins, and the partitioned table from notebook 06_02_05 plays the role of the hypertable’s chunks.


Code
jan = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "nyc-taxi-tiny" / "year=2012" / "month=1" / "part-0.parquet",
                      columns=["pickup_datetime", "pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude"])  # January 2012
jan = jan[jan.pickup_longitude.between(-74.3, -73.6) & jan.pickup_latitude.between(40.45, 41.0)]  # in NYC
pg.load(gpd.GeoDataFrame({"t": jan.pickup_datetime.values}, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(jan.pickup_longitude,
        jan.pickup_latitude), crs=4326), "pickups")  # time-stamped points
pg.load(counties[counties.fips.isin(["36005", "36047", "36061", "36081", "36085"])], "boroughs")

if HAS_TIMESCALE:  # TimescaleDB: hypertable + time_bucket
    pg.execute("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS timescaledb")
    pg.execute("SELECT create_hypertable('pickups', by_range('t', INTERVAL '7 days'), migrate_data => true)")
    bin_expr = "time_bucket('1 hour', p.t)"
else:  # plain PostgreSQL: date_bin
    bin_expr = "date_bin('1 hour', p.t, TIMESTAMP '2012-01-01')"
hourly = q(f"""
SELECT extract(hour FROM {bin_expr})::int AS hour, b.name AS borough, count(*) AS pickups
FROM pickups p JOIN boroughs b ON ST_Intersects(b.geom, p.geom) GROUP BY 1, 2
""")
print("binning with:", bin_expr.split("(")[0])
names = {"New York": "Manhattan", "Kings": "Brooklyn", "Richmond": "Staten Island"}  # county -> borough name
hm = hourly.replace({"borough": names}).pivot(index="borough", columns="hour", values="pickups").fillna(0)  # matrix
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 2.8))
im = ax.imshow(np.log10(hm + 1), aspect="auto", cmap="magma_r")  # heat map
ax.set_yticks(range(len(hm)), hm.index); ax.set_xticks(range(0, 24, 2)); ax.set_xlabel("hour of day")
plt.colorbar(im, label="log10(pickups + 1)"); ax.set_title("Taxi pickups by hour and borough, January 2012 sample"); plt.show()


binning with: date_bin









Manhattan dominates at every hour, with a low between 4:00 and 6:00, a steep rise after 7:00 and the highest counts in the evening; Brooklyn and Queens follow with far fewer pickups, the Bronx has very few and Staten Island none in this sample. With TimescaleDB, a continuous aggregate keeps such hourly counts up to date as new rows arrive (CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WITH (timescaledb.continuous)), and compression and retention policies manage old chunks automatically.
Moving points. In MobilityDB the bus trajectory becomes a tgeompoint, and speed, position at a time and the path are built-in functions. Without MobilityDB, the LINESTRING M functions of PostGIS from the previous section cover the same questions:

    pg.execute("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS mobilitydb CASCADE")
    inst = ", ".join(f"Point({x} {y})@{pd.Timestamp(m, unit='s', tz='UTC').isoformat()}" for x, y, _, m in xyzm)
    pg.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS bus_tgeom")

                   round((twAvg(speed(trip)) * 3.6)::numeric, 1) AS mean_kmh_planar,

else:  # PostGIS only

section: County health time series in a database
text:
County health time series in a database
The USA Health Data Atlas holds several county time series. We store three in one long table, one row per county, year, source and measure:








Source
Years
Measures




NCHS VSRR provisional county drug overdose deaths
2020-2025
deaths, crude rate per 100,000 (small counts suppressed)


State Cancer Profiles, reconstructed annual mortality
2019-2023
age-adjusted cancer mortality per 100,000 (all sites)


County Health Rankings releases
2020-2025
adult obesity, adult smoking, physical inactivity, YPLL, life expectancy



The table is partitioned by year (the same idea as a TimescaleDB hypertable with yearly chunks), so queries for a few years read only those partitions and new releases are added as new partitions.


Code
od = atlas_js("assets/overdose_provisional_data.js")  # drug overdose, county x year
od = pd.DataFrame(od["rows"], columns=od["cols"])
od_long = pd.concat([od.assign(measure="overdose_deaths", value=od.deaths),
                     od.assign(measure="overdose_rate", value=od.crude_rate_per_100k)])[["fips", "year", "measure", "value"]]
od_long["source"] = "NCHS VSRR"

cm = atlas_js("assets/cancer_mortality_timeseries_data.js")  # cancer mortality, county x year x site
cm = pd.DataFrame(cm["rows"], columns=cm["cols"])
cm = cm[cm.cancer_site == "All Cancer Sites"]  # all sites combined
cm_long = cm.assign(measure="cancer_mortality_aa", value=cm.age_adjusted_rate_per_100k, source="State Cancer Profiles")[
    ["fips", "year", "measure", "value", "source"]]

chr_measures = ["adult_obesity_pct", "adult_smoking_pct", "physical_inactivity_pct",
                "years_of_potential_life_lost_rate", "life_expectancy"]  # CHR measures present in all releases
chr_long = pd.concat([chr_county(y).melt(id_vars=["fips", "year"], value_vars=chr_measures, var_name="measure")
                      for y in range(2020, 2026)]).assign(source="County Health Rankings")  # 6 releases
ts = pd.concat([od_long, cm_long, chr_long]).dropna(subset=["value"])  # one long table
ts["year"] = ts.year.astype(int)
print(ts.groupby("source").agg(rows=("value", "size"), years=("year", lambda s: f"{s.min()}-{s.max()}"),
                               counties=("fips", "nunique")))

pg.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS health_ts CASCADE")
pg.execute("""CREATE TABLE health_ts (fips char(5) NOT NULL, year smallint NOT NULL, source text NOT NULL,
           measure text NOT NULL, value double precision, PRIMARY KEY (fips, year, measure))
           PARTITION BY RANGE (year)""")  # long table, partitioned by year
for y in range(ts.year.min(), ts.year.max() + 1):  # one partition per year
    pg.execute(f"CREATE TABLE health_ts_{y} PARTITION OF health_ts FOR VALUES FROM ({y}) TO ({y + 1})")

with conn.cursor() as cur:  # COPY into the parent; rows are routed to their year

Counties with reported counts show overdose deaths rising from 2020 to a peak in 2022-2023 and then falling sharply in 2024 and 2025. Suppression of small counts changes the set of counties from year to year, so these sums are not national totals; the NCHS national provisional counts are the reference for those.
Year-over-year change per county with the window function LAG, and its spatial pattern. Counties whose rate fell from 2023 to 2024 tend to have neighbours whose rate also fell:


Code
chg = q("""
WITH r AS (
    SELECT fips, year, value,
           lag(value) OVER (PARTITION BY fips ORDER BY year) AS prev     -- the previous year of the same county
    FROM health_ts WHERE measure = 'overdose_rate' AND year IN (2023, 2024))
SELECT c.fips, c.name, c.statefp, r.prev AS rate_2023, r.value AS rate_2024,
       100 * (r.value - r.prev) / r.prev AS change_pct, c.geom
FROM r JOIN counties c USING (fips) WHERE r.year = 2024 AND r.prev > 0
""")
print(f"{len(chg):,} counties with rates in both years; median change {chg.change_pct.median():.1f}%; "
      f"{(chg.change_pct < 0).mean():.0%} of them fell")
lower48 = chg[~chg.statefp.isin(["02", "15"])].to_crs(5070)
ax = counties[~counties.statefp.isin(["02", "15", "72"])].to_crs(5070).plot(color="#f0f0f0", figsize=(12, 6))
lower48.plot("change_pct", ax=ax, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-60, vmax=60, legend=True,
             legend_kwds={"label": "% change in overdose death rate, 2023 to 2024", "shrink": 0.6})

1,029 counties with rates in both years; median change -23.9%; 84% of them fell

nbr = q("""
WITH chg AS (
    SELECT fips, 100 * (max(value) FILTER (WHERE year = 2024) / nullif(max(value) FILTER (WHERE year = 2023), 0) - 1) AS pct
    FROM health_ts WHERE measure = 'overdose_rate' AND year IN (2023, 2024) GROUP BY fips)
SELECT (a.pct < 0) AS county_fell, avg((b.pct < 0)::int) AS share_of_neighbours_fell, count(*) AS pairs
FROM chg a
JOIN counties ca ON ca.fips = a.fips
JOIN counties cb ON ST_Touches(ca.geom, cb.geom)
JOIN chg b ON b.fips = cb.fips
WHERE a.pct IS NOT NULL AND b.pct IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1
""")

Among counties whose rate fell, 88% of the neighbours also fell; among counties whose rate rose, 80% of the neighbours fell. The difference is modest because the decline was so widespread (84% of the counties fell, with a median change of -24%), but it points in the direction of regional clustering. Notebook 06_03_04 measures such clustering formally with Moran’s I.
Trends over five years with a regression slope per county in SQL (regr_slope), here for age-adjusted cancer mortality 2019-2023, then summarized by state:


Code
slopes = q("""
SELECT c.fips, c.name, c.statefp, regr_slope(t.value, t.year) AS slope_per_year, avg(t.value) AS mean_rate,
       count(*) AS years, c.geom
FROM health_ts t JOIN counties c USING (fips)
WHERE t.measure = 'cancer_mortality_aa' GROUP BY c.fips, c.name, c.statefp, c.geom HAVING count(*) = 5
""")
print(f"{len(slopes):,} counties; median slope {slopes.slope_per_year.median():.2f} deaths per 100,000 per year; "
      f"{(slopes.slope_per_year < 0).mean():.0%} falling")
ax = slopes[~slopes.statefp.isin(["02", "15"])].to_crs(5070).plot("slope_per_year", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-6, vmax=6,
     figsize=(12, 6), legend=True, legend_kwds={"label": "change per year (age-adjusted deaths per 100,000)", "shrink": 0.6})
ax.set_title("Trend in county cancer mortality, 2019-2023 (State Cancer Profiles, reconstructed annual rates)")
ax.set_axis_off(); plt.show()


3,054 counties; median slope -1.71 deaths per 100,000 per year; 88% falling









Most counties show falling age-adjusted cancer mortality over 2019-2023, consistent with the long national decline. These annual county values are reconstructed by the Atlas from State Cancer Profiles’ pooled five-year rate and its annual percent change (APC), so the county slopes largely restate that APC; they are suitable for mapping direction and size of trends, not for detecting year-to-year shocks.

title: Spatiotemporal data
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

Store event time as timestamp(tz) next to the geometry, and validity time as a range (daterange, tstzrange); a GiST index on (geom, range) serves space-time queries.
Trajectories are LINESTRING M with time in M; ST_IsValidTrajectory, ST_LocateAlong, ST_DumpSegments, ST_ClosestPointOfApproach, ST_DistanceCPA and ST_CPAWithin answer where, how fast and how close.
TimescaleDB (hypertables, time_bucket, continuous aggregates) and MobilityDB (tgeompoint) add specialized features; native partitioning and date_bin cover the basics without them.
County health time series fit a long table partitioned by year; window functions (LAG), regr_slope and spatial self-joins give changes, trends and their spatial pattern.
Respect the data: suppressed small counts, reconstructed annual values and release years that differ from data years limit what changes mean.

Functions used: daterange, @>, generate_series, ST_GeomFromText (M), ST_IsValidTrajectory, ST_LocateAlong, ST_DumpSegments, ST_M, ST_ClosestPointOfApproach, ST_DistanceCPA, ST_CPAWithin, date_bin / time_bucket, lag, regr_slope, PARTITION BY RANGE; pdb.connect, con.load, con.query, con.explain (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

Count the Superfund sites on the National Priorities List in each EPA region at the end of 1990, 2005 and 2025.
Find the PM2.5 monitoring sites whose annual mean rose every year from 2023 to 2025.
Build trajectories for all January 2012 taxi trips between 17:00 and 18:00 and find the pair with the smallest ST_DistanceCPA.
Start the TimescaleDB service from notebook 06_01_02 and rerun the time-bin cell there. Create a continuous aggregate of pickups per hour and borough.
Compute the 2020-2025 overdose rate slope per state from the county table, weighting counties by population.

text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)  # all-NaN windows

import shutil  # find programs
import subprocess  # run raster2pgsql
import time  # timing
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters
import rasterio  # raster I/O
from rasterio.mask import mask as rio_mask  # zonal check in NumPy
import psycopg  # PostgreSQL driver
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

import geolattice.rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing tools (PyRSense)
from geolattice import geolatticedb as pdb  # GeoLattice spatial database tools

rasterio.Env(CPL_LOG="/dev/null").__enter__()  # quiet GDAL messages
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution




Code
import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_03_01"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

def superfund_sites():  # EPA Superfund National Priorities List sites from the Atlas
    """Superfund NPL sites as points (EPSG:4326)."""
    s = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/superfund_npl_data.js")["sites"])  # one row per site
    s = s.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])  # keep sites with coordinates
    s = s[["epa_id", "name", "status", "state", "city", "county", "score", "listed", "lat", "lon"]]  # main fields
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(s, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(s.lon, s.lat), crs=4326)  # points

# PostGIS connection string (see 06_01_02 for the Docker container); override with GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN
PG_DSN = os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN", "postgresql://postgres:geolattice@localhost:5432/geolattice")
print("Repository:", ROOT)  # where the data are read from

# Folder of DATA as the database server sees it (out-db rasters are read by the server).
# Local server: the same path. Docker (06_01_02 compose file): the Data folder is mounted at /data.
SERVER_DATA = Path(os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_SERVER_DATA", str(DATA)))


Repository: /home/zia207/Github/GeoLattice

pg = pdb.connect("postgis", dsn=PG_DSN)  # PostGIS through geolatticedb
q = pg.query  # SQL -> GeoDataFrame / DataFrame
pg.execute("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis_raster")  # raster type and functions
# out-db rasters and COG access must be switched on (per database; new connections pick it up)
pg.execute("ALTER DATABASE " + psycopg.conninfo.conninfo_to_dict(PG_DSN)["dbname"] +
           " SET postgis.enable_outdb_rasters = true")

           " SET postgis.gdal_enabled_drivers = 'GTiff'")

title: Rasters in PostGIS
section: A GeoLattice output: Sentinel-2 NDVI as a COG
text:
A GeoLattice output: Sentinel-2 NDVI as a COG
The red (B04) and near-infrared (B08) bands are 10 m Sentinel-2 L2A surface reflectance stored as integers. The STAC item gives the conversion (raster:bands scale 0.0001 and offset -0.1 for processing baseline 05.11), but also records earthsearch:boa_offset_applied = true: Earth Search already removed the offset, so applying it again would push dark surfaces below zero. The code reads both fields. The scene classification layer (SCL, 20 m) flags clouds, cloud shadows and water. We compute the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index, NDVI = (NIR - red) / (NIR + red), with geolattice.rsense, mask clouds, shadows and water (so that greenness is compared over land only), and write the result as a cloud-optimized GeoTIFF: tiled, compressed and with overviews, so that programs can read just the part and resolution they need.


Code
S2 = GEOLATTICE_DATA / "00_shared" / "data_web_cloud_gis" / "s2_syracuse_2025" / "S2C_18TVN_20250802_0_L2A"  # one scene
item = json.load(open(S2 / "item.json"))  # STAC item of the scene
rb = item["assets"]["red"]["raster:bands"][0]  # scale and offset of the band
offset = 0.0 if item["properties"].get("earthsearch:boa_offset_applied") else rb.get("offset", 0.0)  # avoid double offset
print(f"scale {rb['scale']}, offset {rb['offset']} (already applied: {offset == 0.0})")
ds = xr.Dataset({b: rs.read(S2 / f"{b}.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True) for b in ["red", "nir"]})  # 10 m bands
ds = (ds.where(ds > 0) * rb["scale"] + offset).clip(min=0)  # DN -> surface reflectance (0 = nodata)
ds = ds.rio.write_crs(32618)  # UTM zone 18N
scl = rs.read(S2 / "scl.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True).rio.reproject_match(ds["red"], resampling=0)  # 20 m -> 10 m
bad = scl.isin([0, 1, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10])  # no data, saturated, cloud shadow, water, clouds, cirrus
ndvi = rs.optical.index(ds, "NDVI").where(~bad).astype("float32")  # NDVI with clouds masked
ndvi = ndvi.rio.write_crs(32618).rio.write_nodata(np.nan)
cog = OUT / "ndvi_syracuse_20250802_cog.tif"  # the COG file
rs.write(ndvi, cog, cog=True)  # cloud-optimized GeoTIFF (geolattice.rsense)
print(f"NDVI {ndvi.shape[0]} x {ndvi.shape[1]} cells at 10 m; masked (cloud, shadow, water) {float(bad.mean()):.1%}; "
      f"mean {float(ndvi.mean()):.2f}; file {cog.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB")
with rasterio.open(cog) as src:  # check the COG structure
    print("tiled:", src.profile.get("tiled"), "| block:", src.block_shapes[0], "| overviews:", src.overviews(1),
          "| compression:", src.compression)

In-db vs. out-db rasters









In-db
Out-db (raster2pgsql -R)

Out-db works well with COGs, because each tile reads just its block of the file, and GDAL can read COGs from object storage (/vsis3/, /vsicurl/) when the server is allowed to. We load the NDVI COG both ways:

rows = []  # one row per storage mode
for mode in ["in-db", "out-db"]:
    table = "ndvi_indb" if mode == "in-db" else "ndvi_outdb"
    pg.execute(f"DROP TABLE IF EXISTS {table}")
    path = cog if mode == "in-db" else SERVER_DATA / cog.relative_to(DATA)  # out-db: path as the server sees it
    args = ["raster2pgsql", "-s", "32618", "-t", "256x256", "-I", "-C", "-F"] + (["-R"] if mode == "out-db" else [])
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    pg.execute(tool(*args, path, f"public.{table}"))  # generate and run the SQL
    t_load = time.perf_counter() - t0
    size = q(f"SELECT pg_total_relation_size('{table}') / 1e6 AS mb").mb.iloc[0]  # table + TOAST + index
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    stats = q(f"SELECT (ST_SummaryStatsAgg(rast, 1, true)).* FROM {table}")  # read every pixel once
    rows.append({"storage": mode, "tiles": q(f"SELECT count(*) FROM {table}").iloc[0, 0], "load s": t_load,
                 "table MB": float(size), "full scan s": time.perf_counter() - t0,

ST_Value, ST_Clip and ST_SummaryStats







Function
Returns




ST_Value(rast, band, point)
the cell value under a point (resample => 'bilinear' for interpolation)


ST_Clip(rast, band, geom, crop)
the part of a raster inside a geometry, as a raster


ST_SummaryStats(rast) / ST_SummaryStatsAgg
count, sum, mean, stddev, min, max of a tile / of many tiles


ST_Histogram, ST_Quantile, ST_ValueCount
distributions and class counts



NDVI and elevation at the EPA air quality monitoring sites and Superfund sites that fall inside the scene (one of each: the East Syracuse PM2.5 site and the Onondaga Lake site). The points are in EPSG:4326 and the NDVI in UTM 18N, so the points are transformed to the raster SRID; the spatial join ST_Intersects(rast, geom) finds the tile under each point through the GiST index:


Code

WITH p AS (
    SELECT 'EPA monitor (' || pollutant || ')' AS kind, name, geom FROM aq_sites
    UNION ALL SELECT 'Superfund site', name, geom FROM superfund

SELECT p.kind, p.name,
       round(ST_Value(n.rast, 1, ST_Transform(p.geom, 32618))::numeric, 3)  AS ndvi,
       round(ST_Value(d.rast, 1, p.geom)::numeric)                         AS elevation_m, p.geom
FROM p
JOIN ndvi_indb n ON ST_Intersects(n.rast, ST_Transform(p.geom, 32618))   -- tile under the point
LEFT JOIN ono_dem d ON ST_Intersects(d.rast, p.geom)
""")

title: Rasters in PostGIS
text:
Zonal statistics and raster/vector integration
Zonal statistics summarize a raster within each polygon of a vector layer. In SQL the pattern is: join tiles to zones with ST_Intersects, clip each tile to its zone with ST_Clip, and aggregate with ST_SummaryStatsAgg per zone. geolatticedb.raster.zonal_stats writes that query (and reprojects the zones to the raster SRID). We use 250 m hexagons over the Syracuse scene as zones, then check the result against a NumPy calculation with rasterio.mask.


Code
pg.execute("""DROP TABLE IF EXISTS syr_hex;
CREATE TABLE syr_hex AS
SELECT row_number() OVER () AS hex_id, ST_Transform(h.geom, 4326) AS geom
FROM ST_HexagonGrid(250, (SELECT ST_Union(ST_Envelope(rast)) FROM ndvi_indb)) h
WHERE ST_Within(h.geom, (SELECT ST_Union(ST_Envelope(rast)) FROM ndvi_indb));
CREATE INDEX ON syr_hex USING GIST (geom)""")  # hexagons inside the scene
t0 = time.perf_counter()
zs = pg.raster.zonal_stats("ndvi_indb", "syr_hex", stats=["count", "mean", "min", "max"])  # geolatticedb
print(f"{len(zs):,} hexagons, zonal statistics in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

check = zs.sample(25, random_state=1)  # verify 25 hexagons with rasterio + NumPy
with rasterio.open(cog) as src:
    np_mean = [float(np.nanmean(rio_mask(src, [g], crop=True, nodata=np.nan, all_touched=False)[0]))
               for g in check.to_crs(32618).geometry]
print("max |PostGIS - NumPy| mean NDVI:", round(float(np.nanmax(np.abs(np.array(np_mean) - check["mean"]))), 6))


1,140 hexagons, zonal statistics in 0.4 s
max |PostGIS - NumPy| mean NDVI: 0.0


Both methods count the cells whose centre falls inside each hexagon, so they agree to floating-point precision. A second integration step joins the raster summary to vector layers. Here we flag hexagons that contain an EPA monitoring site or lie within 2 km of a Superfund site, and compare their greenness:

pg.load(zs, "syr_hex_ndvi")  # the zonal result as a table

SELECT CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM superfund s WHERE ST_DWithin(h.geom::geography, s.geom::geography, 2000))
            THEN 'within 2 km of a Superfund site' ELSE 'farther' END AS zone,
       count(*) AS hexagons, round(avg(mean)::numeric, 3) AS mean_ndvi,
       round(avg((mean < 0.3)::int)::numeric, 3) AS share_low_green
FROM syr_hex_ndvi h WHERE count > 400 GROUP BY 1
""")

title: Rasters in PostGIS
section: Map algebra and raster to polygons
text:
Map algebra and raster to polygons
ST_MapAlgebra computes new pixel values from one or more bands with an expression, inside the database. We load the red and NIR bands as a two-band raster, compute NDVI in SQL and compare it with the geolattice.rsense result. ST_Reclass and ST_DumpAsPolygons then turn a class of the raster into vector polygons, here green space with NDVI of at least 0.6.


Code
two_band = OUT / "red_nir_reflectance.tif"  # red and NIR reflectance as one 2-band GeoTIFF
rs.write(ds[["red", "nir"]].to_array("band").astype("float32").rio.write_nodata(np.nan), two_band, cog=False)
pg.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS s2_rednir")
pg.execute(tool("raster2pgsql", "-s", "32618", "-t", "256x256", "-I", "-C", two_band, "public.s2_rednir"))
t0 = time.perf_counter()
pg.execute("""DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ndvi_sql;
CREATE TABLE ndvi_sql AS
SELECT rid, ST_MapAlgebra(rast, 1, rast, 2,                                   -- band 1 = red, band 2 = NIR
         'CASE WHEN [rast1] + [rast2] > 0 THEN ([rast2] - [rast1]) / ([rast2] + [rast1]) END', '32BF') AS rast
FROM s2_rednir""")
print(f"ST_MapAlgebra NDVI in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
sql_vs_py = q("""SELECT (ST_SummaryStatsAgg(rast, 1, true)).mean AS sql_mean FROM ndvi_sql""").iloc[0, 0]
print(f"mean NDVI, SQL map algebra (no cloud mask): {sql_vs_py:.4f} | geolattice.rsense without mask: "
      f"{float(rs.optical.index(ds, 'NDVI').mean()):.4f}")


ST_MapAlgebra NDVI in 3.0 s
mean NDVI, SQL map algebra (no cloud mask): 0.5545 | geolattice.rsense without mask: 0.5545




Code
green = q("""
SELECT (dp).val AS class, ST_Transform((dp).geom, 4326) AS geom, ST_Area((dp).geom) AS area_m2
FROM (SELECT ST_DumpAsPolygons(ST_Reclass(rast, 1, '[-1-0.6):0, [0.6-1]:1', '8BUI', 0)) AS dp FROM ndvi_indb) t
WHERE (dp).val = 1                                                            -- green space only
""")
green_union = q("""SELECT ST_Transform(ST_Union((dp).geom), 4326) AS geom FROM (
    SELECT ST_DumpAsPolygons(ST_Reclass(rast, 1, '[-1-0.6):0, [0.6-1]:1', '8BUI', 0)) AS dp FROM ndvi_indb) t
WHERE (dp).val = 1""")  # merged across tile edges
print(f"{len(green):,} polygon pieces from {len(tiles)} tiles; green space (NDVI >= 0.6): "
      f"{green.area_m2.sum() / 1e6:.1f} km² of {ndvi.count().item() * 100 / 1e6:.1f} km² observed")
ax = green_union.plot(color="#238b45", figsize=(8, 7))  # green space polygons
ax.set_title("Green space (NDVI >= 0.6) as polygons from ST_DumpAsPolygons"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.show()


11,668 polygon pieces from 36 tiles; green space (NDVI >= 0.6): 103.1 km² of 193.0 km² observed









The SQL map algebra reproduces the geolattice.rsense NDVI (both without the cloud mask). The reclassified raster became vector polygons; because each tile is vectorized separately, the pieces are merged with ST_Union to remove tile seams. The polygons can now be buffered, overlaid with parcels or tracts, or used in distance calculations like any vector layer.

Exporting rasters
ST_AsGDALRaster(rast, format) (or ST_AsTIFF, ST_AsPNG) returns a file’s bytes. Union the tiles first to export one image. The result opens in rasterio or xarray directly from memory:


Code
clip_tif = q("""
SELECT ST_AsGDALRaster(ST_Clip(ST_Union(d.rast), 1, c.geom, true), 'GTiff') AS tif
FROM ono_dem d, ny_counties c WHERE c.fips = '36067' AND ST_Intersects(d.rast, c.geom) GROUP BY c.geom
""").tif.iloc[0]  # Onondaga County DEM, clipped to the county, as GeoTIFF bytes
out_tif = OUT / "onondaga_dem_clip.tif"; out_tif.write_bytes(bytes.fromhex(clip_tif) if isinstance(clip_tif, str) else bytes(clip_tif))
dem = rs.read(out_tif).squeeze("band", drop=True)  # back into xarray
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))
dem.plot(ax=ax, cmap="terrain", cbar_kwargs={"label": "elevation (m)"})  # the clipped DEM
counties[counties.fips == "36067"].boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=0.8)  # county outline

title: Rasters in PostGIS
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

postgis_raster stores rasters as tiles in a raster column with a GiST index on the tile footprints; raster2pgsql -t -I -C loads them.
In-db rasters are self-contained and fast to scan; out-db rasters (-R) keep pixels in the file, typically a COG, and need postgis.enable_outdb_rasters and a path the server can read.
ST_Value, ST_Clip and ST_SummaryStats(Agg) sample, cut and summarize rasters inside SQL, so raster values join to points and polygons like attributes.
Zonal statistics (geolatticedb.raster.zonal_stats, or ST_Clip + ST_SummaryStatsAgg) matched a NumPy calculation exactly.
ST_MapAlgebra computes new rasters in the database; ST_Reclass + ST_DumpAsPolygons turn raster classes into vector polygons.
ST_AsGDALRaster exports results to GeoTIFF for geolattice.rsense, rasterio or xarray.

Functions used: raster2pgsql, ST_MetaData, ST_BandMetaData, ST_Envelope, ST_Value, ST_Clip, ST_SummaryStats, ST_SummaryStatsAgg, ST_Histogram, ST_MapAlgebra, ST_Reclass, ST_DumpAsPolygons, ST_Union, ST_AsGDALRaster, ST_HexagonGrid; rs.read, rs.write, rs.optical.index (geolattice.rsense); pdb.connect, con.raster.load, con.raster.info, con.raster.zonal_stats, con.load (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

Load the 23 July and 19 September 2025 scenes as well and compute NDVI change per hexagon in SQL.
Compare ST_Value with resample => 'bilinear' and nearest-neighbour values at the monitoring sites.
Compute the share of each hexagon covered by green space using the green_union polygons and ST_Intersection. Does it agree with the share of cells with NDVI >= 0.6?
Register a remote COG out-db with raster2pgsql -R /vsicurl/https://... and query it. Which server settings are needed?
Summarize the Onondaga DEM within 2 km hexagons and find the steepest hexagon with ST_Slope.

text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import time  # timing
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import shapely  # geometry
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

from geolattice import geolatticedb as pdb  # GeoLattice spatial database tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution




Code
import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_02_04"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

def superfund_sites():  # EPA Superfund National Priorities List sites from the Atlas
    """Superfund NPL sites as points (EPSG:4326)."""
    s = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/superfund_npl_data.js")["sites"])  # one row per site
    s = s.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])  # keep sites with coordinates
    s = s[["epa_id", "name", "status", "state", "city", "county", "score", "listed", "lat", "lon"]]  # main fields
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(s, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(s.lon, s.lat), crs=4326)  # points

# PostGIS connection string (see 06_01_02 for the Docker container); override with GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN
PG_DSN = os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN", "postgresql://postgres:geolattice@localhost:5432/geolattice")
print("Repository:", ROOT)  # where the data are read from
