title: Geometry processing
text:
Buffers
ST_Buffer(geom, d) returns the area within distance d of a geometry. The distance is in SRID units, so buffer in a projected SRID or on geography (metres; PostGIS projects to a suitable UTM or polar system internally and back). Options are passed as a text string:








Option
Values
Effect




quad_segs=n
default 8
segments per quarter circle (smoothness vs. vertex count)


endcap=
round, flat, square
shape at line ends


join=
round, mitre, bevel
shape at line corners


side=
both, left, right
one-sided buffers of lines



A negative distance shrinks polygons (an inner buffer). We compare buffer shapes on a real street, then measure how much the choice of SRID changes a 1 mile buffer around Superfund sites.


Code
opts = {"round (default)": "", "flat ends": "endcap=flat", "square ends, mitre joins": "endcap=square join=mitre",
        "left side only": "side=left", "quad_segs=2": "quad_segs=2"}  # buffer styles
seg = q("SELECT geom FROM ono_streets WHERE \"StreetName\" = 'Highland Park' LIMIT 1")  # one street segment
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(opts), figsize=(16, 3.4))  # one panel per style
for ax, (label, o) in zip(axes, opts.items()):  # every style
    b = q("SELECT ST_Buffer(geom, 60, %s) AS geom, ST_NPoints(ST_Buffer(geom, 60, %s)) AS n "
          "FROM ono_streets WHERE \"StreetName\" = 'Highland Park' LIMIT 1", (o, o))  # 60 m buffer
    b.plot(ax=ax, color="#c6dbef", edgecolor="#2171b5"); seg.plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=1.5)  # buffer and line
    ax.set_title(f"{label}\n{int(b.n.iloc[0])} vertices", fontsize=9); ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()











Code
mile = 1609.344  # one mile in metres
cmp = q(f"""
SELECT s.state,
       avg(ST_Area(ST_Buffer(s.geom::geography, {mile}))) / 1e6                         AS geography_km2,
       avg(ST_Area(ST_Buffer(ST_Transform(s.geom, 5070), {mile}))) / 1e6                AS albers_km2,
       avg(ST_Area(ST_Transform(ST_Buffer(ST_Transform(s.geom, 3857), {mile}), 4326)::geography)) / 1e6
                                                                                   AS mercator_buffer_true_km2,
       avg(ST_Area(ST_Buffer(s.geom, 0.0145)::geography)) / 1e6                          AS degree_buffer_true_km2
FROM superfund s WHERE s.state IN ('FL', 'NY', 'WA', 'AK') GROUP BY s.state ORDER BY 1
""")
cmp.insert(1, "exact circle km2", round(np.pi * mile ** 2 / 1e6, 3))  # πr² for reference
cmp.round(3)  # true area of each kind of 1 mile buffer

A circle with a 1 mile radius covers 8.14 km². Buffers on geography or in Albers cover 8.09 km² everywhere, 0.6% less, because a polygon with 8 segments per quarter circle lies inside the true circle. A 1,609 m buffer drawn in Web Mercator is too small on the ground, by a factor of cos²(latitude), because Mercator metres are shorter than real metres away from the equator; in Alaska the “1 mile” buffer covers less than a quarter of the intended area. A buffer of 0.0145 degrees is an ellipse whose true area also shrinks with latitude. Always buffer on geography or in an appropriate projection.

title: Geometry processing
text:
Unions and dissolve
Dissolve merges polygons that share an attribute into one geometry and removes the internal boundaries. In SQL it is ST_Union as an aggregate with GROUP BY. Related functions:

ST_Collect: groups geometries into a multi-geometry without merging (fast; internal boundaries remain).
ST_Union: merges and removes shared boundaries (overlay; slower).
ST_CoverageUnion: union for a coverage (polygons that share edges exactly and do not overlap, like counties). It skips the overlay work and is much faster.
ST_UnaryUnion: dissolves the parts of one geometry.



Code
rows = []  # timings
for fn in ["ST_Collect", "ST_Union", "ST_CoverageUnion"]:  # three ways to combine counties into states
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # time each
    r = q(f"""SELECT statefp, {fn}(geom) AS geom FROM counties
             WHERE statefp NOT IN ('02', '15', '72') GROUP BY statefp""")  # one row per state
    rows.append({"function": fn, "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 2),
                 "states": len(r), "vertices": int(shapely.get_num_coordinates(r.geometry.values).sum()),
                 "parts": int(shapely.get_num_geometries(r.geometry.values).sum())})
    if fn == "ST_Union":
        states = r  # keep the dissolved states

UNION ALL SELECT 'ST_Union', ST_Union(geom) FROM counties WHERE statefp = '36'""")  # New York both ways
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8))  # two maps
for ax, (_, r) in zip(axes, ny_parts.iterrows()):  # each result
    gpd.GeoSeries([r.geom]).plot(ax=ax, color="#e5f5e0", edgecolor="#238b45", lw=0.6)
    ax.set_title(f"{r.fn}: {shapely.get_num_coordinates(r.geom):,} vertices"); ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()









ST_Collect is fastest but keeps every county outline, so the vertex count does not drop. ST_Union and ST_CoverageUnion both remove the internal boundaries; ST_CoverageUnion is faster because it relies on the counties forming a clean coverage (it would give wrong results for overlapping polygons, so check the coverage first, as shown in the snapping section). States made of islands keep several parts.

title: Geometry processing
text:
Clipping and overlay







Function
Returns




ST_Intersection(A, B)
the part of A inside B


ST_Difference(A, B)
the part of A outside B


ST_SymDifference(A, B)
parts in exactly one of A and B


ST_ClipByBox2D(A, box)
A clipped to a rectangle (fast; may return invalid geometry, fine for display)


ST_Split(A, blade)
A cut into pieces by a line



Traffic-related air pollution is highest close to major roads, and near-road exposure is often defined as living within a few hundred metres of a highway. We build a 500 m zone around the high-speed roads in the Onondaga street layer (speed limit 55 mph or more: I-81, US 20 and their ramps) and split the local streets into the parts inside and outside it:


Code
zone_sql = """SELECT ST_Union(ST_Buffer(geom, 500)) AS g FROM ono_streets WHERE "SPEED" >= 55"""  # 500 m zone
clip = q(f"""
WITH zone AS ({zone_sql}), local AS (SELECT geom FROM ono_streets WHERE "SPEED" < 55)
SELECT 'within 500 m of a highway' AS part, ST_Intersection(l.geom, z.g) AS geom
FROM local l, zone z WHERE ST_Intersects(l.geom, z.g)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'farther away', ST_Difference(l.geom, z.g) FROM local l, zone z
""")
zone = q(zone_sql.replace("AS g", "AS geom"))  # the zone itself, for the map
highways = q('SELECT geom FROM ono_streets WHERE "SPEED" >= 55')  # the high-speed roads
lengths = clip.assign(km=clip.length / 1000).groupby("part").km.sum().round(1)  # street km in each part
total = q('SELECT sum(ST_Length(geom)) / 1000 AS km FROM ono_streets WHERE "SPEED" < 55').km.iloc[0]  # check
print(lengths.to_dict(), f"| sum {lengths.sum():.1f} km = local network {total:.1f} km")
ax = clip.plot(column="part", categorical=True, cmap="Set1", legend=True, figsize=(8, 7), lw=0.8)  # local streets
highways.plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=1.6); zone.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=0.6, ls="--")  # highways, zone
ax.set_title("Local streets within 500 m of a high-speed road (black)"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.show()


{'farther away': 369.1, 'within 500 m of a highway': 26.8} | sum 395.9 km = local network 395.8 km









The parts inside and outside the zone add up to the length of the local network, a quick check that ST_Intersection and ST_Difference partition lines without gaps or overlaps. Merging the highway buffers with ST_Union first keeps streets near two highways from being counted twice. With address points or census blocks instead of streets, the same query estimates how many people live in the near-road zone.

title: Geometry processing
text:
Simplification
Detailed boundaries slow down web maps and spatial joins. Simplification removes vertices:

ST_Simplify(geom, tol): Douglas-Peucker; drops vertices within tol of the simplified line. Can create invalid geometries and gaps.
ST_SimplifyPreserveTopology(geom, tol): the same, but keeps each geometry valid.
ST_SimplifyVW(geom, area): Visvalingam-Whyatt; removes vertices with the smallest triangle area, often looks more natural.
ST_CoverageSimplify(geom, tol) OVER (): simplifies a coverage as a whole, so neighbouring polygons keep identical shared edges (PostGIS 3.4+ with GEOS 3.12+).

The first three simplify each polygon on its own, so a shared border is simplified twice, differently, and gaps and overlaps appear between neighbours. We simplify the New York counties in UTM 18N with a 2 km tolerance and count the damage:


Code
simp = q("""
WITH c AS (SELECT fips, ST_Transform(geom, 32618) AS g FROM counties WHERE statefp = '36')
SELECT fips, 'original' AS method, g AS geom FROM c
UNION ALL SELECT fips, 'ST_Simplify', ST_Simplify(g, 2000) FROM c
UNION ALL SELECT fips, 'ST_SimplifyPreserveTopology', ST_SimplifyPreserveTopology(g, 2000) FROM c
UNION ALL SELECT fips, 'ST_SimplifyVW', ST_SimplifyVW(g, 2000 * 2000) FROM c
UNION ALL SELECT fips, 'ST_CoverageSimplify', ST_CoverageSimplify(g, 2000) OVER () FROM c
""")
rows = []  # one row per method
for m, g in simp.groupby("method", sort=False):  # every method
    union = shapely.union_all(g.geometry.values)  # all counties merged
    total = g.area.sum()  # sum of the county areas
    holes = sum(len(p.interiors) for p in getattr(union, "geoms", [union]))  # gaps inside the state outline
    rows.append({"method": m, "vertices": int(shapely.get_num_coordinates(g.geometry.values).sum()),
                 "invalid": int((~g.is_valid).sum()), "overlap km2": round((total - union.area) / 1e6, 1),
                 "gaps (holes)": holes})

All four methods cut the number of vertices by more than half (from 1,966 to between 687 and 899), and here all results stayed valid. However, only ST_CoverageSimplify keeps the counties a clean coverage. The per-polygon methods simplify each shared border twice, differently, which left 35 to 165 km² of overlapping slivers and 21 to 32 gaps between neighbours (doubled lines in the middle panel). For maps of adjacent areas, choropleths or any later overlay, simplify the coverage as a whole.

title: Geometry processing
text:
Checking and fixing validity
A polygon is valid (OGC rules) when its rings are closed and simple (no self-intersection), holes lie inside the shell and do not overlap each other, and the interior is connected. Invalid polygons make overlay functions fail or return wrong areas. PostGIS offers:

ST_IsValid(geom) and ST_IsValidReason(geom): test and explain.
ST_IsValidDetail(geom): the reason and the location of the problem.
ST_MakeValid(geom, 'method=linework') (default) or 'method=structure': repair. linework keeps every edge and builds valid polygons from them; structure rebuilds the shell and holes by area (XOR of rings).

Real boundary files are usually valid but should be checked; the common problems are easy to create:


Code
bad = {  # classic invalid polygons
    "bow-tie (self-intersection)": "POLYGON((0 0, 2 2, 2 0, 0 2, 0 0))",
    "hole outside shell": "POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0), (3 3, 4 3, 4 4, 3 4, 3 3))",
    "overlapping holes": "POLYGON((0 0, 6 0, 6 6, 0 6, 0 0), (1 1, 4 1, 4 4, 1 4, 1 1), (2 2, 5 2, 5 5, 2 5, 2 2))",
    "spike (zero-width)": "POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 3 3, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))",
    "ring touching itself": "POLYGON((0 0, 4 0, 4 4, 2 0, 0 4, 0 0))",
}
rows = []  # one row per case
for name, wkt in bad.items():  # every case
    r = q("""SELECT ST_IsValid(g) AS valid, (ST_IsValidDetail(g)).reason AS reason,
               ST_AsText((ST_IsValidDetail(g)).location) AS location, ST_Area(g) AS area_before,
               ST_Area(ST_MakeValid(g, 'method=linework')) AS area_linework,
               ST_Area(ST_MakeValid(g, 'method=structure')) AS area_structure,
               GeometryType(ST_MakeValid(g)) AS type_after
        FROM (SELECT ST_GeomFromText(%s) AS g) t""", (wkt,))
    rows.append({"case": name, **r.iloc[0].to_dict()})

For the overlapping holes, structure subtracts the union of the holes from the shell (36 − 14 = 22), while linework builds faces from all edges and alternates inside and outside, so the area where the two holes overlap is filled again (26). The bow-tie has an area of 0 before repair because its two halves have opposite orientation, a typical symptom of invalid input. The spike is removed and the area stays at 4. Check the real layers:

title: Geometry processing
text:
Snapping and topology
Boundaries of the same places from two sources never match exactly. Overlaying them leaves thin slivers where the lines differ. We compare the Atlas (Census cartographic boundary) counties with a second New York county layer from the GeoLattice data folder:


Code
sliv = q("""
WITH a AS (SELECT fips, ST_Transform(geom, 32618) AS g FROM counties WHERE statefp = '36'),
     b AS (SELECT lpad("FIPS"::text, 5, '0') AS fips, ST_Transform(ST_Union(geom), 32618) AS g
           FROM ny_counties_usgs GROUP BY 1)
SELECT a.fips, ST_Area(a.g) / 1e6 AS area_a_km2, ST_Area(b.g) / 1e6 AS area_b_km2,
       ST_Area(ST_SymDifference(a.g, b.g)) / 1e6 AS mismatch_km2,
       ST_HausdorffDistance(ST_Boundary(a.g), ST_Boundary(b.g)) AS max_offset_m
FROM a JOIN b USING (fips)
""")
sliv["mismatch_pct"] = 100 * sliv.mismatch_km2 / sliv.area_a_km2  # mismatch relative to county area
print(f"{len(sliv)} counties matched by FIPS; mismatch: median {sliv.mismatch_pct.median():.1f}% of county area, "
      f"max boundary offset median {sliv.max_offset_m.median() / 1000:.1f} km")
sliv.sort_values("mismatch_pct", ascending=False).head(5).round(2)

Tolerances of 50 and 100 m change almost nothing, so the two Onondaga boundaries do not differ by small offsets. Snapping at 500 m removes 37% of the 75 km² mismatch and at 1 km 56%, but the rest remains because the lines differ by more than 1 km in places (the median maximum offset across counties was 2.8 km). Large tolerances also pull vertices onto the wrong edge, and snapping can create self-intersections, which is why the snapped polygon is repaired with ST_MakeValid before the overlay. Snapping fixes small slivers; for sources this different, choose one as the reference layer instead of merging them.
Within one layer, polygons that should share edges can be checked with ST_CoverageInvalidEdges, which returns the edges that break the coverage (gaps, overlaps, edges that do not match). The Atlas counties of New York form a clean coverage (no invalid edges), so the topology could be built directly: 148 of its 203 edges are shared borders, and its 67 faces are the 62 counties plus island parts. In the topology every shared border between two counties is a single edge with a face on each side, so editing or simplifying that edge changes both counties at once and they can never drift apart. ST_CoverageSimplify gives the same guarantee for one simplification step without building a topology; the topology is worth it when boundaries are edited and maintained over time.

title: Geometry processing
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

Buffer on geography or in a suitable projection; a 1,609 m buffer in Web Mercator covers far less than a square mile on the ground in the north.
ST_Collect groups, ST_Union dissolves, and ST_CoverageUnion dissolves clean coverages faster.
ST_Intersection and ST_Difference partition a layer by a zone; their lengths and areas add up to the original.
Per-polygon simplification creates gaps and overlaps between neighbours; ST_CoverageSimplify keeps shared borders identical.
Check validity with ST_IsValid/ST_IsValidDetail and repair with ST_MakeValid (linework or structure); use ST_ReducePrecision instead of ST_SnapToGrid.
Layers from different sources disagree by a few percent of area; ST_Snap removes small slivers, and postgis_topology stores each shared border once.

Functions used: ST_Buffer, ST_Collect, ST_Union, ST_CoverageUnion, ST_Intersection, ST_Difference, ST_SymDifference, ST_Simplify, ST_SimplifyPreserveTopology, ST_SimplifyVW, ST_CoverageSimplify, ST_IsValid, ST_IsValidDetail, ST_MakeValid, ST_SnapToGrid, ST_ReducePrecision, ST_Snap, ST_HausdorffDistance, ST_CoverageInvalidEdges, CreateTopology, toTopoGeom; pdb.connect, con.load, con.query (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

Repeat the simplification table with tolerances of 500 m and 5 km. At which tolerance does ST_SimplifyPreserveTopology start to produce large overlaps?
Use ST_Buffer(geom, 'side=left') to make a 20 m strip on one side of each Onondaga street. What is the total strip area?
Dissolve the Atlas counties into the four Census regions (Northeast, Midwest, South, West) with ST_CoverageUnion.
Find the NY county pair whose shared border is longest, using the topology edges and ST_Length.
Apply ST_MakeValid with both methods to a figure-eight polygon with a hole in one loop. Plot the results.

title: Spatial SQL fundamentals
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import time  # timing

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

def superfund_sites():  # EPA Superfund National Priorities List sites from the Atlas
    """Superfund NPL sites as points (EPSG:4326)."""
    s = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/superfund_npl_data.js")["sites"])  # one row per site
    s = s.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])  # keep sites with coordinates
    s = s[["epa_id", "name", "status", "state", "city", "county", "score", "listed", "lat", "lon"]]  # main fields
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(s, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(s.lon, s.lat), crs=4326)  # points

title: Spatial SQL fundamentals
text:
Areas and perimeters: ST_Area, ST_Perimeter
ST_Area(geom) returns the planar area in the units of the SRID. For EPSG:4326 that is square degrees, which mean nothing physically. There are three correct ways to get square metres:

ST_Area(geom::geography): area on the WGS84 ellipsoid (exact, slower).
ST_Area(ST_Transform(geom, 5070)): planar area in an equal-area projection (fast, exact for its region).
ST_Area(ST_Transform(geom, 3857)): Web Mercator. Wrong for areas: Mercator preserves shape, not area.

We compare them with the Census land area for the New York counties. (The Census value excludes inland water, so it is the lower bound.)


Code
ny_area = q("""
SELECT name,
       ST_Area(geom)                          AS deg2,          -- square degrees (meaningless)
       ST_Area(geom::geography) / 1e6         AS geography_km2, -- ellipsoid
       ST_Area(ST_Transform(geom, 5070)) / 1e6 AS albers_km2,   -- equal-area projection
       ST_Area(ST_Transform(geom, 3857)) / 1e6 AS mercator_km2, -- Web Mercator
       census_sqmi * 2.589988                 AS census_land_km2
FROM counties WHERE statefp = '36' ORDER BY geography_km2 DESC
""")

SELECT fips, ST_Y(ST_Centroid(geom)) AS lat,
       ST_Area(ST_Transform(geom, 3857)) / ST_Area(geom::geography)  AS mercator_ratio,

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))  # two panels
ax[0].scatter(ratio.lat, ratio.mercator_ratio, s=4, alpha=0.5, label="counties")  # observed inflation

          title="Web Mercator inflates areas with latitude"); ax[0].legend()

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
print(f"Mercator ratio: {ratio.mercator_ratio.min():.2f} to {ratio.mercator_ratio.max():.2f};  "
      f"Albers error: {((ratio.albers_ratio - 1) * 100).abs().max():.4f}% at most")









Mercator ratio: 1.23 to 2.31;  Albers error: 0.0473% at most


Web Mercator inflates county areas by a factor that follows 1/cos²(latitude) exactly, from 1.23 in southern Texas and Florida to 2.31 at the Canadian border. The Albers equal-area projection reproduces the ellipsoidal area of every CONUS county to within a small fraction of a percent, so either geography or ST_Transform(geom, 5070) is correct for areas in the lower 48.
ST_Perimeter follows the same rules. A compactness index (Polsby-Popper, 4πA/P²; 1 for a circle) shows how shape measurements depend on correct units:


Code
q("""
SELECT name, round((ST_Area(geom::geography) / 1e6)::numeric, 0) AS area_km2,
       round((ST_Perimeter(geom::geography) / 1e3)::numeric, 0) AS perimeter_km,
       round((4 * pi() * ST_Area(geom::geography) / ST_Perimeter(geom::geography) ^ 2)::numeric, 3) AS polsby_popper
FROM counties WHERE statefp = '36'
ORDER BY polsby_popper LIMIT 5
""")

Lengths: ST_Length
ST_Length measures lines; for polygons use ST_Perimeter. The Onondaga street centerlines are stored in EPSG:5070 (metres), so the planar length is already in metres. Albers preserves area, not distance, so we check its length against the ellipsoid:


Code
lengths = q("""
SELECT coalesce(nullif("PostType", ''), '(none)') AS street_type, count(*) AS segments,
       round(sum(ST_Length(geom))::numeric / 1e3, 2) AS km_albers,
       round(sum(ST_Length(ST_Transform(geom, 4326)::geography))::numeric / 1e3, 2) AS km_geodesic,
       round(sum(ST_Length(ST_Transform(geom, 32618)))::numeric / 1e3, 2) AS km_utm18n
FROM ono_streets GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY km_geodesic DESC LIMIT 6
""")
lengths["albers err %"] = ((lengths.km_albers / lengths.km_geodesic - 1) * 100).astype(float).round(3)  # error

We measure the distance from downtown Syracuse to every PM2.5 monitor in New York with each method, using the spheroid distance as the reference:


Code
dist = q("""
WITH syr AS (SELECT ST_SetSRID(ST_MakePoint(-76.1474, 43.0481), 4326) AS g)   -- downtown Syracuse
SELECT m.name,
       ST_Distance(m.geom::geography, syr.g::geography) / 1e3                 AS spheroid_km,
       ST_Distance(m.geom::geography, syr.g::geography, false) / 1e3          AS sphere_km,
       ST_DistanceSphere(m.geom, syr.g) / 1e3                                 AS distsphere_km,
       ST_Distance(ST_Transform(m.geom, 32618), ST_Transform(syr.g, 32618)) / 1e3 AS utm18n_km,
       ST_Distance(ST_Transform(m.geom, 5070), ST_Transform(syr.g, 5070)) / 1e3   AS albers_km,
       ST_Distance(ST_Transform(m.geom, 3857), ST_Transform(syr.g, 3857)) / 1e3   AS mercator_km,
       ST_Distance(m.geom, syr.g)                                             AS degrees
FROM pm25 m, syr WHERE m.state = 'New York' ORDER BY spheroid_km
""")
err = dist.drop(columns=["name", "spheroid_km", "degrees"]).div(dist.spheroid_km, axis=0).sub(1).mul(100)  # % error

Centroids and representative points
ST_Centroid returns the centre of mass, which can fall outside a concave or multi-part polygon. ST_PointOnSurface returns a point guaranteed to be inside, which is what labels and point-in-polygon lookups need.


Code
outside = q("""
SELECT fips, name, statefp, ST_Centroid(geom) AS centroid, ST_PointOnSurface(geom) AS on_surface, geom
FROM counties WHERE NOT ST_Intersects(ST_Centroid(geom), geom)
""", geom_col="geom")
print(f"{len(outside)} of {len(counties):,} county centroids fall outside their own county")
ex = outside[outside.statefp != "02"].head(4)  # four examples outside Alaska
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.6))  # four panels
for ax, (_, r) in zip(axes, ex.iterrows()):  # every example
    gpd.GeoSeries([r.geom]).plot(ax=ax, color="#deebf7", edgecolor="#3182bd")  # the county
    gpd.GeoSeries([r.centroid]).plot(ax=ax, color="red", markersize=40, label="ST_Centroid")  # centroid
    gpd.GeoSeries([r.on_surface]).plot(ax=ax, color="green", markersize=40, marker="^", label="ST_PointOnSurface")
    ax.set_title(f"{r['name']} ({r.fips})", fontsize=9); ax.set_axis_off()
axes[0].legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=7); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

Reprojection with ST_Transform
ST_Transform(geom, srid) converts coordinates into another CRS using PROJ and the definitions in spatial_ref_sys. ST_SetSRID(geom, srid) only labels the geometry with an SRID without changing any coordinate. Mixing them up is a common error:


Code
q("""
WITH p AS (SELECT ST_SetSRID(ST_MakePoint(-76.1474, 43.0481), 4326) AS g)   -- Syracuse, lon/lat
SELECT 'ST_Transform(g, 32618)' AS call, ST_AsText(ST_Transform(g, 32618)) AS result FROM p UNION ALL
SELECT 'ST_SetSRID(g, 32618)',  ST_AsText(ST_SetSRID(g, 32618)) FROM p UNION ALL
SELECT 'ST_Transform(g, 5070)', ST_AsText(ST_Transform(g, 5070)) FROM p UNION ALL
SELECT 'ST_Transform(g, 2261)', ST_AsText(ST_Transform(g, 2261)) FROM p
""")

ST_SetSRID(g, 32618) claims that -76.15, 43.05 are UTM metres. In UTM zone 18N that is an easting of about 0 m and a northing of 43 m, a point on the equator about 500 km west of the zone’s central meridian (75°W), in the Pacific Ocean near the coast of Ecuador. ST_SetSRID is right only when the coordinates are correct and the SRID is missing or wrong, e.g. after loading a CSV of lon/lat values: ST_SetSRID(ST_MakePoint(lon, lat), 4326).

title: Spatial SQL fundamentals
text:
Geography vs. geometry calculations
The geography type calculates on the ellipsoid, so radii and areas are always in metres and correct anywhere on Earth. The cost is speed, and fewer functions accept it (measurements, ST_DWithin, ST_Intersects, ST_Buffer, ST_Covers, but not most overlay and processing functions). A common pattern is to keep a projected geometry column for heavy work and cast to geography for measurements.
We count PM2.5 monitors within 50 km of each Superfund site, three ways, and compare results and time. The geography and 5070 versions each get a matching index (an index is used only when the query uses the same expression):


Code
pg.execute("CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS pm25_geog_gix ON pm25 USING GIST ((geom::geography))")  # geography index
pg.execute("CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS pm25_5070_gix ON pm25 USING GIST (ST_Transform(geom, 5070))")  # Albers index
pg.execute("ANALYZE pm25")  # statistics

variants = {
    "geography (exact)": "ST_DWithin(m.geom::geography, s.geom::geography, 50000)",
    "geometry 5070 (Albers)": "ST_DWithin(ST_Transform(m.geom, 5070), ST_Transform(s.geom, 5070), 50000)",
    "geometry 4326 with 0.45 degrees": "ST_DWithin(m.geom, s.geom, 0.45)",   # 50 km ~ 0.45 degrees of latitude
}
res = {}  # counts per variant
for label, pred in variants.items():  # every variant
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # time it
    d = q(f"""SELECT s.epa_id, count(m.site_id) AS n FROM superfund s LEFT JOIN pm25 m ON {pred}
           WHERE s.state NOT IN ('AK', 'HI', 'PR', 'GU', 'VI', 'AS', 'MP') GROUP BY s.epa_id""")
    res[label] = d.set_index("epa_id").n  # monitors per site
    print(f"{label:<34} {time.perf_counter() - t0:6.3f} s, total pairs {d.n.sum():,}")
cmp = pd.DataFrame(res)  # side by side
diff = (cmp.sub(cmp["geography (exact)"], axis=0)).abs()  # disagreement with the exact count
print("sites with a different count than geography:", (diff > 0).sum().to_dict())


geography (exact)                   0.029 s, total pairs 9,372
geometry 5070 (Albers)              0.036 s, total pairs 9,368
geometry 4326 with 0.45 degrees     0.020 s, total pairs 7,862
sites with a different count than geography: {'geography (exact)': 0, 'geometry 5070 (Albers)': 62, 'geometry 4326 with 0.45 degrees': 719}


The Albers version finds almost the same pairs as the exact geography test; the sites that differ have a monitor within a few hundred metres of the 50 km edge, where Albers’ distance error (up to about 0.5%) decides. The degree threshold misses about one pair in six. Its error depends on direction: 0.45° is about 50 km north to south, but only 35 to 40 km east to west in the northern states. Converting a metre threshold into degrees is never safe. At this size all three queries take a few hundredths of a second, because each uses a matching index; without the expression indexes the geography and 5070 versions would scan the table.

Running SQL from Python
There are three common ways to get query results into Python:

Doing the work in SQL and returning only the result is usually much faster than pulling raw rows into pandas. We compare both for the mean 2024 PM2.5 by county (a point-in-polygon join and an aggregate):


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # 1) in the database: join + aggregate, return 1 row per county
in_db = q("""SELECT c.fips, avg(m.pm25_2024) AS pm25 FROM counties c JOIN pm25 m ON ST_Intersects(c.geom, m.geom)
GROUP BY c.fips""")
t_db = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # 2) in Python: pull both tables, then join with GeoPandas
c_all = gpd.read_postgis("SELECT fips, geom FROM counties", engine, geom_col="geom")  # all polygons
m_all = gpd.read_postgis("SELECT pm25_2024, geom FROM pm25", engine, geom_col="geom")  # all points
in_py = gpd.sjoin(m_all, c_all, predicate="intersects").groupby("fips").pm25_2024.mean()  # join + mean
t_py = time.perf_counter() - t0
same = np.allclose(in_db.set_index("fips").pm25.sort_index().dropna(), in_py.sort_index().dropna())  # same answer?
print(f"in the database: {t_db:.2f} s, {len(in_db):,} rows returned | in Python: {t_py:.2f} s, "
      f"{len(c_all) + len(m_all):,} rows transferred | same result: {same}")

FROM counties c LEFT JOIN pm25 m ON ST_Intersects(c.geom, m.geom)
WHERE c.statefp NOT IN ('02', '15', '72') GROUP BY c.fips, c.name, c.geom
""")  # every CONUS county, with or without monitors

Only 627 of the 3,108 counties in the lower 48 (about a fifth) have a PM2.5 monitor, so county averages of monitor values leave most of the map empty (grey). The highest 2024 means are at single monitors in Kenedy County, Texas (21.0 µg/m³) and Harney County, Oregon (15.5 µg/m³), followed by Hidalgo County in the lower Rio Grande Valley and San Bernardino County, California. A county mean from one monitor describes that site more than the county. Filling the gaps needs interpolation (for example kriging, as in the geostatistics module) or satellite-based estimates.

title: Spatial SQL fundamentals
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

ST_Area, ST_Length, ST_Perimeter and ST_Distance work in the units of the SRID; cast to geography or transform to a suitable projection to get metres.
Web Mercator inflated county areas by 1/cos²(latitude) (1.2 to 2.2 in the lower 48) and distances by 1/cos(latitude); never measure in EPSG:3857.
An equal-area projection (EPSG:5070) matched ellipsoidal areas; UTM and Albers matched distances within a few tenths of a percent across New York.
ST_Transform converts coordinates; ST_SetSRID only labels them.
ST_Centroid can fall outside a polygon; ST_PointOnSurface cannot.
Distance thresholds in degrees are direction-dependent and wrong; use geography or a projection, with a matching index.
read_postgis, read_sql and geolatticedb.query return results to Python; pass parameters and push joins and aggregates into SQL.

Functions used: ST_Area, ST_Perimeter, ST_Length, ST_Distance, ST_DistanceSphere, ST_DWithin, ST_Centroid, ST_PointOnSurface, ST_Boundary, ST_Transform, ST_SetSRID, ST_MakePoint, ST_AsText; geopandas.read_postgis, pandas.read_sql; pdb.connect, con.load, con.query, con.execute (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

Repeat the Mercator area plot for Alaska counties (FIPS 02xxx). What ratio do you expect at 65°N?
For each state, compute the length of its boundary from the county polygons (ST_Union then ST_Perimeter(geography)). Which state has the longest boundary?
Find the PM2.5 monitor farthest from any other monitor (hint: a correlated subquery with ORDER BY geom <-> ... LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1).
Count Superfund sites within 5 km of a PM2.5 monitor using geography and using EPSG:5070. Are the two counts equal, and why or why not?

text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import sqlite3  # SQLite (part of the Python standard library)
import threading  # run two writers at the same time
import time  # timing
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import shapely  # geometry encodings
import pyogrio  # fast vector I/O through GDAL/OGR
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

from geolattice import geolatticedb as pdb  # GeoLattice spatial database tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution




Code
import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_01_03"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

def superfund_sites():  # EPA Superfund National Priorities List sites from the Atlas
    """Superfund NPL sites as points (EPSG:4326)."""
    s = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/superfund_npl_data.js")["sites"])  # one row per site
    s = s.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])  # keep sites with coordinates
    s = s[["epa_id", "name", "status", "state", "city", "county", "score", "listed", "lat", "lon"]]  # main fields
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(s, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(s.lon, s.lat), crs=4326)  # points

def chr_county(year):  # County Health Rankings (CHR) county table of one year, from the Atlas
    """County Health Rankings & Roadmaps measures for all counties in one release year (2020-2025)."""
    d = pd.read_csv(fetch(f"data/county_health_ranking/chr_county_{year}.csv"), dtype={"fips": str}, low_memory=False)
    d["fips"] = d["fips"].str.zfill(5)  # restore leading zeros (01001, ...)
    return d[~d["fips"].str.endswith("000")].reset_index(drop=True)  # drop state and national rows

# PostGIS connection string (see 06_01_02 for the Docker container); override with GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN
PG_DSN = os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN", "postgresql://postgres:geolattice@localhost:5432/geolattice")
print("Repository:", ROOT)  # where the data are read from

title: File-based Spatial Databases
text:
SQLite and SpatiaLite basics
SQLite ships with Python as the sqlite3 module. It knows tables, indexes, transactions and SQL, but no geometry. SpatiaLite is a loadable extension (mod_spatialite) that adds about 500 SQL functions, a spatial_ref_sys table with the EPSG registry, geometry columns and R*Tree spatial indexes. Loading an extension has to be allowed explicitly on the connection:


Code
def open_spatialite(path):  # a sqlite3 connection with SpatiaLite loaded
    """Open (or create) a SQLite file and load the SpatiaLite extension."""
    con = sqlite3.connect(path)  # plain SQLite connection
    # Some Python builds omit enable_load_extension; this calls libsqlite3 either way
    pdb._load_spatialite(con, pdb._find_spatialite())  # library names/paths to try (conda, Homebrew, apt)
    return con

db = OUT / "health.sqlite"  # the database file
db.unlink(missing_ok=True)  # start fresh
con = open_spatialite(db)  # create it
con.execute("SELECT InitSpatialMetadata(1)")  # create spatial_ref_sys, geometry_columns, ... (1 = in one transaction)
print("SpatiaLite", con.execute("SELECT spatialite_version()").fetchone()[0],
      "| GEOS", con.execute("SELECT geos_version()").fetchone()[0])
print("EPSG codes in spatial_ref_sys:", con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM spatial_ref_sys").fetchone()[0])


SpatiaLite 5.1.0 | GEOS 3.15.0-CAPI-1.21.0
EPSG codes in spatial_ref_sys: 6559


A geometry column is added with AddGeometryColumn(table, column, srid, type, dimension). SpatiaLite then records the column in geometry_columns and installs triggers that reject geometries of the wrong type or SRID. Geometries are created with SQL functions such as MakePoint(x, y, srid) or GeomFromText(wkt, srid):


Code
con.execute("""CREATE TABLE superfund (
    epa_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, status TEXT, state TEXT, score REAL)""")  # attribute columns
con.execute("SELECT AddGeometryColumn('superfund', 'geom', 4326, 'POINT', 'XY')")  # typed geometry column
con.executemany("INSERT INTO superfund VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, MakePoint(?, ?, 4326))",  # parameters
                sites[["epa_id", "name", "status", "state", "score", "lon", "lat"]].itertuples(index=False))
con.commit()  # save
print(con.execute("SELECT count(*), GeometryType(geom), SRID(geom) FROM superfund").fetchone())  # check

try:  # the triggers enforce the declared type
    con.execute("INSERT INTO superfund (epa_id, geom) VALUES ('X', GeomFromText('LINESTRING(0 0, 1 1)', 4326))")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("rejected:", str(e)[:90])


(1840, 'POINT', 4326)
rejected: superfund.geom violates Geometry constraint [geom-type or SRID not allowed]


Counties come from a GeoDataFrame, so we write their WKB directly. The query below then answers a spatial question in SQL: which New York counties contain Superfund sites with a Hazard Ranking System (HRS) score above 50? SpatiaLite’s ST_Area returns the area in the units of the SRID, so the polygons are transformed to the CONUS Albers projection (EPSG:5070) first to get square metres.


Code
con.execute("CREATE TABLE counties (fips TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, statefp TEXT)")  # attributes
con.execute("SELECT AddGeometryColumn('counties', 'geom', 4326, 'MULTIPOLYGON', 'XY')")  # geometry column
rows = [(r.fips, r.name, r.statefp, shapely.to_wkb(shapely.MultiPolygon([r.geometry])
         if r.geometry.geom_type == "Polygon" else r.geometry)) for r in counties.itertuples()]  # promote to multi
con.executemany("INSERT INTO counties VALUES (?, ?, ?, CastToMulti(GeomFromWKB(?, 4326)))", rows)  # WKB in
con.commit()  # save

q = """
SELECT c.name, count(*) AS sites_hrs_gt50, round(ST_Area(Transform(c.geom, 5070)) / 1e6) AS area_km2
FROM counties c JOIN superfund s ON ST_Within(s.geom, c.geom)
WHERE c.statefp = '36' AND s.score > 50
GROUP BY c.fips ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 5
"""
pd.read_sql(q, con)  # SQL result as a DataFrame

title: File-based Spatial Databases
text:
Spatial indexes in SpatiaLite
The query above tested every site against every New York county. SpatiaLite stores spatial indexes as SQLite **R*Tree virtual tables** named idx_<table>_<column>, holding one bounding box per row. Unlike PostGIS, the index is not used automatically: the query must ask for it, either through the R*Tree table or through the SpatialIndex virtual table.


Code
con.execute("SELECT CreateSpatialIndex('counties', 'geom')")  # builds idx_counties_geom (R*Tree)
con.execute("SELECT CreateSpatialIndex('superfund', 'geom')")  # builds idx_superfund_geom
con.commit()  # save
print(pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM idx_counties_geom LIMIT 3", con))  # what the R*Tree stores: rowid + box

def timed(sql, n=5):  # median run time of a query
    ts = []  # run times
    for _ in range(n):  # repeat
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); res = con.execute(sql).fetchall(); ts.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return res, np.median(ts) * 1000  # result and milliseconds

no_idx = """SELECT c.fips, count(*) FROM counties c JOIN superfund s ON ST_Within(s.geom, c.geom)
GROUP BY c.fips"""  # exact test on every pair
with_idx = """SELECT c.fips, count(*) FROM superfund s JOIN counties c ON ST_Within(s.geom, c.geom)
AND c.ROWID IN (SELECT ROWID FROM SpatialIndex
                WHERE f_table_name = 'counties' AND search_frame = s.geom)
GROUP BY c.fips"""  # R*Tree first, exact test on candidates
r1, t1 = timed(no_idx, 1); r2, t2 = timed(with_idx)  # run both
print(f"without index: {t1:8.0f} ms | with R*Tree: {t2:6.0f} ms | same result: {sorted(r1) == sorted(r2)}")


   pkid        xmin        xmax       ymin       ymax
0    14 -173.120773 -153.001251  58.551842  62.295334
1    19 -171.849991 -159.384750  62.937527  66.581116
2   679 -166.850647 -141.002670  67.998940  71.352562
without index:     2103 ms | with R*Tree:     34 ms | same result: True


The R*Tree turns a scan of millions of point-in-polygon tests into a few thousand box lookups followed by exact tests on the candidates, and gives the same answer. Forgetting the SpatialIndex clause is the most common performance mistake with SpatiaLite; PostGIS and DuckDB use their indexes without being asked.

title: File-based Spatial Databases
text:
GeoPackage: layers and attribute tables
GeoPackage (.gpkg, OGC standard 12-128) is the open replacement for the shapefile. It removes the shapefile’s limits (2 GB, 10-character field names, one layer, no real dates, separate .dbf/.prj/.shx files) and keeps everything in one SQLite file:

feature layers (tables with a geometry column), each with its own SRID;
attribute tables without geometry, such as a table of health measures;
tile matrix sets for raster tiles;
metadata and extensions (R-tree indexes, schemas, related tables).

We write four tables into ny_health.gpkg with pyogrio: counties, Superfund sites and PM2.5 monitors as layers, and the County Health Rankings as an attribute table.


Code
gpkg = OUT / "ny_health.gpkg"  # the GeoPackage file
gpkg.unlink(missing_ok=True)  # start fresh

            "years_of_potential_life_lost_rate", "air_pollution_particulate_matter_average_daily_pm2_5",
            "uninsured", "median_household_income"]  # a few CHR measures
chr_ny = chr24[chr24.state_abbr == "NY"][measures].copy()  # New York counties only

pyogrio.write_dataframe(ny, gpkg, layer="counties")  # layer 1: polygons (EPSG:4326)
pyogrio.write_dataframe(sites[sites.state == "NY"], gpkg, layer="superfund")  # layer 2: points
pyogrio.write_dataframe(pm[pm.state == "New York"].to_crs(32618), gpkg, layer="pm25_monitors")  # layer 3: UTM 18N
pyogrio.write_dataframe(chr_ny, gpkg, layer="chr_2024")  # table 4: attributes only (no geometry)

title: File-based Spatial Databases
text:
Inside a GeoPackage
Because a GeoPackage is an SQLite database, the standard sqlite3 module can open it. The standard defines a few metadata tables:







Table
Contents




gpkg_contents
one row per layer or table: name, type (features, attributes, tiles), extent, SRID


gpkg_geometry_columns
geometry column, type and SRID of each feature layer


gpkg_spatial_ref_sys
coordinate systems used in the file (WKT definitions)


gpkg_extensions
extensions in use, e.g. the R-tree index


rtree_<layer>_<column>
the R-tree index of each layer (SQLite R*Tree)





Code
raw = sqlite3.connect(gpkg)  # open the GeoPackage as plain SQLite (no SpatiaLite needed)
print(pd.read_sql("SELECT table_name, data_type, srs_id, round(min_x, 2) AS min_x, round(max_y, 2) AS max_y "
                  "FROM gpkg_contents", raw))  # the layer catalog
print(pd.read_sql("SELECT srs_id, organization, substr(definition, 1, 45) AS wkt FROM gpkg_spatial_ref_sys", raw))
print([r[0] for r in raw.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE name LIKE 'rtree_%' AND type = 'table'")])

3   32618         EPSG  PROJCS["WGS 84 / UTM zone 18N",GEOGCS["WGS 84
['rtree_counties_geom', 'rtree_counties_geom_rowid', 'rtree_counties_geom_node', 'rtree_counties_geom_parent', 'rtree_superfund_geom', 'rtree_superfund_geom_rowid', 'rtree_superfund_geom_node', 'rtree_superfund_geom_parent', 'rtree_pm25_monitors_geom', 'rtree_pm25_monitors_geom_rowid', 'rtree_pm25_monitors_geom_node', 'rtree_pm25_monitors_geom_parent']


Geometries are stored as GeoPackage binary (GPB): a short header with the magic bytes GP, a version, the SRID and an optional envelope, followed by standard WKB. Decoding one by hand shows the structure:


Code
blob = raw.execute("SELECT geom FROM superfund LIMIT 1").fetchone()[0]  # one geometry blob
flags = blob[3]  # header flags byte
env_len = {0: 0, 1: 32, 2: 48, 3: 48, 4: 64}[(flags >> 1) & 0b111]  # envelope size from the flags
srid = int.from_bytes(blob[4:8], "little" if flags & 1 else "big")  # SRID in the header
geom = shapely.from_wkb(blob[8 + env_len:])  # the rest is ordinary WKB
print(f"magic={blob[:2]!r} version={blob[2]} srid={srid} envelope={env_len} bytes -> {geom}")
raw.close()  # close


magic=b'GP' version=0 srid=4326 envelope=0 bytes -> POINT (-73.657844 40.737337)

title: File-based Spatial Databases
text:
Reading and writing with pyogrio
pyogrio reads GeoPackages (and every other OGR format) much faster than the older Fiona-based path, because it moves whole columns at once, optionally as Apache Arrow. It can also push work into the file: read only some columns, filter by attribute (where) or by bounding box (bbox, which uses the R-tree), or run SQL that joins layers.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # time a full read
full = pyogrio.read_dataframe(gpkg, layer="counties")  # all features and fields
t_full = time.perf_counter() - t0

onondaga_bbox = tuple(ny.loc[ny.fips == "36067"].total_bounds)  # box around Onondaga County
part = pyogrio.read_dataframe(gpkg, layer="counties", bbox=onondaga_bbox, columns=["fips", "name"])  # R-tree filter
big = pyogrio.read_dataframe(gpkg, layer="superfund", where="score > 50")  # attribute filter (SQL WHERE)
arrow = pyogrio.read_dataframe(gpkg, layer="counties", use_arrow=True)  # Arrow transfer
print(f"full read: {len(full)} counties in {t_full * 1000:.0f} ms")
print(f"bbox read: {len(part)} counties touch the Onondaga box -> {', '.join(part.name)}")
print(f"where read: {len(big)} NY Superfund sites with HRS score > 50")

FROM counties c JOIN chr_2024 h ON h.fips = c.fips

title: File-based Spatial Databases
section: When file-based storage is enough, and when to move to PostGIS
text:
When file-based storage is enough, and when to move to PostGIS
SQLite allows many readers but only one writer at a time: a write locks the whole file. The test below starts two threads that each insert 200 rows into the same GeoPackage, the way two people editing a shared file would. With no waiting allowed (timeout=0), one of them fails:


Code
def writer(path, tag, errors, timeout):  # insert rows in many small transactions
    c = sqlite3.connect(path, timeout=timeout)  # timeout: how long to wait for the lock
    try:
        for i in range(200):  # 200 separate commits
            c.execute("INSERT INTO chr_2024 (fips, county) VALUES (?, ?)", (f"T{tag}{i:03d}", "test"))
            c.commit()
    except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:  # typically "database is locked"
        errors.append(f"writer {tag}: {e}")
    finally:
        c.close()

for timeout in (0, 5):  # no waiting, then wait up to 5 s for the lock
    errors = []  # failures of this round
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=writer, args=(gpkg, t, errors, timeout)) for t in "AB"]  # two writers
    [t.start() for t in threads]; [t.join() for t in threads]  # run them at the same time
    print(f"timeout={timeout}s:", errors[0] if errors else "both writers finished (they took turns)")
with sqlite3.connect(gpkg) as c:  # remove the test rows
    c.execute("DELETE FROM chr_2024 WHERE county = 'test'")


timeout=0s: writer A: database is locked
timeout=5s: both writers finished (they took turns)


With a timeout the writers take turns, which works for a few users but serializes all edits. PostgreSQL locks individual rows, so many users and applications can write at once. The same test against PostGIS:


Code
import psycopg  # PostgreSQL driver

def pg_writer(tag, errors):  # same workload against PostGIS
    try:
        with psycopg.connect(PG_DSN) as c:  # each thread has its own connection
            for i in range(200):  # 200 separate commits
                c.execute("INSERT INTO write_test VALUES (%s)", (f"{tag}{i:03d}",)); c.commit()
    except psycopg.Error as e:
        errors.append(str(e))

try:
    with psycopg.connect(PG_DSN, autocommit=True) as c:  # create the test table
        c.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS write_test"); c.execute("CREATE TABLE write_test (id text)")
    errors = []  # failures
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=pg_writer, args=(t, errors)) for t in "AB"]  # two writers
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); [t.start() for t in threads]; [t.join() for t in threads]  # run together
    with psycopg.connect(PG_DSN) as c:
        n = c.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM write_test").fetchone()[0]  # rows written
        c.execute("DROP TABLE write_test"); c.commit()  # clean up
    print(f"PostGIS: {n} rows from 2 concurrent writers in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s, errors: {errors or 'none'}")
except psycopg.OperationalError as e:  # server not running
    print("PostGIS not reachable (see 06_01_02):", str(e).splitlines()[0])


PostGIS: 400 rows from 2 concurrent writers in 0.07 s, errors: none


Use this checklist to decide:








Situation
File (GeoPackage / SpatiaLite)
Server (PostGIS)




Users editing at the same time
one (or a few, taking turns)
many


Data size
up to a few GB per file works well
terabytes, partitioned tables


Where the data live
local disk (not network drives: SQLite locking is unreliable on SMB/NFS)
a server everyone reaches


Access control
whoever has the file has everything
users, roles, row-level security


Web maps and APIs
read-only, small
GeoServer, pg_tileserv, pg_featureserv, OGC API


Functions needed
vector SQL, R*Tree
plus rasters, topology, routing (pgRouting), time series


Delivery
send one file; open in QGIS/ArcGIS
pg_dump, or export to GeoPackage/GeoParquet



A common pattern combines both: PostGIS holds the shared, edited master data, and GeoPackage files carry extracts to field laptops, collaborators and archives. Moving between them is one ogr2ogr command or one geolatticedb call, covered in notebook 06_02_01.


Code
with pdb.connect("postgis", dsn=PG_DSN) as pg:  # copy every GeoPackage layer to PostGIS with geolatticedb
    for name, gtype in pyogrio.list_layers(gpkg):  # every layer
        if gtype is not None:  # feature layers (attribute tables go through pandas, see 06_02_01)
            pg.load(gpkg, f"ny_{name}", layer=name)  # read the layer, keep its SRID, build a GiST index
    loaded = [f"ny_{n}" for n, g in pyogrio.list_layers(gpkg) if g is not None]  # the new tables
    print({t: pg.srid(t) for t in loaded})  # each table kept the SRID of its layer

title: File-based Spatial Databases
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

SQLite stores a whole database in one file; SpatiaLite adds geometry columns, about 500 spatial functions and R*Tree indexes through the mod_spatialite extension.
In SpatiaLite the spatial index must be requested in the query (SpatialIndex or the idx_ R*Tree table); then it gives the same answer as a full scan, much faster.
GeoPackage holds several feature layers (each with its own SRID), attribute tables and tiles in one standard file; its metadata tables and R-trees are ordinary SQLite tables.
pyogrio reads and writes GeoPackages quickly and can filter by columns, attributes, bounding box (R-tree) or SQL across layers.
SQLite allows one writer at a time and is unreliable on network drives. Move to PostGIS for many concurrent editors, large data, access control, web services or advanced functions.

Functions used: InitSpatialMetadata, AddGeometryColumn, MakePoint, GeomFromWKB, CastToMulti, CreateSpatialIndex, Transform, ST_Within (SpatiaLite SQL); pyogrio.write_dataframe, pyogrio.read_dataframe, pyogrio.read_info, pyogrio.list_layers; pdb.connect, con.load, con.srid, con.tables (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

Add a chr_2020 table from the 2020 CHR release to ny_health.gpkg and compute, in one SQL query, the change in adult obesity between the 2020 and 2024 releases for each county.
Rewrite the indexed SpatiaLite query using the idx_counties_geom R*Tree table directly (MbrMinX, MbrMaxX, …). Is it faster than SpatialIndex?
Write all PM2.5 monitors in the US to a GeoPackage with and without SPATIAL_INDEX. Compare file sizes and the time of a bbox read around Syracuse.
Open ny_health.gpkg in QGIS and check that the CHR table appears as a non-spatial table that can be joined to the counties.

import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_01_01"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

def superfund_sites():  # EPA Superfund National Priorities List sites from the Atlas
    """Superfund NPL sites as points (EPSG:4326)."""
    s = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/superfund_npl_data.js")["sites"])  # one row per site
    s = s.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])  # keep sites with coordinates
    s = s[["epa_id", "name", "status", "state", "city", "county", "score", "listed", "lat", "lon"]]  # main fields
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(s, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(s.lon, s.lat), crs=4326)  # points

# PostGIS connection string (see 06_01_02 for the Docker container); override with GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN
PG_DSN = os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN", "postgresql://postgres:geolattice@localhost:5432/geolattice")

title: Spatial Database
text:
Spatial database
A spatial database is a database management system (DBMS) with four additions:

Geometry types that store points, lines and polygons in table columns, next to ordinary attributes.
Spatial functions in SQL (ST_Area, ST_Intersects, ST_Buffer, …), defined by the OGC Simple Features for SQL and ISO 19125 standards.
Spatial indexes that find candidate geometries without scanning the whole table.
A catalog of coordinate reference systems (spatial_ref_sys) so every geometry carries an SRID.

Everything a DBMS already does still applies: many users read and write at the same time, changes happen inside transactions that either complete or roll back, constraints keep the data consistent, and the query planner decides how to answer each question.








Property
Files (Shapefile, GeoJSON, CSV)
Spatial database




Reading one feature
Usually parse the whole file
Index lookup, only matching rows


Several users editing
Last save wins, risk of corruption
Concurrent transactions, row locks


Data larger than memory
Must fit in RAM to analyze
Streams from disk, returns only results


Integrity
None (any value, any geometry)
Types, keys, CHECK constraints, valid SRIDs


Sharing
Copy files around
One copy, access by users and roles


Analysis language
Python/R scripts
SQL, plus Python/R clients



Files remain the right choice for exchange and archiving. The database is the right choice when data are shared, updated or queried repeatedly. We measure the difference on one simple question: which county is a Superfund site in, and how many sites does each New York county have?

File workflow
A GeoJSON file has no index, so finding one county means reading the whole file. The cell below loads geojson_counties_fips.json into a GeoDataFrame (all 3,221 county polygons), builds a FIPS code from the state and county codes, and keeps 36067 (Onondaga County, New York). The clock is the lesson: that one row is available only after every polygon has been parsed.


Code
# File workflow: every question starts by reading the files again
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
c_file = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # parse all 3,221 polygons
c_file["fips"] = c_file["STATE"] + c_file["COUNTY"]  # FIPS code
onondaga_file = c_file[c_file.fips == "36067"]  # keep one county
t_file = time.perf_counter() - t0  # elapsed time
print(f"File: read all {len(c_file):,} features to get 1 county in {t_file*1000:.0f} ms")  # report


File: read all 3,221 features to get 1 county in 94 ms




Database workflow
The counties and Superfund sites are copied once into a DuckDB file, atlas.duckdb. duck.load stores the geometries and builds an R-tree on them, and a B-tree index is added on counties.fips. The same county as above (36067) is then one indexed lookup, and the clock compares that lookup with the full file read.


Code
# Database workflow: load once, then ask questions with SQL
db_path = OUT / "atlas.duckdb"  # a DuckDB database file
db_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)  # start fresh
duck = pdb.connect("duckdb", path=db_path)  # open (create) the database
duck.load(counties, "counties")  # copy the counties into a table (with an R-tree index)
duck.load(sites, "superfund")  # copy the sites
duck.execute("CREATE INDEX counties_fips ON counties (fips)")  # ordinary B-tree index on the FIPS code

t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
onondaga_db = duck.query("SELECT fips, name, geom FROM counties WHERE fips = '36067'")  # one county
t_db = time.perf_counter() - t0  # elapsed time
print(f"Database: indexed lookup of 1 county in {t_db*1000:.1f} ms ({t_file/t_db:.0f} times faster)")
onondaga_db  # the result is a GeoDataFrame

The query counts Superfund sites inside each New York county. counties is aliased c and superfund is aliased s. ST_Within(s.geom, c.geom) keeps a site only when its point lies inside the county polygon, so the join is point-in-polygon. statefp = '36' limits the counties to New York. GROUP BY c.name makes one row per county: count(s.epa_id) is the number of sites, and round(avg(s.score), 1) is the mean Hazard Ranking System score to one decimal place. The rows are sorted by that count, and LIMIT 8 keeps the eight counties with the most sites. duck.query runs the statement and returns the table.

# A spatial question in SQL: Superfund sites per New York county (point-in-polygon)
sql = '''
SELECT c.name AS county, count(s.epa_id) AS n_sites, round(avg(s.score), 1) AS mean_hrs_score
FROM counties c
JOIN superfund s ON ST_Within(s.geom, c.geom)   -- spatial join predicate
WHERE c.statefp = '36'                           -- New York
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY n_sites DESC
LIMIT 8
'''

The file workflow has to parse every polygon before it can return one; the database answers from an index and returns only the requested row. The spatial join reads like the question itself, and the database chooses how to run it (here with the R-tree index on counties.geom). Suffolk and Nassau counties on Long Island have the most Superfund sites in New York, many of them groundwater contamination sites. The HRS score is the EPA Hazard Ranking System score used to list a site.
Transactions protect the data. The cell below counts the county rows, opens a transaction with BEGIN, and deletes every New York county (statefp = '36'). The count falls while that transaction is open. ROLLBACK throws the delete away, and the count returns to the number from before BEGIN. Other sessions do not see the change until COMMIT.


Code
n_before = duck.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM counties")[0][0]  # rows before
duck.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION")  # start a transaction
duck.execute("DELETE FROM counties WHERE statefp = '36'")  # delete New York by mistake
n_during = duck.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM counties")[0][0]  # rows inside the transaction
duck.execute("ROLLBACK")  # undo everything since BEGIN
n_after = duck.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM counties")[0][0]  # rows after the rollback
print(f"before: {n_before:,}   inside transaction: {n_during:,}   after ROLLBACK: {n_after:,}")

title: Spatial Database
section: The OGC Simple Features model: WKT, WKB and EWKB
text:
The OGC Simple Features model: WKT, WKB and EWKB
The Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) Simple Features specification (ISO 19125) defines the geometry types used by every spatial database, GDAL, GEOS and Shapely. Each geometry is built from coordinates joined by straight lines:








Type
Built from
Example in public health




POINT
one coordinate
a hospital, an air quality monitor


LINESTRING
two or more points
a road segment, a river


POLYGON
one closed exterior ring, optional holes
a county, a ZIP code area


MULTIPOINT, MULTILINESTRING, MULTIPOLYGON
collections of one type
the islands of a county


GEOMETRYCOLLECTION
any mix
the result of an intersection



Coordinates can have a third (Z, elevation) and a fourth (M, a measure such as time) dimension. Geometries travel between programs in two encodings:

WKT (Well-Known Text): human-readable, e.g. POINT (-76.15 43.05).
WKB (Well-Known Binary): compact bytes used inside databases and GeoPackage/GeoParquet files.

PostGIS extends both with an SRID: EWKT (SRID=4326;POINT (-76.15 43.05)) and EWKB.


Code
examples = {  # one example of each OGC type (lon/lat)
    "POINT": Point(-76.15, 43.05),

SRIDs and the EPSG registry
Coordinates are only numbers until we know their coordinate reference system (CRS). Databases record the CRS of each geometry column as an integer SRID (spatial reference identifier). The SRIDs normally come from the EPSG registry, which assigns codes to datums, ellipsoids and projections. PostGIS copies the registry into its spatial_ref_sys table; DuckDB and Shapely use PROJ, which ships the same registry.


Code
codes = [4326, 4269, 3857, 5070, 32618, 2261]  # common SRIDs for US work
rows = []  # one row per CRS
for code in codes:  # every code
    crs = CRS.from_epsg(code)  # look it up in the EPSG registry (via PROJ)
    rows.append({"EPSG": code, "name": crs.name, "kind": "geographic" if crs.is_geographic else "projected",
                 "units": crs.axis_info[0].unit_name, "datum": crs.datum.name,
                 "area of use": crs.area_of_use.name[:45]})  # main facts

Web Mercator inflates the area of Onondaga County by 87%, because its scale grows with latitude (about 1/cos²(43°) for areas). UTM and Albers stay within a fraction of a percent of the geodesic area. The Census land area is smaller still because it excludes Onondaga Lake and other water. The rule: store data in EPSG:4326 if you like, but measure in an equal-area projection (areas), a local conformal projection (short distances) or on the ellipsoid (geography).

title: Spatial Database
text:
Geometry vs. geography
PostGIS offers two column types:

geometry: coordinates on a flat plane. Calculations are fast and use Cartesian formulas in the units of the SRID.
geography: coordinates on the WGS84 ellipsoid (lon/lat). Distances, areas and buffers are computed along the curved surface and returned in metres.

Geography is the safe choice for global data and long distances; geometry with a suitable projection is faster and supports every function. We compare distances between county centroids (taken in Albers, then converted to lon/lat):


Code
cent = counties.set_index("fips").to_crs(5070).centroid.to_crs(4326)  # county centroids (lon/lat)
pairs = {"Onondaga - Erie (NY)": ("36067", "36029"),
         "Onondaga - Miami-Dade (FL)": ("36067", "12086"),
         "Onondaga - Los Angeles (CA)": ("36067", "06037")}  # short, medium and long pairs
rows = []  # one row per pair
for label, (a, b) in pairs.items():  # every pair
    pa, pb = cent[a], cent[b]  # the two centroids
    _, _, d_geo = geod.inv(pa.x, pa.y, pb.x, pb.y)  # geodesic distance (geography), metres
    two = gpd.GeoSeries([pa, pb], crs=4326)  # both points as a series
    d_deg = pa.distance(pb) * 111.32e3  # planar distance in degrees x 111 km (a common shortcut)
    d_merc = two.to_crs(3857).iloc[0].distance(two.to_crs(3857).iloc[1])  # Web Mercator
    d_alb = two.to_crs(5070).iloc[0].distance(two.to_crs(5070).iloc[1])  # CONUS Albers
    rows.append({"pair": label, "geodesic km": d_geo / 1e3, "degrees x 111 km": d_deg / 1e3,
                 "Web Mercator km": d_merc / 1e3, "Albers km": d_alb / 1e3})  # store
dist = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("pair")  # as a table
err = dist.drop(columns="geodesic km").div(dist["geodesic km"], axis=0).sub(1).mul(100)  # % error
dist.round(1).join(err.round(1).add_suffix(" err %"))  # distances and errors

Treating degrees as a flat grid overstates the Onondaga to Erie distance by 36%. The pair runs almost east to west, and a degree of longitude spans only about 81 km at 43°N, not 111 km. For the mostly north-south Miami-Dade pair the same shortcut errs by only 1%, so the error depends on direction as well as distance. Web Mercator overstates all three distances by 22 to 36%. The Albers projection stays within 1% for these pairs but still distorts distances away from its standard parallels (29.5°N and 45.5°N). Geography gives the right answer everywhere without choosing a projection, at some cost in speed. The map shows why: the shortest path on the ellipsoid curves northward when drawn on a lon/lat grid.

title: Spatial Database
text:
Vector vs. raster storage
Spatial databases store two kinds of data:









Vector
Raster




Model
discrete features (points, lines, polygons) with attributes
a regular grid of cells with values


PostGIS type
geometry, geography
raster (extension postgis_raster)


Typical data
counties, hospitals, roads
elevation, land cover, satellite images, PM2.5 surfaces


How it is stored
one row per feature
one row per tile (e.g. 100 x 100 cells)



Rasters are cut into tiles so that a query reads only the tiles it needs, through the same spatial index used for vectors. raster2pgsql does this tiling when loading. Rasters can also stay outside the database (out-db) with the table holding only tile footprints and file paths; notebook 06_03_01 compares both. Below we tile the Onondaga County DEM the way raster2pgsql -t 100x100 would:


Code
with rasterio.open(GEOLATTICE_DATA / "00_shared" / "raster_data" / "USA" / "Onondaga_DEM.tif") as src:  # the DEM
    dem = src.read(1, masked=True)  # first band, nodata masked
    tr, crs_dem, nodata = src.transform, src.crs, src.nodata  # georeferencing
print(f"DEM: {dem.shape[0]} rows x {dem.shape[1]} cols, cell {tr.a * 3600:.1f} arc-seconds, CRS {crs_dem}")

tile = 100  # tile size in cells
tiles = []  # one record per tile (what raster2pgsql writes as rows)
for r0 in range(0, dem.shape[0], tile):  # tile rows
    for c0 in range(0, dem.shape[1], tile):  # tile columns
        block = dem[r0:r0 + tile, c0:c0 + tile]  # the cells of this tile
        x0, y0 = tr * (c0, r0); x1, y1 = tr * (c0 + block.shape[1], r0 + block.shape[0])  # footprint
        tiles.append({"rid": len(tiles) + 1, "cells": block.size, "valid": int(block.count()),
                      "geometry": box(min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1), max(x0, x1), max(y0, y1))})
tiles = gpd.GeoDataFrame(tiles, crs=crs_dem)  # tile footprints
print(f"{len(tiles)} tiles; {int((tiles.valid == 0).sum())} contain only nodata and could be skipped")
