title: Spatial Database
section: Spatial indexes: R-tree, GiST and quadtree
text:
Spatial indexes: R-tree, GiST and quadtree
Testing whether each of 1,840 sites lies in each of 3,221 counties means about 5.9 million point-in-polygon tests. A spatial index avoids most of them in two steps:

Filter: compare cheap bounding boxes using the index, and keep only candidate pairs.
Refine: run the exact (expensive) geometric test on the candidates only.

The main index structures are:

R-tree: groups nearby bounding boxes into larger boxes, level by level. Used by SpatiaLite and GeoPackage (SQLite R*Tree), DuckDB spatial and Shapely (STRtree).
GiST (Generalized Search Tree): PostgreSQL’s framework for balanced search trees. PostGIS implements an R-tree on top of GiST, which is why spatial indexes in PostGIS are created USING GIST.
Quadtree / k-d tree: split space recursively into four (or two) parts. PostgreSQL offers them through SP-GiST (space-partitioned GiST).
BRIN (Block Range Index): stores one bounding box per block of table pages. Tiny, and fast for data already sorted in space. Notebook 06_02_05 benchmarks all three in PostGIS.



Code
geoms = np.asarray(counties.geometry)  # county polygons as a NumPy array
pts = np.asarray(sites.geometry)  # site points

t0 = time.perf_counter()  # brute force on a sample: test every site against every county
sample = pts[:200]  # 200 sites keep the brute-force run short
brute = shapely.contains(geoms[None, :], sample[:, None])  # (200 sites x 3,221 counties) exact tests
t_brute = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * len(pts) / len(sample)  # scale up to all sites

t0 = time.perf_counter()  # with an R-tree (Shapely STRtree)
tree = shapely.STRtree(geoms)  # build the index
cand = tree.query(pts)  # filter: bounding boxes only -> candidate (site, county) pairs
hit = tree.query(pts, predicate="within")  # filter + refine: exact test on candidates only
t_tree = time.perf_counter() - t0  # elapsed

print(f"brute force : {len(pts) * len(geoms):>10,} exact tests  ~{t_brute:6.2f} s (extrapolated)")
print(f"R-tree      : {cand.shape[1]:>10,} candidates   {t_tree:6.3f} s  -> {hit.shape[1]:,} matches")
print(f"the index removed {1 - cand.shape[1] / (len(pts) * len(geoms)):.4%} of the tests")


brute force :  5,926,640 exact tests  ~  0.33 s (extrapolated)
R-tree      :      2,755 candidates    0.003 s  -> 1,828 matches
the index removed 99.9535% of the tests


To see what an R-tree looks like, we build one by hand with the Sort-Tile-Recursive (STR) packing used by STRtree: sort the boxes by x, cut them into vertical slices, sort each slice by y, and group neighbours into nodes of at most M entries. Each node stores the box that encloses its children, so a search descends only into nodes whose box overlaps the query.


Code
def str_level(boxes, m=6):  # one level of Sort-Tile-Recursive packing
    """Group boxes (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) into parent nodes of at most m entries."""
    boxes = np.asarray(boxes)  # array of boxes
    n_nodes = int(np.ceil(len(boxes) / m))  # number of parent nodes
    n_slices = int(np.ceil(np.sqrt(n_nodes)))  # vertical slices
    cx = (boxes[:, 0] + boxes[:, 2]) / 2; cy = (boxes[:, 1] + boxes[:, 3]) / 2  # box centres
    parents = []  # enclosing boxes of the new nodes
    for sl in np.array_split(np.argsort(cx), n_slices):  # slices sorted by x
        sl = sl[np.argsort(cy[sl])]  # sort each slice by y
        for grp in np.array_split(sl, int(np.ceil(len(sl) / m))):  # groups of up to m boxes
            b = boxes[grp]  # the children
            parents.append([b[:, 0].min(), b[:, 1].min(), b[:, 2].max(), b[:, 3].max()])  # their MBR
    return np.array(parents)  # one box per parent

ny = counties[counties.statefp == "36"].to_crs(5070)  # New York counties (Albers)
leaf = ny.bounds.values  # level 0: one box per county
level1 = str_level(leaf); level2 = str_level(level1)  # two levels of parent nodes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))  # one map
ny.plot(ax=ax, color="#f0f0f0", edgecolor="0.6", lw=0.4)  # the counties
for boxes, col, lw in [(leaf, "#9ecae1", 0.6), (level1, "#3182bd", 1.3), (level2, "#d95f02", 2.4)]:  # three levels
    for x0, y0, x1, y1 in boxes:  # every box
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, y0), x1 - x0, y1 - y0, fill=False, ec=col, lw=lw))
ax.set_title(f"R-tree of New York counties: {len(leaf)} county boxes -> {len(level1)} nodes -> {len(level2)} nodes")
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); plt.show()  # no ticks, draw









A quadtree partitions space instead of grouping objects: each cell splits into four children whenever it holds more than a set number of points. Dense areas (the Northeast, New Jersey, the Great Lakes industrial belt) get deep, small cells, while empty areas stay as large cells.


Code
def quadtree(xy, x0, y0, x1, y1, cap=25, depth=0, out=None):  # recursive point quadtree
    """Return the leaf cells (x0, y0, x1, y1, n) of a point quadtree with capacity `cap`."""
    out = [] if out is None else out  # list of leaf cells
    inside = xy[(xy[:, 0] >= x0) & (xy[:, 0] < x1) & (xy[:, 1] >= y0) & (xy[:, 1] < y1)]  # points in the cell
    if len(inside) <= cap or depth >= 10:  # small enough: keep as a leaf
        out.append((x0, y0, x1, y1, len(inside))); return out
    xm, ym = (x0 + x1) / 2, (y0 + y1) / 2  # cell centre
    for a, b, c, d in [(x0, y0, xm, ym), (xm, y0, x1, ym), (x0, ym, xm, y1), (xm, ym, x1, y1)]:  # 4 children
        quadtree(inside, a, b, c, d, cap, depth + 1, out)  # recurse
    return out

conus = sites.cx[-125:-66, 24:50].to_crs(5070)  # sites in the lower 48 (lon/lat window), in Albers
xy = np.column_stack([conus.geometry.x, conus.geometry.y])  # coordinates
x0, y0, x1, y1 = xy[:, 0].min(), xy[:, 1].min(), xy[:, 0].max() + 1, xy[:, 1].max() + 1  # root cell
cells = quadtree(xy, x0, y0, x1, y1)  # build the tree
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))  # one map
states.drop(["02", "15", "72"], errors="ignore").to_crs(5070).boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="0.75", lw=0.4)
ax.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], s=3, color="#d95f02")  # the sites
for a, b, c, d, n in cells:  # every leaf cell
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((a, b), c - a, d - b, fill=False, ec="#3182bd", lw=0.5))
ax.set_title(f"Quadtree of {len(xy):,} Superfund sites: {len(cells)} leaf cells, at most 25 sites each")
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); plt.show()  # no ticks, draw

title: Spatial Database
text:
The main options










Engine
Storage
Best for
Spatial index
Limits




PostGIS (PostgreSQL)
server
shared, multi-user data; the most complete function set; rasters, routing (pgRouting), time series
GiST (R-tree), SP-GiST, BRIN
needs a server to run and administer


SpatiaLite (SQLite)
one file
single-user analysis, embedded apps, mobile
R*Tree virtual tables
one writer at a time


GeoPackage (OGC standard on SQLite)
one file
data exchange; replaces the shapefile
R*Tree (rtree_ tables)
a format first, a database second


DuckDB spatial
file or memory, in-process
fast analytics on large files (Parquet, GeoParquet, CSV) on a laptop
R-tree (optional)
single-machine, few concurrent writers


BigQuery GIS
Google Cloud, serverless
petabyte tables, GEOGRAPHY on the sphere
clustering on geography (S2 cells)
pay per data scanned


Snowflake
cloud data warehouse
enterprise analytics, GEOGRAPHY/GEOMETRY types, H3 functions
search optimization
pay per compute time


Apache Sedona
Spark, Flink, Snowflake
distributed processing of billions of geometries
spatial partitioning (KDB-tree, quadtree) + local indexes
needs a cluster for large data



The first four use the same SQL vocabulary (ST_Intersects, ST_Area, …) because they all follow Simple Features for SQL. geolattice.geolatticedb wraps the local engines behind one interface, so the same Python code runs on each. Here the Superfund question from above runs on SpatiaLite, GeoPackage and DuckDB, and on PostGIS if the server from notebook 06_01_02 is running:


Code
ny_c = counties[counties.statefp == "36"]  # New York counties
ny_s = sites[sites.state == "NY"]  # New York Superfund sites
targets = {"spatialite": dict(path=OUT / "demo.sqlite"), "geopackage": dict(path=OUT / "demo.gpkg"),
           "duckdb": dict(path=None), "postgis": dict(dsn=PG_DSN)}  # connection settings per backend
results, times = {}, {}  # per-backend output
for backend, kw in targets.items():  # every backend
    if "path" in kw and kw["path"] is not None:
        kw["path"].unlink(missing_ok=True)  # start each file fresh
    try:
        with pdb.connect(backend, **kw) as con:  # same call for every engine
            con.load(ny_c, "ny_counties"); con.load(ny_s, "ny_sites")  # same loading call
            t0 = time.perf_counter()  # time the join only
            j = con.spatial_join("ny_sites", "ny_counties", predicate="within", right_columns=["name"])  # same join
            times[backend] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # elapsed
            results[backend] = j.groupby("right_name").size()  # sites per county
    except Exception as exc:  # e.g. PostGIS server not running
        print(f"{backend:<11} skipped: {type(exc).__name__}: {str(exc).splitlines()[0][:90]}")
cmp = pd.DataFrame(results).fillna(0).astype(int).sort_values(list(results)[0], ascending=False)  # side by side
print("identical results on all engines:", bool((cmp.nunique(axis=1) == 1).all()))  # check agreement
print({k: f"{v * 1000:.0f} ms" for k, v in times.items()})  # join times
cmp.head(6)  # top counties

title: Spatial Database
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

A spatial database adds geometry types, spatial SQL functions, spatial indexes and an SRID catalog to an ordinary DBMS, which brings transactions, concurrency and integrity to spatial data.
The OGC Simple Features model defines seven geometry types; WKT is for people, WKB (and EWKB with an SRID) for programs.
The SRID decides the meaning of every area and distance. Web Mercator inflated Onondaga County’s area by 87%; equal-area and geodesic calculations agree within a fraction of a percent.
geography calculates on the ellipsoid in metres; geometry on a plane in SRID units.
Rasters are stored as tiles, each a row, found through the same spatial index.
Spatial indexes (R-tree, GiST, quadtree/SP-GiST, BRIN) turn millions of exact tests into a few thousand.
PostGIS, SpatiaLite, GeoPackage and DuckDB share one SQL vocabulary; geolattice.geolatticedb runs the same code on all of them.

Functions used: pdb.connect, con.load, con.query, con.execute, con.spatial_join (geolattice.geolatticedb); shapely.to_wkb, shapely.make_valid, shapely.STRtree; pyproj.CRS, pyproj.Geod.
Exercises

Repeat the area comparison for a county in Alaska (e.g. North Slope Borough, FIPS 02185). How large is the Web Mercator error there, and why?
Add the pair Onondaga to Honolulu (FIPS 15003) to the distance table. Which planar method fails worst?
Change the R-tree node size m from 6 to 3 and to 12. How do the number of levels and the overlap between nodes change?
Build the quadtree with capacity 10 and with capacity 50. Which areas of the country change most?
Write the SQL that counts Superfund sites per state and run it on the DuckDB database atlas.duckdb.

title: GeoLattice: Spatial Databases
text:
Files work until the data grow, several people need them at once, or the same question has to be answered every day. A spatial database stores geometries next to the attributes, indexes them so that “what lies within 5 km of this road?” is answered without reading every row, and lets SQL do joins, overlays, raster statistics and routing where the data live.
These 15 notebooks are chapter 06 of the GeoLattice tutorials. They move from database concepts and setup through spatial SQL, joins, geometry processing and indexing to rasters in PostGIS, routing with pgRouting, space-time data, in-database analytics, DuckDB with GeoParquet and cloud engines, using geolattice.geolatticedb with PostGIS, SpatiaLite, GeoPackage and DuckDB.

title: GeoLattice: Spatial Databases
text:
GeoLattice
GeoLattice is a Python library for geospatial analysis that brings vector and raster processing, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics, spatial databases, web and cloud GIS and remote sensing together under one import. It is built on GDAL, NumPy, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely and xarray, so its functions take and return objects these libraries already use: GeoDataFrames, NumPy arrays and GDAL-readable files.

geolattice


Repository
github.com/zia207/GeoLattice


Python

License
MIT


Author
Zia Ahmed, Upatta Analytics



GDAL and PROJ must be installed first, with Python GDAL bindings that match the GDAL library (conda or your system package manager). Spatial databases are part of the full installation:
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[all]"
The PostGIS notebooks also need a PostgreSQL server with PostGIS (and pgRouting for routing); the environment setup notebook runs one in Docker. DuckDB, SpatiaLite and GeoPackage need no server.

import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import shutil  # find programs on the PATH
import subprocess  # run command-line tools
import importlib.metadata as md  # installed package versions
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data

from geolattice import geolatticedb as pdb  # GeoLattice spatial database tools




Code
import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_01_02"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

# PostGIS connection string (see 06_01_02 for the Docker container); override with GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN
PG_DSN = os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN", "postgresql://postgres:geolattice@localhost:5432/geolattice")
print("Repository:", ROOT)  # where the data are read from

title: Environment setup
text:
Option A: PostGIS in Docker
Docker runs PostgreSQL in an isolated container, so nothing is installed on the host and the same setup works on Linux, macOS and Windows. The official postgis/postgis image contains PostgreSQL and PostGIS. It is built on the official PostgreSQL image, which includes the PostgreSQL Global Development Group (PGDG) package repository, so we add pgRouting, H3 and MobilityDB with apt-get.
The next cell writes three files to Data/docker/:

Dockerfile: PostGIS 3.5 on PostgreSQL 17, plus pgRouting, h3-pg, MobilityDB and the PostGIS command-line loaders.
init.sql: creates the extensions when the database is first initialized.
docker-compose.yml: the database service on port 5432 with a named volume, so data survive restarts. An optional second service runs TimescaleDB (with PostGIS) on port 5433 for notebook 06_03_03.



Code
DOCKER = DATA / "docker"  # folder for the container files
DOCKER.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it

(DOCKER / "Dockerfile").write_text("""\
# PostgreSQL 17 with PostGIS 3.5
FROM postgis/postgis:17-3.5
# pgRouting, h3-pg, MobilityDB and the PostGIS command-line tools from the PGDG repository
# refresh the package index, install those packages, then delete the apt cache
RUN apt-get update \\
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \\
      postgresql-17-pgrouting postgresql-17-h3 postgresql-17-mobilitydb postgis \\
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# run init.sql once, on the first start, after the image's own init scripts
COPY init.sql /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/20_geolattice_extensions.sql
""")  # the image definition

(DOCKER / "init.sql").write_text("""\
-- extensions used in the 06_spatialDB notebooks (runs once, when the volume is empty)
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis;            -- geometry, geography and spatial functions
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis_raster;     -- raster type and raster functions
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis_topology;   -- topology model
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgrouting;          -- shortest paths and other routing
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS h3;                 -- H3 hexagonal index
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS h3_postgis CASCADE; -- H3 functions for PostGIS geometries; CASCADE installs what it depends on
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS mobilitydb CASCADE; -- temporal types for moving objects; CASCADE installs what it depends on
""")  # extension setup

(DOCKER / "docker-compose.yml").write_text("""\
services:                              # the containers Compose starts
  postgis:                             # the PostGIS server the notebooks connect to
    build: .                           # build from the Dockerfile in this folder
    image: geolattice/postgis:17-3.5        # name and tag of the built image
    container_name: geolattice-postgis      # fixed name, so later cells can find it
    environment:                       # settings read by the PostgreSQL image on first start
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres          # superuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: geolattice         # password for local use
      POSTGRES_DB: geolattice               # database created on the first start
    # load PostGIS when the server starts, and allow a larger write-ahead log for bulk loads
    command: ["postgres", "-c", "shared_preload_libraries=postgis-3", "-c", "max_wal_size=2GB"]
    ports: ["5432:5432"]               # host port 5432 to the same port in the container
    volumes:                           # folders shared between the host and the container
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data  # named volume: the database survives restarts
      - ../../Data:/data:ro          # the module data folder, readable inside the container
    healthcheck:                       # Compose uses this to know when the server is ready
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres -d geolattice"]  # ready when the server accepts connections
      interval: 5s                     # seconds between checks
      retries: 20                      # failed checks allowed before the container is unhealthy

  timescale:                           # optional: docker compose --profile timescale up -d
    image: timescale/timescaledb-ha:pg17  # TimescaleDB on PostgreSQL 17
    container_name: geolattice-timescale    # fixed name for the optional server
    profiles: ["timescale"]            # started only when this profile is requested
    environment:                       # settings read on the first start
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: geolattice         # same local password
      POSTGRES_DB: geolattice               # same database name
    ports: ["5433:5432"]               # host port 5433, so it does not clash with PostGIS on 5432

volumes:                               # volumes Compose creates and keeps
  pgdata:
""")  # the services
for f in sorted(DOCKER.iterdir()):  # list what was written
    print(f"{f.relative_to(ROOT)}  ({f.stat().st_size} bytes)")  # path and size of each file

text:
Connecting with psycopg
psycopg (version 3) is the PostgreSQL driver for Python. It sends SQL to the server and returns rows as Python tuples. Everything else in this notebook (SQLAlchemy, GeoAlchemy2, GeoPandas, geolattice.geolatticedb) uses it underneath.


Code
import psycopg  # PostgreSQL driver

with psycopg.connect(PG_DSN) as conn:  # open a connection (closed at the end of the block)
    with conn.cursor() as cur:  # a cursor sends SQL and fetches results
        cur.execute("SELECT version()")  # server version
        print(cur.fetchone()[0][:70])
        cur.execute("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis")  # enable PostGIS in this database
        cur.execute("SELECT postgis_full_version()")  # PostGIS, GEOS, PROJ and GDAL versions
        print(cur.fetchone()[0][:160], "...")


PostgreSQL 18.7 on x86_64-conda-linux-gnu, compiled by x86_64-conda-li
POSTGIS="3.7.0 f3b3ea7" [EXTENSION] PGSQL="180" GEOS="3.15.0-CAPI-1.21.0" PROJ="9.9.0 NETWORK_ENABLED=OFF URL_ENDPOINT=https://cdn.proj.org USER_WRITABLE_DIRECT ...


Extensions are installed on the server but must be enabled in each database with CREATE EXTENSION. The catalog pg_available_extensions shows which ones this server offers:


Code
wanted = ["postgis", "postgis_raster", "postgis_topology", "pgrouting", "h3", "h3_postgis", "mobilitydb", "timescaledb"]
with psycopg.connect(PG_DSN, autocommit=True) as conn:  # autocommit: each statement is its own transaction
    avail = dict(conn.execute("SELECT name, default_version FROM pg_available_extensions").fetchall())  # server
    rows = []  # one row per extension
    for ext in wanted:  # try to enable each one
        status = "not available on this server"  # default
        if ext in avail:  # the server has it
            try:
                conn.execute(f"CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS {ext} CASCADE")  # enable it in this database
                status = "enabled"
            except psycopg.Error as e:  # e.g. TimescaleDB needs shared_preload_libraries
                status = f"error: {e.diag.message_primary[:50]}"
        rows.append({"extension": ext, "version": avail.get(ext, ""), "status": status})  # store
pd.DataFrame(rows)  # show the table

Only the extensions marked enabled are used directly. Notebooks 06_03_03 and 06_03_04 check for TimescaleDB, MobilityDB and h3-pg and use plain PostGIS when they are missing.
Always pass values as parameters, never by formatting them into the SQL string. Parameters are sent separately from the SQL text, so quotes in the data cannot change the statement. A real example: O’Brien County, Iowa.


Code
counties = atlas_counties()  # county polygons
with psycopg.connect(PG_DSN) as conn:  # connect
    conn.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS county_names")  # small demo table
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE county_names (fips text PRIMARY KEY, name text)")  # two columns
    with conn.cursor() as cur:  # a cursor for many inserts
        cur.executemany("INSERT INTO county_names VALUES (%s, %s)",
                        counties[["fips", "name"]].itertuples(index=False))  # parameters: safe for any text
    conn.commit()  # save the table before the experiment below
    name = "O'Brien"  # a county name with an apostrophe
    try:  # string formatting breaks the SQL (and would allow SQL injection)
        conn.execute(f"SELECT fips FROM county_names WHERE name = '{name}'")
    except psycopg.errors.SyntaxError as e:
        print("f-string SQL fails:", e.diag.message_primary)
        conn.rollback()  # clear the failed transaction
    row = conn.execute("SELECT fips, name FROM county_names WHERE name = %s", (name,)).fetchone()  # parameter
    print("parameterized query:", row)


f-string SQL fails: syntax error at or near "Brien"
parameterized query: ('19141', "O'Brien")

text:
Connecting with SQLAlchemy and GeoAlchemy2
SQLAlchemy adds a connection pool (connections are reused instead of opened for every query) and works with pandas and GeoPandas. GeoDataFrame.to_postgis() and geopandas.read_postgis() take a SQLAlchemy engine. The URL scheme postgresql+psycopg:// selects the psycopg 3 driver.


Code
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text  # engine and SQL text

engine = create_engine(PG_DSN.replace("postgresql://", "postgresql+psycopg://", 1), pool_pre_ping=True)  # pool
print(engine.url.render_as_string(hide_password=True))  # never print the password

counties.to_postgis("counties", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False)  # GeoDataFrame -> table
with engine.begin() as con:  # a transaction (committed at the end of the block)
    con.execute(text("CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS counties_geom_gist ON counties USING GIST (geometry)"))
ny = gpd.read_postgis(text("SELECT fips, name, geometry FROM counties WHERE statefp = :st"), engine,
                      params={"st": "36"}, geom_col="geometry")  # table -> GeoDataFrame (named parameter)
print(f"{len(ny)} New York counties, CRS {ny.crs.to_epsg()}")  # the SRID comes back as the CRS
pd.read_sql("SELECT statefp, count(*) AS n FROM counties GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 3", engine)  # plain SQL

GeoAlchemy2 adds PostGIS types (Geometry, Geography, Raster) and functions (func.ST_DWithin, …) to SQLAlchemy. Defining tables in Python gives typed columns, constraints and the spatial index in one place. We build a table of PM2.5 monitors from the EPA AirData sites in the Atlas.


Code
from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, String, Float, select, func  # SQL building blocks
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base, Session  # ORM classes
from geoalchemy2 import Geometry, Geography  # PostGIS column types
from geoalchemy2.shape import to_shape  # database geometry -> Shapely

Base = declarative_base()  # registry of table classes

class Monitor(Base):  # one row per EPA monitor
    __tablename__ = "pm25_monitors"  # table name
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)  # surrogate primary key
    site_id = Column(String(12), nullable=False)  # AQS site id (state-county-site)
    name = Column(String)  # site name
    state = Column(String)  # state name
    pm25_2024 = Column(Float)  # annual mean PM2.5 in 2024 (µg/m³)
    geom = Column(Geometry("POINT", srid=4326))  # typed geometry column; GeoAlchemy2 adds a GiST index

Base.metadata.drop_all(engine, tables=[Monitor.__table__])  # start fresh
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)  # CREATE TABLE ... and CREATE INDEX ... USING gist

aq = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/air_quality_data.js")["sites"])  # all EPA monitors in the Atlas
pm = aq[aq.p == "PM25"].dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])  # PM2.5 monitors with coordinates
with Session(engine) as s:  # an ORM session (a unit of work)
    s.add_all([Monitor(site_id=r.id, name=r.n, state=r.st, pm25_2024=(r.means or {}).get("2024"),
                       geom=f"SRID=4326;POINT({r.lon} {r.lat})") for r in pm.itertuples()])  # EWKT input
    s.commit()  # write all rows in one transaction
    n = s.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(Monitor))  # SELECT count(*)
    print(f"{n:,} PM2.5 monitors stored")


1,546 PM2.5 monitors stored




Code
syracuse = "SRID=4326;POINT(-76.1474 43.0481)"  # downtown Syracuse, NY
with Session(engine) as s:  # query with PostGIS functions written in Python
    q = (select(Monitor.name, Monitor.pm25_2024,
                func.ST_Distance(func.Geography(Monitor.geom), func.Geography(syracuse)).label("dist_m"))
         .where(func.ST_DWithin(func.Geography(Monitor.geom), func.Geography(syracuse), 100_000))  # within 100 km
         .order_by("dist_m"))  # nearest first
    print(q.compile(engine, compile_kwargs={"literal_binds": True}))  # the SQL that GeoAlchemy2 generates
    near = pd.DataFrame(s.execute(q).all(), columns=["monitor", "pm25_2024", "dist_m"])  # run it
near.assign(dist_km=(near.dist_m / 1000).round(1)).drop(columns="dist_m")  # show in km


SELECT pm25_monitors.name, pm25_monitors.pm25_2024, ST_Distance(Geography(pm25_monitors.geom), Geography('SRID=4326;POINT(-76.1474 43.0481)')) AS dist_m 
FROM pm25_monitors 
WHERE ST_DWithin(Geography(pm25_monitors.geom), Geography('SRID=4326;POINT(-76.1474 43.0481)'), 100000) ORDER BY dist_m

The ORM query compiles to ordinary PostGIS SQL with ST_DWithin on geography, so the distance threshold is in metres and the GiST index is used. The monitors around Syracuse report annual mean PM2.5 well below the 2024 EPA annual standard of 9 µg/m³.

section: geolattice.geolatticedb.connect(): one interface for every backend
text:
geolattice.geolatticedb.connect(): one interface for every backend
Each engine has its own driver and quirks: psycopg and SQLAlchemy for PostGIS, sqlite3 plus mod_spatialite for SpatiaLite and GeoPackage, the duckdb module and its spatial extension for DuckDB. geolattice.geolatticedb hides these differences behind one SpatialDB object:







Call
What it does




pdb.connect(backend, ...)
open "postgis" (DSN or host/user/…), "spatialite"/"geopackage" (path=) or "duckdb" (path= or memory)


con.load(data, table)
load a GeoDataFrame or a vector/raster file; detect the SRID; build the spatial index


con.query(sql)
run SQL and return a GeoDataFrame (or a DataFrame when no geometry is returned)


con.execute(sql)
run SQL that changes data or schema


con.tables(), con.columns(t), con.srid(t)
inspect the database


con.spatial_join, con.nearest, con.buffer, con.create_index, con.explain
common spatial operations, written once for all engines


con.raster, con.network, con.tiles
PostGIS raster, pgRouting and vector tiles (PostGIS only)



Backend names have aliases (pg, postgres, sqlite, gpkg, duck). Connections are context managers, so with pdb.connect(...) as con: closes them automatically.


Code
opened = {  # one connection per backend, all with the same call
    "postgis": pdb.connect("postgis", dsn=PG_DSN),
    "spatialite": pdb.connect("spatialite", path=OUT / "geolattice.sqlite"),
    "geopackage": pdb.connect("gpkg", path=OUT / "geolattice.gpkg"),
    "duckdb": pdb.connect("duckdb", path=OUT / "geolattice.duckdb"),
}
for name, con in opened.items():  # every backend
    con.load(counties[counties.statefp == "36"], "ny_counties")  # identical loading code
    print(f"{con!r:<75} tables={con.tables()[:3]}  srid={con.srid('ny_counties')}")


<SpatialDB backend='postgis' at 'postgresql+psycopg://postgres:***@localhost:5432/geolattice'> tables=['counties', 'county_names', 'ny_counties']  srid=4326
<SpatialDB backend='spatialite' at '/home/zia207/Github/GeoLattice/Data/06_spatialDB/outputs/06_01_02/geolattice.sqlite'> tables=['ny_counties']  srid=4326
<SpatialDB backend='geopackage' at '/home/zia207/Github/GeoLattice/Data/06_spatialDB/outputs/06_01_02/geolattice.gpkg'> tables=['ny_counties']  srid=4326
<SpatialDB backend='duckdb' at '/home/zia207/Github/GeoLattice/Data/06_spatialDB/outputs/06_01_02/geolattice.duckdb'> tables=['ny_counties', 'pygis_geometry_columns']  srid=4326




Code
sql = "SELECT name, ST_Area(ST_Transform(geom, 5070)) / 1e6 AS area_km2 FROM ny_counties ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 3"
# DuckDB's ST_Transform takes CRS strings, and always_xy keeps the lon/lat axis order
sql_duck = sql.replace("ST_Transform(geom, 5070)", "ST_Transform(geom, 'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:5070', always_xy := true)")
for name in ["postgis", "spatialite", "duckdb"]:  # three engines
    df = opened[name].query(sql_duck if name == "duckdb" else sql)  # DataFrame (no geometry selected)
    print(f"{name:<10}", ", ".join(f"{r.name} {r.area_km2:,.0f} km²" for r in df.itertuples()))


postgis    St. Lawrence 7,322 km², Essex 4,981 km², Hamilton 4,668 km²
spatialite St. Lawrence 7,322 km², Essex 4,981 km², Hamilton 4,668 km²
duckdb     St. Lawrence 7,322 km², Essex 4,981 km², Hamilton 4,668 km²


PostGIS and SpatiaLite ran the identical statement, and all three engines return the same areas. DuckDB follows the same function names but differs in details: its ST_Transform takes the source and target CRS as strings, and always_xy := true tells it that coordinates are stored as longitude/latitude (the EPSG definition of 4326 lists latitude first). Such differences are why geolatticedb writes the engine-specific SQL for its own methods (loading, indexes, joins, nearest neighbours). With echo=True it prints every statement it sends:


Code
with pdb.connect("postgis", dsn=PG_DSN) as con:  # PostGIS connection
    con.echo = True  # from now on, print every SQL statement
    nb_ = con.spatial_join("ny_counties", "ny_counties", predicate="touches", right_columns=["name"])  # neighbours
print(f"{len(nb_):,} rows: each shared county boundary appears twice (A touches B, B touches A)")


SELECT f_geometry_column FROM geometry_columns WHERE f_table_schema=%s AND f_table_name=%s UNION ALL SELECT f_geography_column FROM geography_columns WHERE f_table_schema=%s AND f_table_name=%s
SELECT f_geometry_column FROM geometry_columns WHERE f_table_schema=%s AND f_table_name=%s UNION ALL SELECT f_geography_column FROM geography_columns WHERE f_table_schema=%s AND f_table_name=%s
SELECT column_name FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema=%s AND table_name=%s ORDER BY ordinal_position
SELECT Find_SRID(%s, %s, %s)
SELECT l."fips", l."statefp", l."name", l."census_sqmi", l."geom", r."name" AS "right_name" FROM "ny_counties" AS l JOIN "ny_counties" AS r ON ST_Touches(l."geom", r."geom")
284 rows: each shared county boundary appears twice (A touches B, B touches A)




Code
for con in opened.values():  # close every connection
    con.close()
engine.dispose()  # close the SQLAlchemy pool

title: Environment setup
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

Docker gives a complete PostGIS server (plus pgRouting, h3-pg and MobilityDB) with three files and one command; conda installs PostgreSQL, PostGIS and pgRouting without Docker.
Extensions are installed on the server and enabled per database with CREATE EXTENSION.
psycopg sends SQL; SQLAlchemy adds pooling and pandas/GeoPandas integration; GeoAlchemy2 adds PostGIS types and functions to Python table definitions.
Pass values as parameters (%s, :name), never by string formatting.
geolattice.geolatticedb.connect() opens PostGIS, SpatiaLite, GeoPackage or DuckDB with one call, and the same methods work on all four.

Functions used: psycopg.connect, sqlalchemy.create_engine, GeoDataFrame.to_postgis, geopandas.read_postgis, geoalchemy2.Geometry; pdb.connect, con.load, con.query, con.tables, con.srid, con.nearest (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

Start the optional TimescaleDB service (docker compose --profile timescale up -d) and connect to it on port 5433 with pdb.connect("postgis", port=5433, ...). Which extensions are available there?
Add a CHECK (pm25_2024 >= 0) constraint to the Monitor class and try to insert a negative value.
Use GeoAlchemy2 to find the five PM2.5 monitors with the highest 2024 mean within 200 km of New York City.
Connect to a GeoPackage with pdb.connect("gpkg", path=...), load the PM2.5 monitors and open the file in QGIS.

title: Loading and Exporting Data
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import bz2  # decompress .bz2 files
import io  # in-memory text buffers
import shutil  # find programs on the PATH
import subprocess  # run command-line tools
import time  # timing
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import shapely  # geometry encodings
import pyogrio  # vector file I/O
import psycopg  # PostgreSQL driver
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text  # SQLAlchemy engine for GeoPandas
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

from geolattice import geolatticedb as pdb  # GeoLattice spatial database tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution




Code
import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_02_01"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

def superfund_sites():  # EPA Superfund National Priorities List sites from the Atlas
    """Superfund NPL sites as points (EPSG:4326)."""
    s = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/superfund_npl_data.js")["sites"])  # one row per site
    s = s.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])  # keep sites with coordinates
    s = s[["epa_id", "name", "status", "state", "city", "county", "score", "listed", "lat", "lon"]]  # main fields
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(s, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(s.lon, s.lat), crs=4326)  # points

def chr_county(year):  # County Health Rankings (CHR) county table of one year, from the Atlas
    """County Health Rankings & Roadmaps measures for all counties in one release year (2020-2025)."""
    d = pd.read_csv(fetch(f"data/county_health_ranking/chr_county_{year}.csv"), dtype={"fips": str}, low_memory=False)
    d["fips"] = d["fips"].str.zfill(5)  # restore leading zeros (01001, ...)
    return d[~d["fips"].str.endswith("000")].reset_index(drop=True)  # drop state and national rows

# PostGIS connection string (see 06_01_02 for the Docker container); override with GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN
PG_DSN = os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN", "postgresql://postgres:geolattice@localhost:5432/geolattice")
print("Repository:", ROOT)  # where the data are read from


Repository: /home/zia207/Github/GeoLattice




Code
PG = psycopg.conninfo.conninfo_to_dict(PG_DSN)  # host, port, dbname, user, password from the DSN
OGR_PG = "PG:" + " ".join(f"{k}={PG[k]}" for k in ("host", "port", "dbname", "user", "password") if k in PG)  # GDAL form
ENV = {**os.environ, "PGPASSWORD": PG.get("password", "")}  # password for psql/pg_dump without a prompt
engine = create_engine(PG_DSN.replace("postgresql://", "postgresql+psycopg://", 1))  # for GeoPandas
conn = psycopg.connect(PG_DSN, autocommit=True)  # for SQL and COPY (each statement commits)

def sql(q, params=None):  # run SQL, return a DataFrame if rows come back
    """Execute SQL on the PostGIS connection; return rows as a DataFrame when there are any."""
    cur = conn.execute(q, params)  # run
    return pd.DataFrame(cur.fetchall(), columns=[d.name for d in cur.description]) if cur.description else None

def tool(*args, stdin=None):  # run a command-line tool
    """Run ogr2ogr, shp2pgsql, raster2pgsql, pg_dump, ... and return its standard output."""
    if shutil.which(str(args[0])) is None:  # not installed on this machine
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"{args[0]} not found: install GDAL/PostGIS tools (06_01_02) "
                                f"or run it inside the container with docker exec")
    r = subprocess.run([str(a) for a in args], capture_output=True, text=True, input=stdin, env=ENV)  # run
    if r.returncode != 0:  # failed: show the error message
        raise RuntimeError(r.stderr[-1000:])
    return r.stdout  # what the tool printed

sql("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis"); sql("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis_raster")  # extensions
print(sql("SELECT postgis_lib_version() AS postgis, version() AS server").iloc[0].str[:40].to_dict())


{'postgis': '3.7.0', 'server': 'PostgreSQL 18.7 on x86_64-conda-linux-gn'}

title: Loading and Exporting Data
section: Reference datasets: TIGER/Line, Natural Earth, OSM
text:
Reference datasets: TIGER/Line, Natural Earth, OSM
Three public datasets cover most needs for boundaries and base data:



Dataset
What it has
Where




TIGER/Line (US Census Bureau)
full-resolution legal boundaries (states, counties, tracts, blocks), roads, water; yearly
www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/TIGER2024/


Cartographic boundary files (US Census Bureau)
the same areas generalized for mapping (1:500k, 1:5m, 1:20m), clipped to the shoreline
www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2024/


Natural Earth
world countries, provinces, cities, rivers at 1:10m, 1:50m and 1:110m; public domain
naturalearthdata.com


OpenStreetMap
roads, buildings, points of interest, health facilities; worldwide; ODbL licence
extracts from Geofabrik, BBBike



TIGER/Line counties are a large download (about 80 MB). Set GET_TIGER = True to fetch them; the rest of the notebook uses the Census cartographic boundaries that the USA Health Data Atlas already distributes, and a CONUS county shapefile from the GeoLattice data folder.


Code
GET_TIGER = False  # set True to download the 2024 TIGER/Line county file (~80 MB) from the Census Bureau
TIGER_URL = "https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/TIGER2024/COUNTY/tl_2024_us_county.zip"  # national county file
tiger_zip = DATA / "census" / "tl_2024_us_county.zip"  # local copy
if GET_TIGER and not tiger_zip.exists():  # download once
    tiger_zip.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(TIGER_URL, tiger_zip)
if tiger_zip.exists():  # GDAL reads zipped shapefiles directly through /vsizip/
    print(pyogrio.read_info(f"/vsizip/{tiger_zip}")["features"], "TIGER/Line counties")
else:
    print("TIGER/Line download skipped (GET_TIGER = False)")

title: Loading and Exporting Data
text:
Loading from Python: GeoDataFrame.to_postgis()
When data are already in a GeoDataFrame, to_postgis() creates the table, writes the geometry as WKB and registers its SRID. It is convenient but does not add a primary key or a spatial index; add them afterwards. chunksize sends rows in batches.


Code
counties = atlas_counties()  # US counties (EPSG:4326)
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # time the load
counties.rename_geometry("geom").to_postgis("counties_cb", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False,
                                           chunksize=1000)  # create the table and write 3,221 rows
sql("ALTER TABLE counties_cb ADD PRIMARY KEY (fips)")  # primary key on the FIPS code
sql("CREATE INDEX ON counties_cb USING GIST (geom)")  # spatial index
sql("ANALYZE counties_cb")  # update planner statistics
print(f"to_postgis: {len(counties):,} rows in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")
sql("SELECT f_table_name, f_geometry_column, coord_dimension, srid, type FROM geometry_columns "
    "WHERE f_table_name = 'counties_cb'")  # how PostGIS registered the column

The column was registered as the generic type GEOMETRY because the GeoDataFrame mixes Polygon and MultiPolygon. A typed column (geometry(MultiPolygon, 4326)) is better: PostGIS then rejects wrong types and SRIDs. We build typed tables in the schema design section.
geolattice.geolatticedb wraps the same steps (load, SRID, spatial index) in one call, with reprojection on the way in:

pg = pdb.connect("postgis", dsn=PG_DSN)  # geolatticedb connection to the same database
pg.load(counties, "counties_5070", srid=5070)  # reproject to CONUS Albers, load and index

title: Loading and Exporting Data
text:
Loading with ogr2ogr
ogr2ogr converts between any two GDAL vector formats, and PostGIS is one of them (PG: connection string). It is the most flexible loader: it reads GeoJSON, KML, File Geodatabases, OSM, WFS services and zipped files, and can reproject, filter, rename and run SQL on the way in. The main options:







Option
Meaning




-f PostgreSQL PG:"..."
output driver and connection


-nln name
name of the new table


-nlt PROMOTE_TO_MULTI
store polygons and multipolygons in one MultiPolygon column


-t_srs EPSG:5070
reproject while loading


-lco GEOMETRY_NAME=geom -lco FID=gid
names of the geometry and primary key columns


-select, -where, -sql
choose fields and rows


-overwrite, -append
replace or extend an existing table


--config PG_USE_COPY YES
use COPY instead of INSERT (faster; the default for new tables)





Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # time the load
tool("ogr2ogr", "-f", "PostgreSQL", OGR_PG, ne_countries, "-nln", "ne_countries", "-overwrite",
     "-nlt", "PROMOTE_TO_MULTI", "-lco", "GEOMETRY_NAME=geom", "-lco", "FID=gid",
     "-select", "NAME,ISO_A3,CONTINENT,POP_EST,GDP_MD")  # five attribute fields
tool("ogr2ogr", "-f", "PostgreSQL", OGR_PG, ne_places, "-nln", "ne_places", "-overwrite",
     "-lco", "GEOMETRY_NAME=geom", "-lco", "FID=gid", "-where", "pop_max > 1000000")  # cities above 1 million
print(f"ogr2ogr: 2 layers in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")
sql("""SELECT c.continent, count(p.gid) AS cities_over_1m, round(sum(p.pop_max) / 1e6) AS pop_millions
FROM ne_countries c JOIN ne_places p ON ST_Contains(c.geom, p.geom)
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC""")  # a first query across the two layers

title: Loading and Exporting Data
text:
Loading shapefiles with shp2pgsql
shp2pgsql ships with PostGIS and converts a shapefile into SQL: a CREATE TABLE followed by the rows. Its output can be piped into psql, or saved, reviewed and run later. The main options:







Option
Meaning




-s 5070 (or -s 5070:4326)
SRID of the data (and, after the colon, the SRID to reproject to)


-I
create a GiST spatial index


-D
PostgreSQL dump format (COPY): much faster, but needs psql to run


-d / -a / -p
drop and recreate / append / prepare the table only


-g geom
name of the geometry column


-W LATIN1
character encoding of the .dbf



We use the INSERT format (no -D) so the SQL can run through psycopg as well as psql.


Code
shp = GEOLATTICE_DATA / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "USA" / "US_COUNTY.shp"  # CONUS counties, EPSG:5070
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # time conversion + load
sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS us_county_shp")  # start fresh (-d would also drop, but fails if the table is missing)
ddl = tool("shp2pgsql", "-s", "5070", "-I", "-g", "geom", shp, "public.us_county_shp")  # SQL text
print(f"shp2pgsql wrote {len(ddl) / 1e6:.1f} MB of SQL; first lines:")
print("\n".join(l[:110] for l in ddl.splitlines()[:9]))  # the generated statements
conn.execute(ddl)  # run all statements (BEGIN ... COMMIT) through psycopg
print(f"loaded in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s:", sql("SELECT count(*) AS n, ST_SRID(geom) AS srid "
      "FROM us_county_shp GROUP BY 2").to_dict("records"))


shp2pgsql wrote 7.4 MB of SQL; first lines:
SET CLIENT_ENCODING TO UTF8;
SET STANDARD_CONFORMING_STRINGS TO ON;
BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE "public"."us_county_shp" ("gid" serial,
"fips" numeric,
"x" numeric,
"y" numeric,
"region_id" numeric,
"division_i" numeric,
loaded in 0.2 s: [{'n': 3108, 'srid': 5070}]


With psql on the PATH, the faster dump format is a one-liner in a terminal:
shp2pgsql -d -D -s 5070 -I -g geom Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/US_COUNTY.shp public.us_county_shp | psql -h localhost -U postgres -d geolattice

title: Loading and Exporting Data
text:
Loading rasters with raster2pgsql
raster2pgsql cuts a raster into tiles and writes one row per tile into a raster column. The main options are -t 100x100 (tile size), -I (GiST index on tile footprints), -C (raster constraints: SRID, pixel size, alignment, recorded in raster_columns), -M (VACUUM ANALYZE after loading), -F (a column with the file name) and -R (out-db: store only references to the file). Notebook 06_03_01 covers raster analysis.


Code
dem = GEOLATTICE_DATA / "00_shared" / "raster_data" / "USA" / "Onondaga_DEM.tif"  # Onondaga County DEM (EPSG:4326)

rsql = tool("raster2pgsql", "-s", "4326", "-t", "100x100", "-I", "-C", "-F", dem, "public.onondaga_dem")  # SQL text
conn.execute(rsql)  # run the generated SQL (one transaction)
sql("VACUUM ANALYZE onondaga_dem")  # what -M adds; VACUUM must run outside a transaction
sql("""SELECT r_table_name, srid, scale_x, blocksize_x, blocksize_y, num_bands, pixel_types,
(SELECT count(*) FROM onondaga_dem) AS tiles FROM raster_columns WHERE r_table_name = 'onondaga_dem'""")

title: Loading and Exporting Data
text:
Bulk loading with COPY
Inserting rows one at a time costs a network round trip, a statement parse and, if each row is committed separately, a write to the transaction log per row. COPY streams rows in a simple text or binary format, and the server writes them without parsing SQL for each. For the 2012 NYC taxi pickups we compare four methods: INSERT with a commit after every row (the naive loop, on 2,000 rows), executemany inside one transaction (on 10,000 rows), GeoDataFrame.to_postgis(), and COPY with the geometry sent as hexadecimal EWKB.


Code
files = sorted((DATA / "nyc-taxi-tiny" / "year=2012").glob("month=*/part-0.parquet"))  # 12 monthly files
taxi = pd.concat([pd.read_parquet(f, columns=["pickup_datetime", "passenger_count", "trip_distance",
                                              "fare_amount", "pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude"])
                  for f in files], ignore_index=True)  # all 2012 trips in the sample
taxi = taxi[taxi.pickup_longitude.between(-74.3, -73.6) & taxi.pickup_latitude.between(40.45, 41.0)]  # inside NYC
print(f"{len(taxi):,} pickups with valid coordinates from {len(files)} files")
DDL = """DROP TABLE IF EXISTS {t};
CREATE TABLE {t} (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, pickup_time timestamp, passengers smallint,
                  distance_mi real, fare real, geom geometry(Point, 4326))"""  # target table
ewkb = shapely.to_wkb(shapely.set_srid(shapely.points(taxi.pickup_longitude, taxi.pickup_latitude), 4326),
                      hex=True, include_srid=True)  # geometry as hex EWKB (text that PostGIS parses directly)
rows = list(zip(taxi.pickup_datetime.astype(str), taxi.passenger_count, taxi.trip_distance,
                taxi.fare_amount, ewkb))  # Python tuples, one per trip
timing = {}  # rows per second by method

conn.execute(DDL.format(t="taxi_insert"))  # 0) one INSERT and one commit per row, on 2,000 rows
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for r in rows[:2_000]:  # autocommit connection: every execute is its own transaction
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO taxi_insert (pickup_time, passengers, distance_mi, fare, geom) "
                 "VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s)", r)
timing["INSERT, commit per row"] = 2_000 / (time.perf_counter() - t0)
sql("TRUNCATE taxi_insert")  # empty it again

# 1) executemany INSERT in one transaction, on 10,000 rows
t0 = time.perf_counter()
with conn.cursor() as cur:  # one INSERT per row (batched into one transaction)
    with conn.transaction():
        cur.executemany("INSERT INTO taxi_insert (pickup_time, passengers, distance_mi, fare, geom) "
                        "VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s)", rows[:10_000])
timing["executemany INSERT"] = 10_000 / (time.perf_counter() - t0)

conn.execute(DDL.format(t="taxi_gpd"))  # 2) GeoPandas
gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(taxi[["pickup_datetime", "passenger_count", "trip_distance", "fare_amount"]].set_axis(
    ["pickup_time", "passengers", "distance_mi", "fare"], axis=1),
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(taxi.pickup_longitude, taxi.pickup_latitude), crs=4326).rename_geometry("geom")
t0 = time.perf_counter()
gdf.to_postgis("taxi_gpd", engine, if_exists="append", index=False, chunksize=50_000)
timing["GeoDataFrame.to_postgis"] = len(gdf) / (time.perf_counter() - t0)

conn.execute(DDL.format(t="taxi_copy"))  # 3) COPY from an in-memory CSV
t0 = time.perf_counter()
buf = io.StringIO()  # CSV text in memory
pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv(buf, index=False, header=False)  # write all rows
with conn.cursor() as cur:
    with cur.copy("COPY taxi_copy (pickup_time, passengers, distance_mi, fare, geom) FROM STDIN (FORMAT csv)") as cp:
        cp.write(buf.getvalue())  # stream the CSV to the server
timing["COPY"] = len(rows) / (time.perf_counter() - t0)

speed = pd.Series(timing, name="rows per second").round(0)  # results
print(speed.to_string())
print(f"COPY vs commit per row: {speed['COPY'] / speed['INSERT, commit per row']:.0f}x, "
      f"vs executemany: {speed['COPY'] / speed['executemany INSERT']:.1f}x")


174,253 pickups with valid coordinates from 12 files
INSERT, commit per row       5464.0
executemany INSERT         135965.0
GeoDataFrame.to_postgis    142064.0
COPY                       232451.0
COPY vs commit per row: 43x, vs executemany: 1.7x


Committing every row is by far the slowest pattern, because each commit waits for the transaction log to reach disk. executemany in one transaction is much faster: psycopg 3 sends the statements in a pipeline instead of waiting for each reply. COPY is fastest even though its time here includes building the CSV text in pandas, and GeoPandas (which also writes in batches) is close behind. For millions of rows the usual order of work is:

Create the table without indexes.
COPY the data.
Create the primary key and the GiST index (one bulk sort is much faster than updating the index row by row).
Run ANALYZE so the planner knows the row count and value distribution.

We time step 3 against a load into a table that already has its GiST index:


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter(); sql("CREATE INDEX taxi_copy_gix ON taxi_copy USING GIST (geom)"); sql("ANALYZE taxi_copy")
t_after = time.perf_counter() - t0  # index built once, after loading
conn.execute(DDL.format(t="taxi_idx")); sql("CREATE INDEX ON taxi_idx USING GIST (geom)")  # index first
t0 = time.perf_counter()
with conn.cursor() as cur:
    with cur.copy("COPY taxi_idx (pickup_time, passengers, distance_mi, fare, geom) FROM STDIN (FORMAT csv)") as cp:
        cp.write(buf.getvalue())  # same COPY, but every row also updates the index
t_with = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"COPY then index: {len(rows) / speed['COPY'] + t_after:.2f} s  |  COPY into an indexed table: {t_with:.2f} s")
print("Index build alone:", f"{t_after:.2f} s for {len(rows):,} points")
sql("DROP TABLE taxi_insert, taxi_gpd, taxi_idx")  # keep only taxi_copy


COPY then index: 1.10 s  |  COPY into an indexed table: 1.06 s
Index build alone: 0.35 s for 174,253 points


At 174,253 points both orders take about the same time, and the index build itself takes well under a second. The advantage of indexing after the load appears with tens of millions of rows and with several indexes per table, because then every inserted row would update every index.

title: Loading and Exporting Data
section: Schema design: keys, typmods and constraints
text:
Schema design: keys, typmods and constraints
A good schema lets the database reject bad data. For a small county health database we use:

a schema (health) to group the tables;
primary keys (FIPS code, EPA site id) and a foreign key from sites to counties;
geometry typmods: geometry(MultiPolygon, 4326) fixes the type and SRID of a column;
CHECK constraints for valid codes, valid geometries and value ranges;
a generated column for the county area on the ellipsoid;
a long table for health measures (one row per county, year and measure), which holds any number of measures and years without changing the schema.



Code
conn.execute("""
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS health CASCADE;
CREATE SCHEMA health;

CREATE TABLE health.county (
    fips      char(5) PRIMARY KEY CHECK (fips ~ '^[0-9]{5}$'),          -- 5-digit FIPS code
    statefp   char(2) NOT NULL,
    name      text    NOT NULL,
    geom      geometry(MultiPolygon, 4326) NOT NULL CHECK (ST_IsValid(geom)),
    area_km2  double precision GENERATED ALWAYS AS (ST_Area(geom::geography) / 1e6) STORED
);
CREATE INDEX county_geom_gix ON health.county USING GIST (geom);

CREATE TABLE health.superfund_site (
    epa_id      text PRIMARY KEY,
    name        text NOT NULL,
    status      text CHECK (status IN ('NPL Site', 'Proposed NPL Site', 'Deleted NPL Site')),
    hrs_score   real CHECK (hrs_score BETWEEN 0 AND 100),             -- Hazard Ranking System score
    county_fips char(5) REFERENCES health.county (fips),               -- filled by a spatial join
    geom        geometry(Point, 4326) NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX site_geom_gix ON health.superfund_site USING GIST (geom);

CREATE TABLE health.chr_measure (
    fips    char(5) REFERENCES health.county (fips),
    year    smallint CHECK (year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2030),               -- CHR release year
    measure text,
    value   double precision,
    PRIMARY KEY (fips, year, measure)
);
COMMENT ON TABLE health.chr_measure IS 'County Health Rankings measures, long format (USA Health Data Atlas)';
""")
sql("SELECT f_table_schema AS schema, f_table_name AS table, f_geometry_column AS col, type, srid "
    "FROM geometry_columns WHERE f_table_schema = 'health'")  # typed geometry columns

Now the data move from the loose staging table counties_cb into the typed table. ST_Multi promotes polygons to multipolygons and ST_MakeValid repairs any invalid ring, so every row satisfies the constraints. The Superfund sites get their county by a spatial join in the same INSERT.


Code
conn.execute("""INSERT INTO health.county (fips, statefp, name, geom)
SELECT fips, statefp, name, ST_Multi(ST_CollectionExtract(ST_MakeValid(geom), 3))   -- valid MultiPolygon
FROM counties_cb""")
sites = superfund_sites()  # Superfund sites from the Atlas
sites.rename_geometry("geom").to_postgis("stage_sites", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False)  # staging
conn.execute("""INSERT INTO health.superfund_site (epa_id, name, status, hrs_score, county_fips, geom)
SELECT s.epa_id, s.name, s.status, s.score, c.fips, s.geom
FROM stage_sites s LEFT JOIN health.county c ON ST_Intersects(c.geom, s.geom)   -- point in county
ON CONFLICT (epa_id) DO NOTHING""")  # a site on a shared boundary is kept once
chr24 = chr_county(2024)  # County Health Rankings 2024
keep = ["adult_obesity_pct", "adult_smoking_pct", "physical_inactivity_pct", "years_of_potential_life_lost_rate",
        "uninsured", "median_household_income", "air_pollution_particulate_matter_average_daily_pm2_5"]
long = chr24.melt(id_vars=["fips", "year"], value_vars=keep, var_name="measure").dropna()  # long format
long = long[long.fips.isin(counties.fips)]  # only counties present in the boundary file
with conn.cursor() as cur:  # COPY the measures
    with cur.copy("COPY health.chr_measure (fips, year, measure, value) FROM STDIN") as cp:
        for r in long.itertuples(index=False):
            cp.write_row((r.fips, int(r.year), r.measure, float(r.value)))
sql("""SELECT 'county' AS t, count(*) FROM health.county UNION ALL
SELECT 'superfund_site', count(*) FROM health.superfund_site UNION ALL
SELECT 'sites without county', count(*) FROM health.superfund_site WHERE county_fips IS NULL UNION ALL
SELECT 'chr_measure', count(*) FROM health.chr_measure""")

The constraints now protect the tables. Each statement below breaks one rule and is rejected with a clear message:


Code
tests = {  # statement -> the rule it breaks
    "wrong geometry type": "INSERT INTO health.superfund_site (epa_id, name, geom) "
                           "VALUES ('T1', 'test', 'SRID=4326;LINESTRING(0 0, 1 1)')",
    "wrong SRID": "INSERT INTO health.superfund_site (epa_id, name, geom) VALUES ('T2', 'test', 'SRID=3857;POINT(0 0)')",
    "invalid geometry": "INSERT INTO health.county (fips, statefp, name, geom) "
                        "VALUES ('99999', '99', 'x', 'SRID=4326;MULTIPOLYGON(((0 0, 2 2, 2 0, 0 2, 0 0)))')",
    "bad FIPS code": "INSERT INTO health.county (fips, statefp, name, geom) "
                     "VALUES ('ABCDE', '99', 'x', 'SRID=4326;MULTIPOLYGON(((0 0, 1 0, 1 1, 0 0)))')",
    "unknown county (foreign key)": "INSERT INTO health.chr_measure VALUES ('99999', 2024, 'x', 1)",
    "score out of range": "INSERT INTO health.superfund_site (epa_id, name, hrs_score, geom) "
                          "VALUES ('T3', 'test', 140, 'SRID=4326;POINT(0 0)')",
}
for rule, stmt in tests.items():  # try each one
    try:
        conn.execute(stmt); print(f"{rule:<30} ACCEPTED (unexpected)")
    except psycopg.Error as e:
        print(f"{rule:<30} rejected: {e.diag.message_primary[:85]}")


wrong geometry type            rejected: Geometry type (LineString) does not match column type (Point)
wrong SRID                     rejected: Geometry SRID (3857) does not match column SRID (4326)
invalid geometry               rejected: new row for relation "county" violates check constraint "county_geom_check"
bad FIPS code                  rejected: new row for relation "county" violates check constraint "county_fips_check"
unknown county (foreign key)   rejected: insert or update on table "chr_measure" violates foreign key constraint "chr_measure_
score out of range             rejected: new row for relation "superfund_site" violates check constraint "superfund_site_hrs_s


A long table is easy to reshape in SQL. The generated area column and the foreign key let one query combine boundaries, sites and measures:

title: Loading and Exporting Data
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

GeoDataFrame.to_postgis() and geolatticedb.load() load data that are already in Python; add keys and indexes afterwards (geolatticedb adds the spatial index).
ogr2ogr loads any GDAL format, including GeoJSON, OSM PBF and zipped shapefiles, and can reproject and filter on the way.
shp2pgsql and raster2pgsql produce SQL for shapefiles and tiled rasters; -I adds the index, -D (dump format) is fastest with psql.
COPY loaded the 2012 taxi pickups fastest, and committing each row separately was slowest by far; build indexes after large loads and run ANALYZE.
Typed geometry columns (geometry(Point, 4326)), keys and CHECK constraints let the database reject wrong types, SRIDs, invalid geometries and impossible values.
Export with ogr2ogr/GeoPandas to GeoPackage, FlatGeobuf or GeoParquet, with COPY ... TO to CSV, and with pg_dump for whole schemas.

Functions and tools used: GeoDataFrame.to_postgis, ogr2ogr, shp2pgsql, raster2pgsql, COPY, pg_dump; ST_Multi, ST_MakeValid, ST_CollectionExtract, ST_Intersects, ST_Area; pdb.connect, con.load, con.srid, con.columns (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

Set GET_TIGER = True, load the TIGER/Line counties with ogr2ogr (/vsizip/ path) and compare their total area with the cartographic boundaries. Why do they differ?
Load the 2020 and 2022 CHR releases into health.chr_measure and list the 10 counties whose adult obesity rose most.
Repeat the COPY benchmark with the binary format (COPY ... FROM STDIN (FORMAT binary) and cp.set_types). Is it faster than CSV?
Add a CHECK (ST_Y(geom) BETWEEN 18 AND 72) constraint to health.superfund_site. Which existing rows would violate it (NOT VALID lets you add it anyway)?
Export health.superfund_site to FlatGeobuf and open it in QGIS directly from a web server.

import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_02_03"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

def superfund_sites():  # EPA Superfund National Priorities List sites from the Atlas
    """Superfund NPL sites as points (EPSG:4326)."""
    s = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/superfund_npl_data.js")["sites"])  # one row per site
    s = s.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])  # keep sites with coordinates
    s = s[["epa_id", "name", "status", "state", "city", "county", "score", "listed", "lat", "lon"]]  # main fields
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(s, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(s.lon, s.lat), crs=4326)  # points

def chr_county(year):  # County Health Rankings (CHR) county table of one year, from the Atlas
    """County Health Rankings & Roadmaps measures for all counties in one release year (2020-2025)."""
    d = pd.read_csv(fetch(f"data/county_health_ranking/chr_county_{year}.csv"), dtype={"fips": str}, low_memory=False)
    d["fips"] = d["fips"].str.zfill(5)  # restore leading zeros (01001, ...)
    return d[~d["fips"].str.endswith("000")].reset_index(drop=True)  # drop state and national rows

# PostGIS connection string (see 06_01_02 for the Docker container); override with GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN
PG_DSN = os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN", "postgresql://postgres:geolattice@localhost:5432/geolattice")
print("Repository:", ROOT)  # where the data are read from

title: Spatial relationships and joins
section: Spatial predicates and the DE-9IM model
text:
Spatial predicates and the DE-9IM model
Every predicate is defined by the Dimensionally Extended 9-Intersection Model (DE-9IM): for geometries A and B, it records the dimension of the intersection of their interiors (I), boundaries (B) and exteriors (E), a 3 x 3 matrix written as a 9-character string by ST_Relate. The named predicates are patterns on that matrix:








Predicate
True when
Typical use




ST_Intersects(A, B)
A and B share at least one point
general overlap test (the default)


ST_Disjoint(A, B)
no shared point
rarely used; cannot use an index


ST_Contains(A, B)
no point of B is outside A, and the interiors meet
polygon contains point


ST_Within(A, B)
ST_Contains(B, A)
point within polygon


ST_Covers(A, B)
no point of B is outside A (boundary allowed)
containment that counts boundary points


ST_Touches(A, B)
boundaries meet, interiors do not
neighbouring polygons


ST_Crosses, ST_Overlaps
lines cross / same-dimension partial overlap
road crosses county line


ST_DWithin(A, B, d)
distance ≤ d
proximity, buffers without buffering



The differences matter only at boundaries, and boundaries are where real data are messy. A unit square and five test points show them:


Code
square = "POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))"  # a 2 x 2 square
tests = {"inside": "POINT(1 1)", "on edge": "POINT(2 1)", "on corner": "POINT(2 2)",
         "outside": "POINT(3 1)", "line crossing": "LINESTRING(1 1, 3 1)", "neighbour square": "POLYGON((2 0, 4 0, 4 2, 2 2, 2 0))"}
rows = []  # one row per test geometry
for name, wkt in tests.items():  # evaluate every predicate in PostGIS
    r = q("""SELECT ST_Intersects(a, b) AS intersects, ST_Contains(a, b) AS contains, ST_Covers(a, b) AS covers,
                ST_Touches(a, b) AS touches, ST_Crosses(a, b) AS crosses, ST_Relate(a, b) AS de9im
         FROM (SELECT ST_GeomFromText(%s) AS a, ST_GeomFromText(%s) AS b) t""", (square, wkt))
    rows.append({"B": name, **r.iloc[0].to_dict()})  # store
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("B")  # truth table (A = the square)

A point on the edge intersects and is covered by the square, but the square does not contain it, because containment requires the interiors to meet. With real data this decides whether a Superfund site recorded exactly on a county line belongs to a county at all. ST_Intersects (or ST_Covers) assigns it; ST_Contains drops it. When polygons share boundaries, as counties do, ST_Intersects may assign a boundary point to two polygons, so check for duplicates.

Point-in-polygon joins
A spatial join is an ordinary JOIN with a spatial predicate in the ON clause. PostGIS first uses the GiST index to find county boxes that contain each point, then runs the exact test. Counting sites per county and attaching county attributes is then plain SQL:

title: Spatial relationships and joins
text:
Distance joins with ST_DWithin
ST_DWithin(A, B, d) is the index-friendly way to ask “within distance d”. It is equivalent to ST_Distance(A, B) <= d but much faster, because PostGIS expands the bounding boxes by d and uses the index before measuring. Cast to geography for a distance in metres; the index must then be built on the same geography expression. Which PM2.5 monitors are within 10 km of an active Superfund site?


Code
pg.execute("CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS superfund_geog_gix ON superfund USING GIST ((geom::geography))")  # index
pg.execute("CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS pm25_geog_gix ON pm25 USING GIST ((geom::geography))")  # on the cast
pg.execute("ANALYZE superfund; ANALYZE pm25")  # statistics for the planner

t0 = time.perf_counter()  # index-assisted distance join
near = q("""
SELECT m.site_id, m.name, m.state, m.pm25_2024, count(s.epa_id) AS superfund_within_10km
FROM pm25 m JOIN superfund s
  ON ST_DWithin(m.geom::geography, s.geom::geography, 10000) AND s.status = 'NPL Site'
GROUP BY m.site_id, m.name, m.state, m.pm25_2024 ORDER BY superfund_within_10km DESC
""")
t_dw = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # the same test written with ST_Distance (no index)
slow = q("""SELECT count(*) AS n FROM pm25 m JOIN superfund s
ON ST_Distance(m.geom::geography, s.geom::geography) <= 10000 AND s.status = 'NPL Site'""")
t_d = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"ST_DWithin: {t_dw:.2f} s, {near.superfund_within_10km.sum():,} pairs | ST_Distance <= d: {t_d:.2f} s, "
      f"{slow.n.iloc[0]:,} pairs")

title: Spatial relationships and joins
text:
Polygon overlay joins
Overlay joins combine two polygon layers and measure the shared area with ST_Intersection. Here we ask what share of each New Jersey county lies within 3 km of an active Superfund site. The 3 km buffers are merged with ST_Union first, so overlapping buffers are not counted twice; the buffers and areas are computed in the New Jersey State Plane projection (EPSG:3424, US feet), converted to km².


Code
overlay = q("""
WITH zone AS (                                   -- one merged polygon: land within 3 km of an active site
    SELECT ST_Union(ST_Buffer(ST_Transform(geom, 3424), 3000 / 0.3048006)) AS g
    FROM superfund WHERE state = 'NJ' AND status = 'NPL Site'
), nj AS (
    SELECT fips, name, ST_Transform(geom, 3424) AS g FROM counties WHERE statefp = '34'
)
SELECT nj.fips, nj.name,
       ST_Area(nj.g) * 0.3048006 ^ 2 / 1e6                              AS county_km2,
       ST_Area(ST_Intersection(nj.g, zone.g)) * 0.3048006 ^ 2 / 1e6     AS within_3km_km2,
       ST_Transform(nj.g, 4326) AS geom
FROM nj CROSS JOIN zone
""")
overlay["share_pct"] = (100 * overlay.within_3km_km2 / overlay.county_km2).round(1)  # share of county area
overlay = overlay.merge(svi[["fips", "RPL_THEMES"]], on="fips")  # add SVI
zone = q("""SELECT ST_Transform(ST_Union(ST_Buffer(ST_Transform(geom, 3424), 3000 / 0.3048006)), 4326) AS geom
FROM superfund WHERE state = 'NJ' AND status = 'NPL Site'""")  # the zone itself, for the map
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 8))  # map
overlay.plot("share_pct", ax=ax, cmap="Oranges", legend=True, edgecolor="0.4", lw=0.5,
             legend_kwds={"label": "% of county area within 3 km of an active NPL site", "shrink": 0.6})
zone.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=0.5)  # outline of the 3 km zone
ax.set_title("New Jersey: land within 3 km of active Superfund sites"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.show()
overlay.drop(columns="geom").sort_values("share_pct", ascending=False).head(6).round(2)
