title: Spatial relationships and joins
text:
Neighbour joins with ST_Touches
Joining a table to itself with ST_Touches lists neighbouring polygons. That is the first step of spatial statistics: a spatial weights matrix, and the spatial lag (the average of a variable over a unit’s neighbours). Notebook 06_03_04 computes Moran’s I from these neighbour lists.


Code
lag = q("""
SELECT a.fips, a.name, a.statefp, h.adult_obesity_pct AS obesity,
       avg(hn.adult_obesity_pct) AS neighbour_mean_obesity, count(*) AS n_neighbours
FROM counties a
JOIN counties b ON ST_Touches(a.geom, b.geom)              -- queen contiguity (shared edge or vertex)
JOIN chr24 h  ON h.fips = a.fips
JOIN chr24 hn ON hn.fips = b.fips
WHERE a.statefp NOT IN ('02', '15', '72')
GROUP BY a.fips, a.name, a.statefp, h.adult_obesity_pct
""")
r = lag[["obesity", "neighbour_mean_obesity"]].corr().iloc[0, 1]  # correlation (pairs with missing values dropped)
print(f"{len(lag):,} counties, median {lag.n_neighbours.median():.0f} neighbours; "
      f"correlation of obesity with the neighbour mean: r = {r:.2f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5))  # scatter plot
ax.scatter(lag.obesity, lag.neighbour_mean_obesity, s=3, alpha=0.4)  # each county
ax.set(xlabel="adult obesity (%), county", ylabel="mean of neighbouring counties (%)",
       title="Obesity is spatially clustered (CHR 2024)"); plt.show()


3,106 counties, median 6 neighbours; correlation of obesity with the neighbour mean: r = 0.77









A county’s adult obesity rate is strongly correlated with the average of its neighbours, a sign of positive spatial autocorrelation. ST_Touches treats counties that meet at a single corner as neighbours (queen contiguity); requiring a shared edge (rook contiguity) needs ST_Relate(a.geom, b.geom, 'F***1****').

title: Spatial relationships and joins
text:
Nearest-neighbour search with <->
“Which PM2.5 monitor is closest to each Superfund site?” cannot be answered with a fixed distance, because the nearest monitor may be 1 km or 300 km away. The KNN operator <-> returns the distance between two geometries and, in an ORDER BY with a LIMIT, makes PostgreSQL walk the GiST index outward from the query point, stopping after k results. A LATERAL join runs that search once per row of the outer table.
On geometry in EPSG:4326, <-> orders by planar distance in degrees, which can pick the wrong neighbour away from the equator. On geography it orders by distance on the sphere, which is what we want. We index the geography expression and search with it:


Code
pg.execute("CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS pm25_geog_gix ON pm25 USING GIST ((geom::geography))")  # geography index
pg.execute("ANALYZE pm25")  # statistics

knn_sql = """
SELECT s.epa_id, s.name, s.state, n.site_id AS nearest_monitor, n.pm25_2024, n.dist_m, s.geom
FROM superfund s
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT m.site_id, m.pm25_2024, ST_Distance(m.geom::geography, s.geom::geography) AS dist_m
    FROM pm25 m
    ORDER BY m.geom::geography <-> s.geom::geography     -- KNN: index-ordered by distance
    LIMIT 1
) n
"""
t0 = time.perf_counter(); knn = q(knn_sql); t_knn = time.perf_counter() - t0  # KNN
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # brute force: compute every distance, keep the minimum
brute = q("""SELECT DISTINCT ON (s.epa_id) s.epa_id, m.site_id AS nearest_monitor,
ST_Distance(m.geom::geography, s.geom::geography) AS dist_m
FROM superfund s CROSS JOIN pm25 m ORDER BY s.epa_id, dist_m""")
t_brute = time.perf_counter() - t0
pair = knn.set_index("epa_id").dist_m.to_frame("knn").join(brute.set_index("epa_id").dist_m.rename("brute"))  # align
same = np.isclose(pair.knn, pair.brute, atol=0.01).mean()  # share of sites with the same nearest distance
print(f"KNN <->: {t_knn:.2f} s | brute force over {len(sites) * len(pm):,} pairs: {t_brute:.2f} s | "
      f"same nearest distance for {same:.1%} of sites")


KNN <->: 0.06 s | brute force over 1,933,840 pairs: 4.07 s | same nearest distance for 99.8% of sites




Code
plan = pg.explain(knn_sql.replace("SELECT s.epa_id", "SELECT s.epa_id", 1) + " LIMIT 5")  # query plan
print("\n".join(l for l in plan.splitlines() if "Index" in l or "Limit" in l or "Nested" in l)[:600])


Limit  (cost=0.14..65.68 rows=5 width=101)
  ->  Nested Loop  (cost=0.14..24115.68 rows=1840 width=101)
        ->  Limit  (cost=0.14..13.03 rows=1 width=36)
              ->  Index Scan using pm25_geog_gix on pm25 m  (cost=0.14..13545.30 rows=1051 width=36)


The plan shows an Index Scan on the geography index inside the nested loop: for each site PostgreSQL reads only a few index entries, ordered by the <-> distance. Brute force computed all 1.9 million distances and found the same nearest monitor for 99.8% of the sites; the few differences are near-ties, because <-> on geography measures on a sphere while ST_Distance uses the spheroid. The KNN query was about 70 times faster, and the gap grows with the product of the two table sizes.


Code
km = knn.dist_m / 1000  # nearest-monitor distance in km
print(f"distance from a Superfund site to the nearest PM2.5 monitor: median {km.median():.1f} km, "
      f"90th percentile {km.quantile(0.9):.1f} km, max {km.max():.0f} km")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 2]})  # histogram + map
axes[0].hist(km.clip(upper=150), bins=50, color="#3182bd")  # distribution (clipped at 150 km)
axes[0].set(xlabel="km to nearest PM2.5 monitor (clipped at 150)", ylabel="Superfund sites")
k48 = knn.cx[-125:-66, 24:50].to_crs(5070)  # lower 48
k48.assign(km=k48.dist_m / 1000).plot("km", ax=axes[1], cmap="viridis_r", markersize=6, legend=True,
                                      vmax=100, legend_kwds={"label": "km to nearest monitor", "shrink": 0.7})
counties[~counties.statefp.isin(["02", "15", "72"])].dissolve("statefp").to_crs(5070).boundary.plot(
    ax=axes[1], color="0.8", lw=0.4)  # state outlines
axes[1].set_axis_off(); axes[1].set_title("Superfund sites coloured by distance to the nearest PM2.5 monitor")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


distance from a Superfund site to the nearest PM2.5 monitor: median 15.2 km, 90th percentile 58.1 km, max 6106 km









Half of the Superfund sites have a PM2.5 monitor within 15 km, and 90% within 58 km, but sites in the rural Mountain West and Great Plains are often far from any monitor (the maximum, about 6,100 km, is a site on Guam, which has no monitor in the Atlas data). Monitor values far from a site say little about the air at the site.
<-> also supports k > 1 and a distance cap. geolatticedb.nearest writes the LATERAL query for us. Its ranking uses <-> on the stored geometries, so we store both tables in a projected SRID (EPSG:5070, metres) to rank by true distance. title: Spatial relationships and joins
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

Spatial predicates are patterns on the DE-9IM matrix; they differ only at boundaries. ST_Intersects/ST_Covers keep boundary points, ST_Contains/ST_Within drop them, and shared boundaries can match twice.
A spatial join is a JOIN ... ON <predicate>; the GiST index filters candidates and the predicate refines them. LEFT JOIN keeps polygons with no matches.
ST_DWithin (on geography for metres) uses the index and is much faster than ST_Distance(...) <= d.
Overlay joins use ST_Intersection and ST_Area; merge buffers with ST_Union to avoid double counting.
Self-joins with ST_Touches give neighbour lists and spatial lags.
ORDER BY a <-> b LIMIT k in a LATERAL join finds k nearest neighbours through the index; use geography (or a projected SRID) so “nearest” means nearest in metres.

Functions used: ST_Intersects, ST_Contains, ST_Covers, ST_Touches, ST_Crosses, ST_Relate, ST_DWithin, ST_Distance, ST_Buffer, ST_Union, ST_Intersection, ST_Area, <->, LATERAL; pdb.connect, con.load, con.query, con.explain, con.nearest (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

Rewrite the point-in-polygon join with ST_Contains and with ST_Covers. How many sites does each version match?
Repeat the 3 km overlay for California with EPSG:3310 (California Albers). Which county has the largest share?
Build rook (shared edge) neighbour lists with ST_Relate(a.geom, b.geom, 'F***1****'). How many fewer neighbour pairs are there than with queen contiguity?
Find, for every county, the distance from its centroid to the nearest active Superfund site, and map it.
Compare ORDER BY m.geom <-> s.geom (EPSG:4326 degrees) with the geography version. For how many sites does the nearest monitor change?

import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import io  # in-memory buffers
import re  # read numbers from query plans
import time  # timing
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import shapely  # geometry
import psycopg  # PostgreSQL driver
import duckdb  # DuckDB
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

from geolattice import geolatticedb as pdb  # GeoLattice spatial database tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution




Code
import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_02_05"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

# PostGIS connection string (see 06_01_02 for the Docker container); override with GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN
PG_DSN = os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN", "postgresql://postgres:geolattice@localhost:5432/geolattice")
print("Repository:", ROOT)  # where the data are read from


Repository: /home/zia207/Github/GeoLattice




Code
conn = psycopg.connect(PG_DSN, autocommit=True)  # psycopg for timing and plans
pg = pdb.connect("postgis", dsn=PG_DSN)  # geolatticedb for loading and GeoDataFrame results

def sql(q, params=None):  # run SQL, return a DataFrame when rows come back
    cur = conn.execute(q, params)
    return pd.DataFrame(cur.fetchall(), columns=[d.name for d in cur.description]) if cur.description else None

def timed(q, n=3):  # median wall time of a query (after one warm-up run)
    conn.execute(q).fetchall()  # warm-up: loads pages into the cache
    ts = []
    for _ in range(n):
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); conn.execute(q).fetchall(); ts.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return float(np.median(ts))

def plan(q):  # EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) as text
    return "\n".join(r[0] for r in conn.execute(f"EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF) {q}").fetchall())

taxi_glob = str(DATA / "nyc-taxi-tiny" / "year=*" / "month=*" / "part-0.parquet")  # partitioned Parquet files

GiST, SP-GiST and BRIN indexes









Index
Structure
Good for
Size




GiST
balanced R-tree of bounding boxes
all geometry types, overlapping boxes, KNN (<->)
large


SP-GiST
space-partitioning tree (quadtree / k-d tree)
points and non-overlapping data
medium


BRIN
one bounding box per range of table blocks (default 128 pages)
very large tables already ordered in space or time
tiny



We build each on the 1.16 million pickups (one at a time, so the planner can only use that one) and time a typical query: the pickups inside a 1 km box around Times Square.


Code
box_q = """SELECT count(*) FROM taxi
WHERE geom && ST_MakeEnvelope(-73.9915, 40.7535, -73.9795, 40.7625, 4326)"""  # about 1 km x 1 km
sql("SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0")  # single process: clearer, comparable timings

for name, ddl in [("GiST", "USING GIST (geom)"), ("SP-GiST", "USING SPGIST (geom)"), ("BRIN", "USING BRIN (geom)")]:
    sql("DROP INDEX IF EXISTS taxi_geom_idx")  # only one index at a time
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); sql(f"CREATE INDEX taxi_geom_idx ON taxi {ddl}"); build = time.perf_counter() - t0
    size = float(sql("SELECT pg_relation_size('taxi_geom_idx') / 1e6 AS mb").mb.iloc[0])  # index size
    rows.append({"index": name, "build s": build, "size MB": size, "query ms": timed(box_q) * 1000})
n_box = sql(box_q).iloc[0, 0]  # how many pickups are in the box
idx = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("index").round(2)  # compare

SP-GiST is often recommended for points, but on this dataset it was larger, slower to build and about half as fast to query as GiST, so measure both on your own data. title: Indexing and performance
section: Reading query plans with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
text:
Reading query plans with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimizer chose; EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and reports the actual time and rows of each step; BUFFERS adds how many 8 kB pages were read from the cache (shared hit) or from disk (read). The most common nodes:







Node
Meaning




Seq Scan
reads every row of the table


Index Scan
walks the index and fetches matching rows one by one


Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan
collects matching row locations from the index, then reads the pages in physical order; Recheck Cond runs the exact test, because the index only compares boxes


Nested Loop
for each row of the outer input, probes the inner input (with an index: fast)


Hash Join, Merge Join
equality joins; not usable for spatial predicates


Aggregate, HashAggregate
count, sum, GROUP BY



With the GiST index back in place, the plan of the box query is:


Code
sql("DROP INDEX IF EXISTS taxi_geom_idx"); sql("CREATE INDEX taxi_geom_idx ON taxi USING GIST (geom)"); sql("ANALYZE taxi")
print(plan(box_q))


Aggregate (actual time=18.347..18.348 rows=1.00 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=11870 read=368
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on taxi (actual time=5.794..16.422 rows=66763.00 loops=1)
        Recheck Cond: (geom && '0103000020E61000000100000005000000FA7E6ABC747F52C09CC420B072604440FA7E6ABC747F52C09A99999999614440A69BC420B07E52C09A99999999614440A69BC420B07E52C09CC420B072604440FA7E6ABC747F52C09CC420B072604440'::geometry)
        Heap Blocks: exact=11870
        Buffers: shared hit=11870 read=368
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on taxi_geom_idx (actual time=4.630..4.630 rows=66763.00 loops=1)
              Index Cond: (geom && '0103000020E61000000100000005000000FA7E6ABC747F52C09CC420B072604440FA7E6ABC747F52C09A99999999614440A69BC420B07E52C09A99999999614440A69BC420B07E52C09CC420B072604440FA7E6ABC747F52C09CC420B072604440'::geometry)

The plan reads from the bottom up. The Bitmap Index Scan on taxi_geom_idx found the matching row locations, and the Bitmap Heap Scan read only the pages that hold them. Buffers: shared hit=... counts the pages read, much less than the table’s size. The planner estimates row counts from statistics collected by ANALYZE; comparing the estimated rows= (shown without COSTS OFF) with the actual rows is the first check when a plan looks wrong.
Now a spatial join, pickups per hexagon. The plan shows a Nested Loop: for each hexagon, an index scan finds the pickups inside it.

title: Indexing and performance
text:
ST_Subdivide for large polygons
An index finds candidate polygons by their bounding box, then the exact test runs against the whole polygon. For countries with tens of thousands of vertices each point-in-polygon test is expensive, and the boxes are huge: the box of Canada or Russia contains a lot of ocean and other countries, so many candidates fail the exact test. ST_Subdivide(geom, max_vertices) splits each polygon into pieces with at most max_vertices vertices. The pieces have small boxes and cheap tests, and the join gives the same answer. We join Natural Earth 1:10m countries with two point sets: the 7,342 populated places, and 500,000 random test points spread over the globe (synthetic, with a fixed seed), which stand for a large global table such as geocoded records or sensor readings.


Code
NE = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvkelso/natural-earth-vector/master/geojson"  # Natural Earth on GitHub
countries = gpd.read_file(fetch("ne_10m_admin_0_countries.geojson", base=NE, folder="natural_earth"))[
    ["ADMIN", "ISO_A3", "geometry"]]  # detailed countries
places = gpd.read_file(fetch("ne_10m_populated_places_simple.geojson", base=NE, folder="natural_earth"))[
    ["name", "pop_max", "geometry"]]  # 7,342 populated places
pg.load(countries, "ne10_countries"); pg.load(places, "ne10_places")  # load and index
sql("""SELECT setseed(0.42); DROP TABLE IF EXISTS random_pts;
CREATE TABLE random_pts AS SELECT ST_SetSRID(ST_MakePoint(random() * 360 - 180, random() * 150 - 60), 4326) AS geom
FROM generate_series(1, 500000);                               -- 500,000 random points, 60°S to 90°N
CREATE INDEX ON random_pts USING GIST (geom); ANALYZE random_pts""")
print(sql("SELECT count(*) AS countries, sum(ST_NPoints(geom)) AS vertices, max(ST_NPoints(geom)) AS max_vertices "
          "FROM ne10_countries").to_dict("records"))
rows = []  # one row per variant
for maxv in [None, 1024, 256, 64]:  # no subdivision, then smaller and smaller pieces
    if maxv:
        sql(f"""DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ne10_sub; CREATE TABLE ne10_sub AS
               SELECT "ADMIN", ST_Subdivide(geom, {maxv}) AS geom FROM ne10_countries;
               CREATE INDEX ON ne10_sub USING GIST (geom); ANALYZE ne10_sub""")  # subdivided copy
    tbl = "ne10_sub" if maxv else "ne10_countries"
    row = {"max vertices": maxv or "not subdivided", "pieces": sql(f"SELECT count(*) FROM {tbl}").iloc[0, 0]}
    for pts_tbl, label in [("ne10_places", "places"), ("random_pts", "random points")]:  # both point sets
        q_ = f"SELECT count(*) AS n FROM {tbl} c JOIN {pts_tbl} p ON ST_Intersects(c.geom, p.geom)"
        row[f"{label}: join s"] = timed(q_, n=1); row[f"{label}: matched"] = int(sql(q_).n.iloc[0])
    rows.append(row)

Every variant matches exactly the same points. For the 7,342 populated places, subdivision gains little: most places are cities inside their country’s bounding box, and PostGIS caches the prepared (pre-indexed) polygon while it tests many points against the same country. For the 500,000 points spread over the globe, many fall inside the bounding box of a large country without being in it, and subdividing to 1,024 or 256 vertices makes the join 9 to 13 times faster (from 4.7 s to 0.5 and 0.4 s). Cutting further, to 64 vertices, made the join slower than no subdivision at all (11.6 s): 21,043 pieces mean many more index entries and candidate pairs, which outweighs the cheaper tests. A few hundred vertices per piece is a good starting point. Keep the subdivided table next to the original (with the country key) for joins, and use the original for display and area calculations.

title: Indexing and performance
text:
CLUSTER and physical order
The table was loaded in time order, so the 66,763 pickups in the Times Square box are spread over almost every page of the table. CLUSTER table USING index rewrites the table in the order of an index, and pickups that are close in space then share pages. Another way is to load the rows sorted by a space-filling curve such as ST_GeoHash(geom). We measure both layouts with a GiST index and with a BRIN index (with 16 pages per block range instead of the default 128, so each range covers a smaller area):


Code
def pages(q):  # pages read by a query: shared hit + read of the top plan node
    m = re.search(r"Buffers: shared(?: hit=(\d+))?(?: read=(\d+))?", plan(q))
    return int(m.group(1) or 0) + int(m.group(2) or 0)

def measure(table):  # pages and time of the box query with a GiST index, then with a BRIN index
    q_ = box_q.replace("FROM taxi", f"FROM {table}")
    out = {}
    for kind, ddl in [("GiST", "USING GIST (geom)"), ("BRIN", "USING BRIN (geom) WITH (pages_per_range = 16)")]:
        sql(f"DROP INDEX IF EXISTS {table}_m_idx"); sql(f"CREATE INDEX {table}_m_idx ON {table} {ddl}"); sql(f"ANALYZE {table}")
        out[f"pages read ({kind})"] = pages(q_); out[f"query ms ({kind})"] = timed(q_) * 1000
        if kind == "BRIN":
            out["BRIN size kB"] = sql(f"SELECT pg_relation_size('{table}_m_idx') / 1e3 AS kb").kb.iloc[0]
        sql(f"DROP INDEX {table}_m_idx")
    return out

layouts = {"time order (as loaded)": measure("taxi")}  # 1) as loaded
sql("DROP INDEX IF EXISTS taxi_geom_idx"); sql("CREATE INDEX taxi_geom_idx ON taxi USING GIST (geom)")
t0 = time.perf_counter(); sql("CLUSTER taxi USING taxi_geom_idx"); t_cluster = time.perf_counter() - t0  # 2) CLUSTER
sql("DROP INDEX taxi_geom_idx"); layouts["CLUSTER on GiST"] = measure("taxi")
sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS taxi_geohash")  # 3) a copy sorted by GeoHash
sql("CREATE TABLE taxi_geohash AS SELECT * FROM taxi ORDER BY ST_GeoHash(geom)"); layouts["sorted by ST_GeoHash"] = measure("taxi_geohash")
sql("CREATE INDEX taxi_geom_idx ON taxi USING GIST (geom)"); sql("ANALYZE taxi")  # keep a GiST index on taxi
print(f"CLUSTER took {t_cluster:.1f} s")
pd.DataFrame(layouts).astype(float).round(1)  # compare the three layouts

In time order the GiST query reads more than 12,000 pages to collect the 66,763 matching rows, and BRIN cannot help: every block range holds pickups from all over the city, so its bounding box overlaps the query box and almost every page is read. Clustering on the GiST index cuts the pages read by the GiST query tenfold (to 1,235) and its time from 21 to 8 ms. The R-tree order still mixes distant areas within some block ranges, so BRIN improves only partly. Sorting by GeoHash, a space-filling curve, keeps each block range compact: BRIN then reads about 1,100 pages and answers in 21 ms, as fast as GiST did on the time-ordered table, with an index of 49 kB instead of 48 MB. That makes BRIN attractive for very large, append-only tables that can be loaded in spatial order. CLUSTER is a one-time rewrite (it takes an exclusive lock and new rows are not kept in order), so it suits tables that are loaded in batches.

title: Indexing and performance
text:
Table partitioning
A partitioned table is split into child tables by a key, here one partition per year of pickup_time. Queries that filter on the key skip the other partitions (partition pruning), each partition has its own smaller indexes, and old years can be detached or dropped in a moment instead of deleted row by row. Partitioning by time is common for monitoring data, sensor streams and trajectories (see notebook 06_03_03); partitioning by region (list of states) suits national datasets.


Code
sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS taxi_part CASCADE")
sql("""CREATE TABLE taxi_part (id bigint, pickup_time timestamp NOT NULL, passengers smallint, fare real,
                                 geom geometry(Point, 4326)) PARTITION BY RANGE (pickup_time)""")
for y in range(2009, 2016):  # one partition per year
    sql(f"CREATE TABLE taxi_{y} PARTITION OF taxi_part FOR VALUES FROM ('{y}-01-01') TO ('{y + 1}-01-01')")
t0 = time.perf_counter()
sql("INSERT INTO taxi_part SELECT * FROM taxi")  # rows are routed to their partition
sql("CREATE INDEX ON taxi_part USING GIST (geom)"); sql("ANALYZE taxi_part")  # creates one index per partition
print(f"partitioned copy built in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
print(sql("""SELECT c.relname AS partition, c.reltuples::bigint AS rows FROM pg_inherits i
JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.inhrelid WHERE i.inhparent = 'taxi_part'::regclass ORDER BY 1""").T.to_string(header=False))
q_year = box_q.replace("FROM taxi", "FROM taxi_part") + " AND pickup_time >= '2013-01-01' AND pickup_time < '2014-01-01'"
p = plan(q_year)
print("\n".join(l for l in p.splitlines() if "taxi_" in l or "Append" in l))  # which partitions were scanned


partitioned copy built in 2.9 s
partition  taxi_2009  taxi_2010  taxi_2011  taxi_2012  taxi_2013  taxi_2014  taxi_2015
rows          168468     165137     172471     174253     169887     161728     143743
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on taxi_2013 taxi_part (actual time=0.616..1.327 rows=9634.00 loops=1)
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on taxi_2013_geom_idx (actual time=0.595..0.595 rows=9634.00 loops=1)


The plan scans only taxi_2013: the other six partitions were pruned before execution because their ranges cannot contain 2013 pickups. Retiring the oldest year is a metadata change, ALTER TABLE taxi_part DETACH PARTITION taxi_2009, instead of a DELETE of 168,000 rows followed by a VACUUM.

title: Indexing and performance
text:
VACUUM and ANALYZE
PostgreSQL never overwrites a row in place: UPDATE and DELETE leave the old version as a dead tuple until VACUUM marks its space reusable (VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and returns the space to the operating system). ANALYZE refreshes the statistics the planner uses to estimate row counts. The autovacuum daemon runs both automatically, but after a large load or delete it is worth running them by hand. We delete the 2009 and 2010 pickups from the unpartitioned table:


Code
sql("ALTER TABLE taxi SET (autovacuum_enabled = false)")  # keep autovacuum out of the experiment
def state():  # dead rows, size and the planner's estimate for a 2009 query
    st = sql("SELECT n_live_tup AS live, n_dead_tup AS dead, pg_size_pretty(pg_table_size('taxi')) AS size "
             "FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'taxi'").iloc[0].to_dict()
    est = conn.execute("EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM taxi WHERE pickup_time < '2011-01-01'").fetchone()[0]
    st["planner estimate, rows before 2011"] = int(re.search(r"rows=(\d+)", est).group(1))
    return st
steps = {"loaded": state()}
sql("DELETE FROM taxi WHERE pickup_time < '2011-01-01'"); time.sleep(0.5)  # delete two years
steps["after DELETE"] = state()
sql("ANALYZE taxi"); steps["after ANALYZE"] = state()
sql("VACUUM taxi"); steps["after VACUUM"] = state()
sql("VACUUM FULL taxi"); sql("ANALYZE taxi"); steps["after VACUUM FULL"] = state()
sql("ALTER TABLE taxi RESET (autovacuum_enabled)")  # back to normal

After the DELETE the statistics still describe the old table, so the planner expects hundreds of thousands of 2009-2010 rows that no longer exist; wrong estimates like this lead to wrong plans. ANALYZE fixes the estimate. VACUUM clears the dead tuples so their space can be reused, but the file keeps its size; only VACUUM FULL (which locks the table) shrinks it.

title: Indexing and performance
section: Benchmark: PostGIS vs. GeoPandas vs. DuckDB
text:
Benchmark: PostGIS vs. GeoPandas vs. DuckDB
The same job, counting 2011-2015 pickups (all rows remaining in taxi) per 400 m hexagon, in three engines:

PostGIS: data in tables with GiST indexes; the query runs on the server.
GeoPandas: data in memory as GeoDataFrames; sjoin builds an STRtree on the fly.
DuckDB spatial: in-process, columnar and multi-threaded; its spatial join operator builds a temporary R-tree.

We time the join itself and, separately, getting the data into each engine.


Code
pts = taxi[taxi.pickup_time >= "2011-01-01"]  # the rows left in the PostGIS table
hexes = pg.query("SELECT hex_id, geom FROM hex")  # hexagons as a GeoDataFrame
res, times = {}, {}  # results and timings

sql("RESET max_parallel_workers_per_gather")  # let PostGIS use parallel workers, as in normal operation
pg_q = "SELECT h.hex_id, count(*) AS n FROM hex h JOIN taxi t ON ST_Intersects(h.geom, t.geom) GROUP BY h.hex_id"
times["PostGIS"] = {"load s": np.nan, "join s": timed(pg_q, n=1)}  # data already loaded and indexed
res["PostGIS"] = sql(pg_q).set_index("hex_id").n

t0 = time.perf_counter()
gpts = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(pts.lon, pts.lat), crs=4326)  # points in memory
t_load = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
res["GeoPandas"] = gpd.sjoin(gpts, hexes, predicate="intersects").groupby("hex_id").size()  # STRtree join
times["GeoPandas"] = {"load s": t_load, "join s": time.perf_counter() - t0}

ddb = duckdb.connect(); ddb.load_extension("spatial")  # DuckDB in memory
t0 = time.perf_counter()
ddb.register("pts_df", pts[["lon", "lat"]])  # zero-copy view of the pandas columns
ddb.execute("CREATE TABLE pts AS SELECT ST_Point(lon, lat) AS geom FROM pts_df")  # point geometries
hex_df = pd.DataFrame({"hex_id": hexes.hex_id, "wkb": shapely.to_wkb(hexes.geometry.values)})  # hexagons as WKB
ddb.register("hexes_df", hex_df)
ddb.execute("CREATE TABLE hex AS SELECT hex_id, ST_GeomFromWKB(wkb) AS geom FROM hexes_df")
t_load = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
res["DuckDB"] = ddb.sql("SELECT h.hex_id, count(*) AS n FROM hex h JOIN pts p ON ST_Intersects(h.geom, p.geom) "
                        "GROUP BY h.hex_id").df().set_index("hex_id").n  # spatial join
times["DuckDB"] = {"load s": t_load, "join s": time.perf_counter() - t0}

agree = pd.DataFrame(res).fillna(0)  # pickups per hexagon from each engine
print("identical counts in all engines:", bool((agree.nunique(axis=1) == 1).all()), f"({int(agree.PostGIS.sum()):,} pickups)")
bench = pd.DataFrame(times).T.round(2); bench

ax.set_xlabel("seconds (join only)"); ax.set_title(f"{len(pts):,} points x {len(hexes):,} hexagons")

All three engines produce identical counts, and at this size all finish the join in well under a second. GeoPandas was fastest once the points were in memory (0.3 s), and DuckDB and PostGIS took about 0.6 s each; the differences are small next to the time it takes to get data into each engine and change with data size, hardware and parallel settings. Choose by setting rather than by these seconds: DuckDB for large files and one analyst, because it reads Parquet directly and works out of core (notebook 06_03_05); GeoPandas for small and medium data already in Python; PostGIS for shared, updated data and for queries that reuse its indexes, while serving other users at the same time.

title: Indexing and performance
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

GiST indexes any geometry and supports KNN; SP-GiST is an alternative for points (here it lost to GiST); BRIN is tiny but works only when rows are stored in spatial order, e.g. sorted by ST_GeoHash.
Read plans from the bottom up; check scan types, estimated vs. actual rows and buffers. Index use needs index-friendly predicates (&&, ST_Intersects, ST_DWithin).
ST_Subdivide speeds up joins of many scattered points against large polygons without changing the result.
CLUSTER cuts the pages read by index scans; loading in ST_GeoHash order makes BRIN as fast as GiST.
Partitioning by time prunes partitions in queries and makes deleting old data instant.
After large loads and deletes, run ANALYZE (statistics) and VACUUM (dead tuples); only VACUUM FULL shrinks the file.
PostGIS, GeoPandas and DuckDB gave identical spatial join results in under a second each; choose by setting (shared data, files, Python workflow), not by small timing differences.

Functions and commands used: CREATE INDEX ... USING GIST/SPGIST/BRIN, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), ST_MakeEnvelope, &&, ST_HexagonGrid, ST_Subdivide, CLUSTER, PARTITION BY RANGE, VACUUM, VACUUM FULL, ANALYZE, pg_relation_size, pg_stat_user_tables; pdb.connect, con.load, con.query (geolattice.geolatticedb); geopandas.sjoin; DuckDB ST_Intersects.
Exercises

Repeat the index comparison for a query box 10 km wide. Does the ranking of GiST and SP-GiST change? When does the planner prefer a sequential scan?
Load the pickups sorted by ST_GeoHash(geom) instead of using CLUSTER, and compare BRIN query times.
Try ST_Subdivide with 16 and 4096 vertices. Where is the optimum for this dataset?
Partition taxi_part by borough (PARTITION BY LIST) instead of year. Which queries benefit?
Run the benchmark with only 100,000 points. Does the ranking of the three engines change?

title: Network analysis with pgRouting
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 2 (core plus spatial analysis): pip install "geolattice[analysis]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning)

import time  # timing
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import networkx as nx  # graph algorithms in Python (to check pgRouting)
import osmnx as ox  # OpenStreetMap networks
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

from geolattice import geolatticedb as pdb  # GeoLattice spatial database tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution




Code
import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_03_02"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

# PostGIS connection string (see 06_01_02 for the Docker container); override with GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN

pg.execute("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgrouting")  # routing functions

def to_edges_table(G, table, cost="travel_time"):  # OSMnx graph -> pgRouting edges + vertices tables
    """Write a directed OSMnx graph as `table` (id, source, target, cost, reverse_cost, geom) and `table`_vertices."""
    nodes, edges = ox.convert.graph_to_gdfs(G)  # nodes (osmid) and edges (u, v, key)
    e = edges.reset_index()[["u", "v", "highway", "length", "speed_kph", cost, "geometry"]].copy()
    e["highway"] = e["highway"].astype(str)  # lists of road types -> text
    e = e.rename(columns={"u": "source", "v": "target", cost: "cost"})  # pgRouting column names
    e["reverse_cost"] = -1.0  # OSMnx lists each direction as its own edge, so block the reverse
    e.insert(0, "id", np.arange(1, len(e) + 1))  # edge id
    pg.load(gpd.GeoDataFrame(e, geometry="geometry", crs=edges.crs), table)  # edges table
    v = nodes.reset_index()[["osmid", "geometry"]].rename(columns={"osmid": "id"})  # vertices table
    pg.load(gpd.GeoDataFrame(v, geometry="geometry", crs=nodes.crs), f"{table}_vertices")
    pg.execute(f"CREATE INDEX ON {table} (source); CREATE INDEX ON {table} (target); ANALYZE {table}")
    return len(e), len(v)

title: Network analysis with pgRouting
section: From OSM to a routable graph
text:
From OSM to a routable graph
OSM stores roads as ways (lists of node references) tagged with highway=*, oneway, maxspeed and so on. A routing graph needs edges that run between intersections, each with a source and target vertex and a cost. Two common tools do the conversion:

osm2pgrouting: a command-line tool that reads an .osm file and writes ways and ways_vertices_pgr tables directly (osm2pgrouting -f city.osm -c mapconfig.xml -d geolattice -U postgres).
OSMnx: downloads or reads OSM data in Python, simplifies the graph to intersections, and fills missing speeds; we then write its edges to PostGIS.

We use OSMnx on a real OSM extract of West Oakland, California. Missing maxspeed tags are filled with typical speeds per road type, and the travel time of each edge (seconds) becomes the routing cost:


Code
osm = fetch("West-Oakland.osm.bz2", base="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gboeing/osmnx/main/tests/input_data",
            folder="osm")  # real OSM XML (bz2)
G_osm = ox.graph_from_xml(osm, simplify=True)  # ways -> graph of intersections
G_osm = ox.routing.add_edge_speeds(G_osm, hwy_speeds={"residential": 40, "secondary": 50, "tertiary": 50,
                                                      "service": 20, "unclassified": 40}, fallback=30)  # km/h
G_osm = ox.routing.add_edge_travel_times(G_osm)  # seconds per edge
G_osm = ox.projection.project_graph(G_osm, to_crs=32610)  # UTM zone 10N (metres)
n_e, n_v = to_edges_table(G_osm, "oakland_edges")  # write to PostGIS
print(f"West Oakland: {n_v} vertices, {n_e} directed edges")
q("""SELECT highway, count(*) AS edges, round(sum(length)) AS metres, round(avg(speed_kph)) AS kph,
       round((sum(cost) / 60)::numeric, 1) AS minutes FROM oakland_edges GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 3 DESC""")

A routable graph must be connected: a vertex in a separate piece cannot be reached from the rest. pgr_connectedComponents (for undirected graphs) and pgr_strongComponents (for directed graphs, where one-way streets matter) label every vertex with its component:


Code
comp = q("""SELECT component, count(*) AS vertices FROM pgr_strongComponents(
    'SELECT id, source, target, cost, reverse_cost FROM oakland_edges') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC""")
print(f"{len(comp)} strongly connected components; the largest holds {comp.vertices.iloc[0]} of {n_v} vertices "
      "(the others are dead ends and one-way pieces cut off at the edge of the extract)")

SELECT d.seq, d.agg_cost, e.geom FROM pgr_dijkstra(
    'SELECT id, source, target, cost, reverse_cost FROM oakland_edges',
    (SELECT id FROM oakland_edges_vertices ORDER BY ST_X(geom) LIMIT 1),       -- westernmost vertex
    (SELECT id FROM oakland_edges_vertices ORDER BY ST_X(geom) DESC LIMIT 1),  -- easternmost vertex
    directed => true) d JOIN oakland_edges e ON e.id = d.edge
""")
ax = q("SELECT geom FROM oakland_edges").plot(color="0.7", lw=1, figsize=(7, 5))  # the network
route.plot(ax=ax, color="#d95f02", lw=3)  # the route
ax.set_title(f"West Oakland OSM network: west-east route, {route.agg_cost.max() / 60:.1f} min"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.show()

    G_real = ox.routing.add_edge_travel_times(ox.routing.add_edge_speeds(G_real))  # speeds and travel times
    G_real = ox.projection.project_graph(G_real)  # local UTM zone
    fac = ox.features_from_place(PLACE, tags={"amenity": ["hospital", "clinic"]})  # health facilities

title: Network analysis with pgRouting
section: Routable graphs from any line layer
text:
Routable graphs from any line layer
Street centerlines from a county or state GIS office have no topology: they are just lines. A graph is built by giving every line end a vertex, merging ends that coincide (within a tolerance), and writing the vertex ids into source and target. geolatticedb.network.prepare() does this (the same steps as pgRouting’s pgr_extractVertices). The Onondaga County centerlines have a speed limit (SPEED, mph) and a one-way flag, so the cost can be travel time:


Code
streets = gpd.read_file(GEOLATTICE_DATA / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "USA" / "Ononda_Street_PROJ.shp")[
    ["StreetName", "PostType", "SPEED", "OneWay", "geometry"]]  # NYS street centerlines (EPSG:5070)
pg.load(streets.explode(index_parts=False), "ono_edges")  # single LineStrings
vtab = pg.network.prepare("ono_edges", tolerance=0.5,  # merge ends within 0.5 m
                          cost='ST_Length(geom) / (greatest(coalesce("SPEED", 30), 15) * 0.44704)')  # seconds at the limit
print(q(f"SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ono_edges) AS edges, (SELECT count(*) FROM {vtab}) AS vertices"))
comp = q("""SELECT component, count(*) AS n FROM pgr_connectedComponents(
    'SELECT id, source, target, cost, reverse_cost FROM ono_edges') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC""")
print(f"{len(comp)} connected components; largest {comp.n.iloc[0]} vertices ({comp.n.iloc[0] / comp.n.sum():.0%})")


   edges  vertices
0    999       861
8 connected components; largest 839 vertices (97%)


This layer is a 999-segment extract, so it falls apart into several components where the extract cut through streets. Small components are normal along the edge of any extract; routes should start and end in the largest component, which is easy to enforce by keeping only its vertices when snapping points to the network. Gaps inside the network (lines that should meet but do not, or roads that cross at bridges without an intersection) are found the same way and fixed with a larger tolerance or with pgr_separateCrossing / pgr_separateTouching.

title: Network analysis with pgRouting
text:
Shortest paths: pgr_dijkstra
From here on we use the study region: 439 intersections and 1,416 directed road segments with speed limits (50 to 100 km/h), 20 towns, 101 census tracts and 5 hospitals, all in UTM zone 18N. Every pgRouting function takes an edges SQL string, so the cost can be changed (distance, time, a penalty for road types) without changing the table.


Code
NET = GEOLATTICE_DATA / "00_shared" / "data_spatial_net"  # study region data
G = ox.load_graphml(NET / "roads.graphml") if not DOWNLOAD_OSM else G_real  # road graph
G = ox.routing.add_edge_travel_times(ox.routing.add_edge_speeds(G))  # km/h and seconds per edge
n_e, n_v = to_edges_table(G, "roads")  # edges and vertices tables
hosp = gpd.read_file(NET / "hospitals.geojson") if not DOWNLOAD_OSM else fac.assign(
    hospital=fac.get("name", "facility"), beds=np.nan)[["hospital", "beds", "geometry"]]  # facilities
tracts = gpd.read_file(NET / "tracts.geojson")  # tracts with population
towns = gpd.read_file(NET / "towns.geojson")  # towns
pg.load(hosp, "hospitals"); pg.load(tracts, "tracts"); pg.load(towns, "towns")
for t in ["hospitals", "towns"]:  # snap each point to its nearest network vertex (KNN)
    pg.execute(f"ALTER TABLE {t} ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS vid bigint")
    pg.execute(f"UPDATE {t} p SET vid = (SELECT v.id FROM roads_vertices v ORDER BY v.geom <-> p.geom LIMIT 1)")
EDGES = "SELECT id, source, target, cost, reverse_cost FROM roads"  # the edges SQL used below
print(f"{n_v} vertices, {n_e} directed edges, {len(hosp)} hospitals, {len(tracts)} tracts")

Code
path = q(f"""
SELECT d.seq, d.node, d.edge, d.cost, d.agg_cost, e.highway, e.geom
FROM pgr_dijkstra('{EDGES}',
                  (SELECT vid FROM towns WHERE town = 'Southport'),
                  (SELECT vid FROM hospitals WHERE hospital = 'Lakeview Community Hospital'),
                  directed => true) d
JOIN roads e ON e.id = d.edge ORDER BY d.seq
""")
s_vid = q("SELECT vid FROM towns WHERE town = 'Southport'").vid.iloc[0]  # check with NetworkX
t_vid = q("SELECT vid FROM hospitals WHERE hospital = 'Lakeview Community Hospital'").vid.iloc[0]
nx_time = nx.shortest_path_length(G, s_vid, t_vid, weight="travel_time")
print(f"pgr_dijkstra: {path.agg_cost.iloc[-1] + path.cost.iloc[-1]:.1f} s over {len(path)} edges "
      f"({path.geometry.length.sum() / 1000:.1f} km) | NetworkX: {nx_time:.1f} s")
print((path.assign(km=path.length / 1000).groupby("highway").km.sum().round(1)).to_dict(), "km by road type")

title: Network analysis with pgRouting
text:
Travel-time matrices: pgr_dijkstraCost
pgr_dijkstraCost returns only the total cost between many origins and many destinations, which is the input of accessibility measures, location-allocation and gravity models. One call computes the matrix from all 20 towns to all 5 hospitals. Pairs whose origin and destination snap to the same vertex are left out of the result, so their travel time is set to 0:


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
od = q(f"""
SELECT t.town, h.hospital, round((c.agg_cost / 60)::numeric, 1) AS minutes
FROM pgr_dijkstraCost('{EDGES}', ARRAY(SELECT vid FROM towns), ARRAY(SELECT vid FROM hospitals), directed => true) c
JOIN towns t ON t.vid = c.start_vid JOIN hospitals h ON h.vid = c.end_vid
""")
print(f"{len(od)} origin-destination pairs in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")
mat = od.pivot(index="town", columns="hospital", values="minutes")  # matrix
same = q("SELECT t.town, h.hospital FROM towns t JOIN hospitals h ON h.vid = t.vid")  # town and hospital on one vertex
for r in same.itertuples():  # pgr_dijkstraCost omits pairs with start = end; their travel time is 0
    mat.loc[r.town, r.hospital] = 0.0
mat.assign(nearest=mat.idxmin(axis=1), min_minutes=mat.min(axis=1)).sort_values("min_minutes", ascending=False).head(6)

title: Network analysis with pgRouting
text:
Isochrones and service areas: pgr_drivingDistance
pgr_drivingDistance(edges, start, limit) returns every vertex reachable from start within a cost limit, with the cost to reach it. Wrapping the reached vertices in a hull gives an isochrone (here with ST_ConcaveHull). Starting from all hospitals at once with equicost => true assigns each vertex to the hospital it reaches first, which partitions the network into service areas (catchments).


Code
iso = q(f"""
WITH dd AS (
    SELECT d.agg_cost, v.geom FROM pgr_drivingDistance('{EDGES}',
        (SELECT vid FROM hospitals WHERE hospital = 'Centerville Medical Center'), 1200, directed => true) d
    JOIN roads_vertices v ON v.id = d.node)
SELECT m AS minutes, count(*) AS vertices, ST_ConcaveHull(ST_Collect(geom), 0.5) AS geom
FROM dd, unnest(ARRAY[5, 10, 15, 20]) AS m WHERE agg_cost <= m * 60 GROUP BY m ORDER BY m DESC
""")
ax = iso.plot(column="minutes", cmap="YlGnBu_r", alpha=0.6, edgecolor="k", lw=0.5, legend=True, categorical=True,
              figsize=(8, 8), legend_kwds={"title": "minutes", "loc": "lower left"})  # isochrones
q("SELECT geom FROM roads").plot(ax=ax, color="0.5", lw=0.3)  # roads
hosp[hosp.hospital == "Centerville Medical Center"].plot(ax=ax, color="red", marker="P", markersize=150)
ax.set_title("Drive-time isochrones from Centerville Medical Center"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.show()

title: Network analysis with pgRouting
section: Example: travel time to health facilities
text:
Example: travel time to health facilities
Travel time to the nearest hospital is a standard measure of geographic access to care. For every tract we snap the tract’s representative point to the nearest network vertex, compute the travel time to every hospital in one pgr_dijkstraCost call (hospitals as origins, travelling to the tracts), keep the minimum, and summarize by population. Ambulance and patient trips both matter; with one-way streets the direction is part of the definition.


Code
pg.execute("ALTER TABLE tracts ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS vid bigint")  # nearest vertex of each tract
pg.execute("UPDATE tracts t SET vid = (SELECT v.id FROM roads_vertices v ORDER BY v.geom <-> ST_PointOnSurface(t.geom) LIMIT 1)")
access = q(f"""
WITH c AS (
    SELECT end_vid, min(agg_cost) / 60 AS minutes FROM pgr_dijkstraCost('{EDGES}',
           ARRAY(SELECT vid FROM hospitals), ARRAY(SELECT DISTINCT vid FROM tracts), directed => true)
    GROUP BY end_vid)
SELECT t.tract_id, t.population, t.pct_over65, t.median_income,
       CASE WHEN t.vid IN (SELECT vid FROM hospitals) THEN 0 ELSE c.minutes END AS minutes,  -- same vertex: 0
       (SELECT min(ST_Distance(ST_PointOnSurface(t.geom), h.geom)) FROM hospitals h) / 1000 AS straight_km,
       t.geom
FROM tracts t LEFT JOIN c ON c.end_vid = t.vid
""")
access["over65"] = access.population * access.pct_over65 / 100  # residents aged 65+
w = access.population  # population weights
print(f"{len(access)} tracts, {int(w.sum()):,} residents")
print(f"population-weighted mean travel time: {np.average(access.minutes, weights=w):.1f} min; "
      f"residents beyond 15 min: {w[access.minutes > 15].sum() / w.sum():.1%}; "
      f"residents 65+ beyond 15 min: {access.over65[access.minutes > 15].sum() / access.over65.sum():.1%}")

            legend_kwds={"label": "minutes to the nearest hospital"})  # travel time by tract

title: Network analysis with pgRouting
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

A routable graph is an edges table (id, source, target, cost, reverse_cost) plus vertices; OSMnx or osm2pgrouting build it from OSM, and geolatticedb.network.prepare() from any line layer.
Check connectivity with pgr_connectedComponents / pgr_strongComponents, and route only within the main component.
pgr_dijkstra returns a path; its total time matched NetworkX exactly. pgr_dijkstraCost returns whole origin-destination matrices in one call.
pgr_drivingDistance gives reachable vertices for isochrones (with ST_ConcaveHull) and, with several starts and equicost, service areas.
Network travel time to the nearest hospital, weighted by population, is a practical access measure; it differs from straight-line distance where roads are indirect or slow.

Functions used: pgr_strongComponents, pgr_connectedComponents, pgr_dijkstra, pgr_dijkstraCost, pgr_drivingDistance, ST_ConcaveHull, <->; ox.graph_from_xml, ox.load_graphml, ox.routing.add_edge_speeds, ox.routing.add_edge_travel_times, ox.features_from_place; pdb.connect, con.load, con.network.prepare, con.network.shortest_path, con.network.isochrone (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

title: In-database spatial analytics
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 3 (core, spatial analysis and spatial statistics): pip install "geolattice[statistics]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README. It also uses esda, h3, which no GeoLattice option installs: pip install esda h3.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning)

import time  # timing
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import shapely  # geometry
import h3  # Uber H3 hexagonal index (h3-py)
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, KMeans  # reference implementations
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score  # compare two clusterings
import libpysal  # PySAL spatial weights
import esda  # PySAL exploratory spatial data analysis
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

from geolattice import geolatticedb as pdb  # GeoLattice spatial database tools
import geolattice.spatial_statistics as sstat  # GeoLattice spatial statistics (PySpatialStats port)

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution




Code
import os  # environment variables
import json  # JSON parsing
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

# The GeoLattice repository root: the first folder above this notebook that holds data/ and Tutorials/
HERE = Path.cwd()  # folder of this notebook
ROOT = next(p for p in [HERE, *HERE.parents] if (p / "Data").is_dir() and (p / "Tutorials").is_dir())
GEOLATTICE_DATA = ROOT / "Data"  # shared GeoLattice data folder
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "06_spatialDB"  # data folder of this module
OUT = DATA / "outputs" / "06_03_04"  # outputs written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# USA Health Data Atlas (https://zia207.github.io/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/): raw files on GitHub
ATLAS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zia207/USA-Health-Data-Atlas/main"

def fetch(rel, base=ATLAS, folder="atlas"):  # download helper
    """Download a file once (default: from the Atlas repository) and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / folder / rel  # local cache path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the cache folder
        print(f"Downloading {rel} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/{rel}", path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

def atlas_js(rel):  # read an Atlas data file
    """Atlas data files are JavaScript (`window.X = {...};`); return the JSON object inside."""
    text = fetch(rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")  # whole file as text
    return json.loads(text[text.index("=") + 1:].strip().rstrip(";"))  # strip the assignment and parse

def atlas_counties():  # county polygons of the Atlas
    """US county polygons (Census cartographic boundaries, EPSG:4326) with a 5-digit FIPS code."""
    g = gpd.read_file(fetch("assets/geojson_counties_fips.json"))  # GeoJSON from the Atlas
    g["fips"] = g["STATE"] + g["COUNTY"]  # state + county code = FIPS
    g = g.rename(columns={"NAME": "name", "STATE": "statefp", "CENSUSAREA": "census_sqmi"})  # tidy names
    return g[["fips", "statefp", "name", "census_sqmi", "geometry"]].set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)

def superfund_sites():  # EPA Superfund National Priorities List sites from the Atlas
    """Superfund NPL sites as points (EPSG:4326)."""
    s = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/superfund_npl_data.js")["sites"])  # one row per site
    s = s.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])  # keep sites with coordinates
    s = s[["epa_id", "name", "status", "state", "city", "county", "score", "listed", "lat", "lon"]]  # main fields
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(s, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(s.lon, s.lat), crs=4326)  # points

def chr_county(year):  # County Health Rankings (CHR) county table of one year, from the Atlas
    """County Health Rankings & Roadmaps measures for all counties in one release year (2020-2025)."""
    d = pd.read_csv(fetch(f"data/county_health_ranking/chr_county_{year}.csv"), dtype={"fips": str}, low_memory=False)
    d["fips"] = d["fips"].str.zfill(5)  # restore leading zeros (01001, ...)
    return d[~d["fips"].str.endswith("000")].reset_index(drop=True)  # drop state and national rows

# PostGIS connection string (see 06_01_02 for the Docker container); override with GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN
PG_DSN = os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_PG_DSN", "postgresql://postgres:geolattice@localhost:5432/geolattice")
print("Repository:", ROOT)  # where the data are read from


Repository: /home/zia207/Github/GeoLattice

pg = pdb.connect("postgis", dsn=PG_DSN)  # PostGIS through geolatticedb
q = pg.query  # SQL -> GeoDataFrame / DataFrame

counties = atlas_counties()  # county polygons
lower48 = ~counties.statefp.isin(["02", "15", "72"])  # contiguous US
sites = superfund_sites().cx[-125:-66, 24:50]  # Superfund sites in the lower 48
aq = pd.DataFrame(atlas_js("assets/air_quality_data.js")["sites"])  # EPA monitors
pm = aq[(aq.p == "PM25") & (aq.st != "Country Of Mexico")].dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"]).copy()
pm["pm25_2024"] = [(m or {}).get("2024") for m in pm["means"]]  # 2024 annual mean
pm = pm.groupby("id").agg(name=("n", "first"), pm25_2024=("pm25_2024", "mean"), lon=("lon", "first"),
                          lat=("lat", "first")).reset_index().dropna(subset=["pm25_2024"]).rename(columns={"id": "site_id"})
pm = gpd.GeoDataFrame(pm.drop(columns=["lon", "lat"]), geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(pm.lon, pm.lat), crs=4326).cx[-125:-66, 24:50]

pg.load(counties[lower48], "counties48", srid=5070)  # CONUS Albers (metres) for all distance-based work
pg.load(sites, "superfund48", srid=5070); pg.load(pm, "pm25_48", srid=5070)

pg.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS chr24"); chr24.to_sql("chr24", pg._engine, index=False)  # attribute table

title: In-database spatial analytics
text:
Density-based clusters: ST_ClusterDBSCAN
DBSCAN groups points that have at least minpoints neighbours within distance eps, and labels isolated points as noise (NULL). In PostGIS it is a window function: ST_ClusterDBSCAN(geom, eps, minpoints) OVER () returns a cluster id for every row, so the clustering runs where the data are and can be partitioned (OVER (PARTITION BY state)). We cluster Superfund sites with eps = 15 km and at least 5 sites:


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
db = q("""
SELECT epa_id, name, state, ST_ClusterDBSCAN(geom, eps => 15000, minpoints => 5) OVER () AS cluster, geom
FROM superfund48
""")
t_sql = time.perf_counter() - t0
xy = np.column_stack([db.geometry.x, db.geometry.y])  # same points in Python
sk = DBSCAN(eps=15000, min_samples=5).fit_predict(xy)  # scikit-learn DBSCAN (-1 = noise)
pg_lab = db.cluster.fillna(-1).astype(int).values  # PostGIS labels with noise as -1
print(f"PostGIS: {db.cluster.nunique()} clusters, {db.cluster.isna().mean():.0%} noise, {t_sql:.2f} s | "
      f"scikit-learn: {len(set(sk)) - (-1 in sk)} clusters | adjusted Rand index {adjusted_rand_score(pg_lab, sk):.3f}")
top = db.dropna(subset=["cluster"]).groupby("cluster").agg(sites=("epa_id", "size"),
      states=("state", lambda s: ", ".join(sorted(set(s))))).sort_values("sites", ascending=False)
top.head(6)  # largest clusters

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6.5))  # one map
pg.query("SELECT ST_Union(geom) AS geom FROM counties48").boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="0.7", lw=0.4)  # outline
noise = db[db.cluster.isna()]; clus = db.dropna(subset=["cluster"])
noise.plot(ax=ax, color="0.6", markersize=3, label="noise")  # unclustered sites
clus.plot(ax=ax, column="cluster", cmap="tab20", markersize=8, categorical=True)  # clustered sites

PostGIS and scikit-learn find identical clusters (adjusted Rand index 1.000; a value just below 1 would come from border points within eps of two clusters, which either implementation may assign). With these settings 63% of the sites are noise, and the 49 clusters sit in old industrial and metropolitan areas: the largest is the Delaware Valley around Philadelphia (138 sites in Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey and Pennsylvania), followed by the New York-northern New Jersey area (79), a central New Jersey group, Silicon Valley and the Twin Cities. DBSCAN needs no number of clusters in advance, but its result depends strongly on eps: try 10 and 25 km.

title: In-database spatial analytics
text:
Partitioning clusters: ST_ClusterKMeans
K-means splits points into k groups so that each point is closest to its group’s centre. ST_ClusterKMeans(geom, k) OVER () runs it in SQL; the optional max_radius limits the size of each cluster. We partition the PM2.5 monitoring sites into 10 regions and compare their mean 2024 concentrations:


Code
km = q("""
SELECT site_id, pm25_2024, ST_ClusterKMeans(geom, 10) OVER () AS region, geom FROM pm25_48
""")
km["x"], km["y"] = km.geometry.x, km.geometry.y  # coordinates for labels
regions = km.groupby("region").agg(sites=("site_id", "size"), mean_pm25=("pm25_2024", "mean"), x=("x", "mean"), y=("y", "mean"))
skm = KMeans(n_clusters=10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(np.column_stack([km.geometry.x, km.geometry.y]))
print(f"adjusted Rand index PostGIS vs scikit-learn: {adjusted_rand_score(km.region, skm):.2f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6.5))
pg.query("SELECT ST_Union(geom) AS geom FROM counties48").boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="0.7", lw=0.4)
km.plot(ax=ax, column="region", cmap="tab10", markersize=10, categorical=True)  # sites by region
for r, row in regions.iterrows():  # label each region with its mean PM2.5
    ax.annotate(f"{row.mean_pm25:.1f}", (row.x, row.y), fontsize=10, weight="bold", ha="center",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round", fc="w", alpha=0.8))
ax.set_title("ST_ClusterKMeans: 10 regions of PM2.5 monitoring sites, mean 2024 PM2.5 (µg/m³)"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.show()


adjusted Rand index PostGIS vs scikit-learn: 0.66









K-means depends on its random starting centres, so PostGIS and scikit-learn agree on the broad regions but not on every boundary (adjusted Rand index 0.66). Both are valid local optima; fix random_state in Python, or keep one PostGIS run, when results must be reproducible. Mean 2024 PM2.5 is highest in the Texas and Gulf Coast region (9.3 µg/m³) and the southern California and Arizona region (8.1), and lowest in the interior West (5.5) and the Northeast (6.2).

title: In-database spatial analytics
text:
Hexagon grids: ST_HexagonGrid
Counties differ in size by three orders of magnitude, so maps of counts per county mostly show county size. A hexagon grid gives equal-area cells (in an equal-area projection) with the same neighbours in every direction. ST_HexagonGrid(size, bounds) returns the hexagons covering a box; ST_SquareGrid does the same with squares.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
hexes = q("""
WITH grid AS (SELECT (h).geom, (h).i, (h).j FROM (
    SELECT ST_HexagonGrid(40000, ST_SetSRID(ST_Extent(geom)::geometry, 5070)) AS h FROM counties48) g),  -- 40 km edge
     land AS (SELECT ST_Union(geom) AS g FROM counties48)
SELECT grid.i, grid.j, grid.geom,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM superfund48 s WHERE ST_Intersects(grid.geom, s.geom))           AS superfund,
       (SELECT avg(pm25_2024) FROM pm25_48 m WHERE ST_Intersects(grid.geom, m.geom))         AS pm25
FROM grid, land WHERE ST_Intersects(grid.geom, land.g)
""")
print(f"{len(hexes):,} hexagons of {hexes.area.iloc[0] / 1e6:,.0f} km² in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s; "
      f"{(hexes.superfund > 0).sum()} contain a Superfund site")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 5.5))
hexes.plot(column=np.where(hexes.superfund > 0, hexes.superfund, np.nan), ax=axes[0], cmap="Reds", legend=True,
           missing_kwds={"color": "#f2f2f2"}, legend_kwds={"label": "Superfund sites per hexagon", "shrink": 0.6})
hexes.plot("pm25", ax=axes[1], cmap="YlOrRd", legend=True, missing_kwds={"color": "#f2f2f2"},
           legend_kwds={"label": "mean 2024 PM2.5 of monitors (µg/m³)", "shrink": 0.6})
for ax, t in zip(axes, ["Superfund NPL sites", "PM2.5 monitors"]): ax.set_title(t); ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


2,063 hexagons of 4,157 km² in 0.3 s; 593 contain a Superfund site

title: In-database spatial analytics
text:
H3 indexing
H3 is a global grid of hexagons at 16 resolutions, each cell identified by a 64-bit index. Points are indexed once (lat/lng -> cell) and then aggregated with an ordinary GROUP BY on the index, with no spatial join; neighbouring cells, parents and children are integer operations. The h3-pg extension adds H3 to PostgreSQL (the Dockerfile in notebook 06_01_02 installs it). Without it, the cells are computed with h3-py in Python and stored as a column, and the rest stays in SQL:


Code
HAS_H3PG = bool(q("SELECT count(*) AS n FROM pg_available_extensions WHERE name = 'h3'").n.iloc[0])  # extension?
RES = 4  # H3 resolution 4: cells of about 1,770 km²
if HAS_H3PG:  # compute cells in the database
    pg.execute("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS h3; CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS h3_postgis CASCADE")
    pg.execute("ALTER TABLE superfund48 ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS h3 h3index")
    pg.execute(f"UPDATE superfund48 SET h3 = h3_lat_lng_to_cell(ST_Transform(geom, 4326), {RES})")
    print("H3 cells computed with h3-pg")
else:  # compute cells with h3-py and write them back as a text column
    ll = sites.geometry  # lon/lat points (EPSG:4326)
    cells = [h3.latlng_to_cell(p.y, p.x, RES) for p in ll]  # one cell per site
    pg.execute("ALTER TABLE superfund48 ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS h3 text")
    with pg._engine.begin() as con:  # update by primary key (epa_id)
        con.exec_driver_sql("CREATE TEMP TABLE h3map (epa_id text, h3 text)")
        con.exec_driver_sql("INSERT INTO h3map VALUES " + ",".join(f"('{e}', '{c}')" for e, c in zip(sites.epa_id, cells)))
        con.exec_driver_sql("UPDATE superfund48 s SET h3 = m.h3 FROM h3map m WHERE m.epa_id = s.epa_id")
    print("H3 cells computed with h3-py (h3-pg not installed on this server)")
h3_counts = q("SELECT h3::text AS h3, count(*) AS sites FROM superfund48 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC")  # no spatial join

Hexagon grids from ST_HexagonGrid are local to one projection; H3 cells are global, stable identifiers, so the same cell id can link a Superfund count from PostGIS, a population estimate from another source and a satellite summary from a third, with plain joins on the id. Neighbourhood operations (grid_disk, here a 1-ring sum) are lookups, not geometric tests.

title: In-database spatial analytics
section: Spatial weights and Moran’s I in SQL
text:
Spatial weights and Moran’s I in SQL
Global Moran’s I measures whether similar values cluster in space:
\[I = \frac{n}{S_0}\,\frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}\, z_i z_j}{\sum_i z_i^2}, \qquad z_i = x_i - \bar{x},\quad S_0 = \sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}\]
With row-standardized weights (\(w_{ij} = 1/k_i\) for the \(k_i\) neighbours of i), \(S_0 = n\) and the numerator is the covariance between each county and the average of its neighbours. All parts are SQL aggregates. The weights come from a queen-contiguity self-join, stored once as a table:


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
pg.execute("""DROP TABLE IF EXISTS w_queen;
CREATE TABLE w_queen AS
SELECT a.fips AS i, b.fips AS j
FROM counties48 a JOIN counties48 b ON a.fips <> b.fips AND ST_Intersects(a.geom, b.geom)   -- shared edge or vertex
     AND ST_Touches(a.geom, b.geom);
CREATE INDEX ON w_queen (i)""")
print(f"queen weights built in SQL in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s:",
      q("SELECT count(*) AS links, count(DISTINCT i) AS counties, round(count(*)::numeric / count(DISTINCT i), 2) AS mean_k FROM w_queen").to_dict("records")[0])


queen weights built in SQL in 0.2 s: {'links': 18162, 'counties': 3106, 'mean_k': Decimal('5.85')}




Code
def moran_sql(var):  # global Moran's I of a CHR measure, entirely in SQL
    return q(f"""
    WITH x AS (SELECT c.fips, h.{var} AS v FROM counties48 c JOIN chr24 h USING (fips) WHERE h.{var} IS NOT NULL),
         w AS (SELECT w.i, w.j FROM w_queen w JOIN x xi ON xi.fips = w.i JOIN x xj ON xj.fips = w.j),  -- both observed
         k AS (SELECT i, count(*) AS k FROM w GROUP BY i),                                            -- neighbours of i
         z AS (SELECT x.fips, x.v - avg(x.v) OVER () AS z FROM x JOIN k ON k.i = x.fips)              -- no islands
    SELECT count(*) AS n,
           (SELECT sum(zi.z * zj.z / k.k) FROM w JOIN z zi ON zi.fips = w.i JOIN z zj ON zj.fips = w.j
                                           JOIN k ON k.i = w.i) / sum(z.z * z.z) AS moran_i
    FROM z""")
measures = {"adult_obesity_pct": "adult obesity", "adult_smoking_pct": "adult smoking",
            "years_of_potential_life_lost_rate": "premature death (YPLL)"}
sql_I = pd.concat({label: moran_sql(var) for var, label in measures.items()}).droplevel(1)
sql_I.round(4)  # Moran's I computed in PostGIS

title: In-database spatial analytics
section: Inference and local statistics with PySAL and geolattice.spatial_statistics
text:
Inference and local statistics with PySAL and geolattice.spatial_statistics
SQL gives the statistic; its significance needs a permutation test (shuffle the values over the counties many times and see how often I is as large as observed), and local statistics need a vector of results per county. Both are natural in Python. We read the neighbour list from the database once, build the same weights for PySAL (libpysal, esda) and for geolattice.spatial_statistics, and check that all three give the same I:


Code
wl = q("SELECT i, j FROM w_queen")  # neighbour list from SQL
rows = {}  # one row per measure
for var, label in measures.items():  # every measure
    d = chr24.set_index("fips")[var].dropna()  # observed values
    nbrs = wl[wl.i.isin(d.index) & wl.j.isin(d.index)].groupby("i").j.apply(list).to_dict()  # observed pairs only
    ids = sorted(nbrs)  # counties with at least one observed neighbour (as in the SQL)
    y = d.loc[ids].values  # values in id order
    w_pg = sstat.W({i: nbrs[i] for i in ids}, ids=ids, transform="row")  # geolattice.spatial_statistics weights
    w_ps = libpysal.weights.W({i: nbrs[i] for i in ids}, id_order=ids, silence_warnings=True); w_ps.transform = "r"
    m_pg = sstat.Moran(y, w_pg, permutations=999, seed=0)  # geolattice.spatial_statistics
    np.random.seed(0); m_ps = esda.Moran(y, w_ps, permutations=999)  # PySAL esda (seeded through NumPy)
    rows[label] = {"I (SQL)": float(sql_I.loc[label, "moran_i"]), "I (geolattice)": m_pg.I, "I (esda)": m_ps.I,
                   "z (normal)": m_ps.z_norm, "p (999 permutations)": m_ps.p_sim, "n": len(ids)}
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(4)  # identical statistic, with inference

The SQL, geolattice.spatial_statistics and PySAL values agree to four decimals, and no permutation reached the observed value (p = 0.001, the smallest possible with 999 permutations). All three measures are strongly clustered among counties: adult smoking most of all (I = 0.66), then adult obesity (0.61) and premature death (0.53).
Local Moran’s I (LISA) splits that clustering into hot spots (high values among high neighbours, HH), cold spots (LL) and spatial outliers (HL, LH). PySAL’s esda.Moran_Local runs the conditional permutation test: each county’s value is held fixed while the values of its neighbours are drawn from the other counties. We label counties with a pseudo p-value of at most 0.05 and also report how many survive a false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The labels go back to the database as a table and join to the county geometry for the map:


Code
var = "years_of_potential_life_lost_rate"  # premature death
d = chr24.set_index("fips")[var].dropna()
nbrs = wl[wl.i.isin(d.index) & wl.j.isin(d.index)].groupby("i").j.apply(list).to_dict(); ids = sorted(nbrs)
w_ps = libpysal.weights.W({i: nbrs[i] for i in ids}, id_order=ids, silence_warnings=True); w_ps.transform = "r"
np.random.seed(0); lisa = esda.Moran_Local(d.loc[ids].values, w_ps, permutations=999)  # conditional permutations
quad = {1: "HH", 2: "LH", 3: "LL", 4: "HL"}  # esda quadrant codes
res = pd.DataFrame({"fips": ids, "Ii": lisa.Is, "p_sim": lisa.p_sim,
                    "label": [quad[k] if p <= 0.05 else "NS" for k, p in zip(lisa.q, lisa.p_sim)]})
fdr_cut = esda.fdr(lisa.p_sim, 0.05)  # Benjamini-Hochberg threshold for the pseudo p-values
print(f"significant at p <= 0.05: {(res.label != 'NS').sum()}; after FDR (p <= {fdr_cut:.4f}): {(lisa.p_sim <= fdr_cut).sum()}")
pg.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS lisa_ypll"); res.to_sql("lisa_ypll", pg._engine, index=False)  # back to PostGIS
lmap = q('SELECT c.fips, c.name, l.label, l."Ii", c.geom FROM counties48 c LEFT JOIN lisa_ypll l USING (fips)')
print(res.label.value_counts().to_dict())
colors = {"HH": "#d7191c", "LL": "#2c7bb6", "HL": "#fdae61", "LH": "#abd9e9", "NS": "#eeeeee"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6.5))
lmap.plot(ax=ax, color=lmap.label.map(colors).fillna("white"), edgecolor="none")  # clusters
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(color=c, label=l) for l, c in colors.items()], loc="lower left", title="LISA (p <= 0.05)")
ax.set_title("Local Moran clusters of premature death (YPLL), County Health Rankings 2024"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.show()

Of the 2,861 counties, 1,133 have a pseudo p-value of at most 0.05 and 479 remain after the FDR correction; without any clustering about 140 would reach p <= 0.05 by chance, so the uncorrected map shows the pattern but overstates its extent. High-high clusters of premature death cover the Deep South and the Mississippi Delta (most HH counties are in Mississippi, Tennessee, Kentucky, Alabama, Georgia, Arkansas and Louisiana), the Appalachian parts of Kentucky and West Virginia, the Four Corners region of Arizona and New Mexico and parts of the northern Plains, the last two with large American Indian reservations. title: In-database spatial analytics
text:
Summary and exercises
Main points

ST_ClusterDBSCAN and ST_ClusterKMeans are window functions that cluster points in SQL; DBSCAN matched scikit-learn exactly, K-means agreed on the broad regions (it depends on random starts).
ST_HexagonGrid and ST_SquareGrid give regular, equal-area cells for mapping counts and means without the size bias of counties.
H3 assigns points to global hexagonal cells; aggregation is a GROUP BY on the cell id and neighbourhoods are lookups. Use h3-pg in the database, or h3-py and a stored cell column.
Spatial weights are a SQL self-join (ST_Touches) stored as a table; global Moran’s I is a few aggregates over it and matched PySAL and geolattice.spatial_statistics.
Permutation tests and LISA (esda.Moran_Local, conditional permutations) run in Python on one value per county; the results go back to PostGIS as a table for joins and maps.

Functions used: ST_ClusterDBSCAN, ST_ClusterKMeans, ST_HexagonGrid, ST_Extent, ST_Touches, ST_Union, window functions OVER (); h3.latlng_to_cell, h3.cell_to_boundary, h3.grid_disk (h3-py) or h3_lat_lng_to_cell (h3-pg); esda.Moran, esda.Moran_Local, esda.fdr, libpysal.weights.W; sstat.W, sstat.Moran (geolattice.spatial_statistics); pdb.connect, con.load, con.query (geolattice.geolatticedb).
Exercises

Rerun ST_ClusterDBSCAN with eps = 10 km and 25 km. How do the number of clusters and the share of noise change?
Use ST_ClusterKMeans(geom, 10, max_radius => 400000). What happens to the regions in the West?
Build the hexagon map with ST_SquareGrid and compare the counts per cell. Which grid hides fewer clusters along coastlines?
Compute Moran’s I in SQL with rook weights (ST_Relate(a.geom, b.geom, 'F***1****')). How much does I change?
Run the LISA for adult smoking and overlay its HH clusters with the YPLL HH clusters. Where do they coincide?
